We first booked a hotel in hatton beacuse they have mentioned in booking.com that there is only 10.3km to adams peak which is actually 34 km away.we cancelled it and came to dellhouse also called Nallathaniya in where many nice hotels serve rooms and only 600m away from adamspeak.Be ware that you should book a hotel in Nallathannya to do the climb  with pleasure

We did the hike at 2 in the morning.sunrise was amazing and at abt 6.we booked a hotel by booking.com which showed 11km from adamspeak..but it is 35 km away.we had to find another hotel in nallathanniya and we found a nice hotel which is just 500m away from adamspeak.check the distance hotel when you make the booking. Hatton is 35 km away from adamspeak.we must book a hotel in NALLATHANNIYA to do adamspeak NOT IN HATTON

a must when traveling in srilanka ,nice with great views be sure you book a hotel in adam's peak normally in booking.com they says 8.8 km from adam'speak but actually the hotel was 40km so we didn't stay we arrived to nallathanniya we saw many hotel am stay there,it was much comfortable because we were near the base of the climb there was no tranportation fee when you book be sure you book a hotel in nallathanniya not in maskeliya or hatton or anywhere else

We traveled to adams peak from kandy. We get bus and go to hattan and then get bus again and go to adams peak . The bus ticket was abiut 40 rupees we arrived at night and found a cozy hotell and stay for 2 nights there . The hotels reservations said to us we should go to climb on 2 am and watch sunrise and back in early morning . But we feel sleepy too mich and we missed sunrise 😂 and we started climbing at 7 am . In the way we feel paradise big trees big flowers big waterfalls everything is big there and beautiful. We visited temples in way and they give 1500 rupees for donations!!! After climbing for 5 or 6 hours ( I should say very very hard hours) we arrived but the temple was closed!!! And any body said to us !! In first 6 months of year the adams peak temple was closed !!! But we werent angry or unhappy because we had alot of wonderful view in our way .

And you're not the only ones, pilgrim season has a fair few travellers, so you'll never be alone. It is dark, so take a torch! You'll need all your phone battery for photos. It's tough. It's constant stairs for 2 to 4 hours. We managed it in just over 2. And coming back down is just as tough. Make sure you stretch before and after. Take warm clothing as it's freezing and very windy at the top, a blanket to sit on is useful, snacks and drinks. Sugary drinks are useful for the energy. Trainers are perfectly adequate and we found walking poles helped.

I climbed with children aged 11 and 12, so it took us four hours to reach the top. I decided to climb in the daylight, not wanting to climb in the dark with children.  The most difficult thing is not knowing how much further there is to go as we were off peak season for climbing and there were very few other people around to tell us, which in some ways is an advantage. It was a very wet day so there was no view from the top and it was not possible to get in to see the footprint. This is a taxing climb, but we enjoyed the challenge. We were followed by a small dog all the way up and down which made the trip even better.

I've read quite a lot of reviews saying that it's raining season, mating season for animals and off season where the temple of footprint is closed. But I decided to go simply because the Peak Wilderness Sanctuary is a part of UNESCO Heritage Site (which I'm collecting) and set it as a goal to reach the top. We started off late at 4am expecting not to see the sunrise because we saw the peak was surrounded by cloud the day before and knew that there won't be any sunrise. We also started light only with our rain jackets, a bottle of of water that we barely drink due to the rain, and our smartphone as torchlight as there's no light on the road. We spot no animals on the way but heard a lot of frogs croaking from the bushes. It was raining and foggy. Our sport shoes got wet quickly but it didn't affect much of the ascent. The climb was not so hard as there are proper stairs either made of rocks or concrete. When we're half way up we already saw some hikers coming down. We've been told there's no sunrise and the temple is locked. It didn't bother us much as we already knew that and our main goal was just to reach the top. We arrived at the top at around 7:30am and found it really foggy, and the temple was closed. While we're taking photos from the gap of the gate, a man from the shelter opened the door and told us it's off season and it's closed. We replied with smiles and he went back to the shelter. Surprisingly with a minute or two he opened the door and came up to the temple with his jacket on. He opened the side entrance and told us to take off our shoes and enter. We were shocked but followed his lead to the site where the "footprint" was situated. There's a door locked but you could peek into it from bottom. It's just amazing to get to see the real thing in front of our eyes, after so many people had told us that the temple was closed, nothing to see and asked us to turn back! It's just unbelievable! We gave some donation before we left. There's some other donation in the bowl (which was not wet) and we knew that we're not the only lucky ones. We went down with great joyfulness because we had accomplished our goal, seeing the unexpected and starting to see the greenery of the forest in the mist. The trees were really beautiful in the mist, just like in fairy tales. And the tea valley and waterfalls at the bottom of the mountain was a bonus to the hike. To conclude, it's not easy to reach the top as it takes hours to reach the top and not easy while raining, but as long as you're optimistic who knows what's waiting for you ahead. Just go for it! It's definitely something memorable, at least your legs soreness will remind you for a few days, but it's worth it.

A great experience that everyone should do in his life time its a mix between hiking, climbing and cultural knowledge you'll meet many monks along the way and visit many temples till you arrive to the top for the grand temple after passing on 5500 stairs step !! its a little bit hard to get up there but am sure its much harder to get down because your legs will be numb :D and it will stay numb for 2-3 days after but if you ever visited Sri lanka ... don't miss Adam's peak challenge :)

“Sri Pada” Adams peak though not the highest mountain of Sri Lanka, the striking pyramid of Adam's Peak (7,360 ft) is certainly the most remarkable. A depression in the rocky summit resembles a huge footprint, which has been venerated as a sacred sigh from remote antiquity. This was identified by Buddhists as the Buddha's footprint, by Hindus as that of Shiva, and by Muslims as Adam's. Later the Portuguese attributed it to St. Thomas the Apostle. Lovely amazing and historical place to see...

Climbing the Adams peak is surely a must do activity if you are in Sri Lanka. It is not an easy climb and we saw many people who were really struggling along the way. There are supposed to be around 5500 steps and it gets quite steep at times. The view of the sunrise is very beautiful from the peak and this is the reason most people  start climbing at night. We started climbing at 2:00AM and were able to reach the top at 4:45AM. This meant we had to wait in the cold weather for more than an hour before sunrise (around 6AM); but this wasnt so bad as it gave us some time to catch our breath and also meet many of the others who had come from different parts of the world. We made friends with a group of Chinese youngsters, one of whom was celebrating her birthday. We cut a cake and sang for her :) The sunrise itself was really beautiful and the view of the valley from the peak is amazing. We spent about half an hour just soaking it all up and taking pics. Getting down is obviously an easier task and we managed it in about 2 hours. We had a few aches the next day, but it was well worth it.

A must visit for an adventurer visiting Sri Lanka. Recommended to start climbing at night, so you can reach the top for sunrise. I used 2,5 hours for a medium speed ascend. In addition to all the natural dimensions of the experience, this is also really a pure cultural experience. If you don't like buddhism, this is maybe not for you. Really memorable visit.

We climbed Sri Pada in August, normally the off season and often has hazy views. We were very lucky and got up for the sunrise walk and had absolutely spectacular views. It rained a bit but was still excellent. Definitely stretch your legs afterwards though, all those stairs on the way down were a killer

On our planning trip to Sri Lanka, this was something we read about it and decided not to do. First we do not have any religion, second we do not really tried climbing and third we wanted surf, beach and sun! Well Budah, Shiva and Adam had a different plan for us! due to bad weather conditions and floods we had to adjust our journey and decided to stopover at Adam´s peak before going to Colombo. Must say without being a believers, a treeking lover, it was one of the best chanlange i have done in my life! Although very demanding, you can really feel your mind getting empty by being focus on the walking steps along the way! it was raining all night, didn't´t have the chance to visit the temple as it was close in low season! But worthy as personal achievement.We were 2 at start become 4 on the first steps and a dog we walked with us all the way up who we named Adam. Adam didn't´t came down is karma said so. :)It took us 2 hours and half to go up, and maybe another 2 to came down.

We decided to climb Adams Peak at the start of August, after we had seen it was highly recommended by the guide books and other travellers. We climbed as a group of 3 on a Saturday, starting our ascent at 1:30am and reaching the summit at 4:30am We did have a look at other reviews/discussions from this time of year and noted a few things that were mentioned, which I have covered below. Animals: We did not see any wildlife on our climb, although as the first climbers of the day we were followed up by 2 dogs (one of which was at the bottom starting the climb with another group as we came back down). However, the climb is very eerie in the dark and when visibility is particularly poor I would suggest a group of 3 or more is best for a night climb Lighting: As has been mentioned on here the climb is not lit all year round, despite what some guide books say. If climbing at night I would recommend using head torches, as due to the gradient of the climb at some points it would be best to have both hands free. Neither of our 3 torches ran low on batteries during the climb, but it's probably worth taking at least one spare set. The climb: The start of the climb is pretty poor, with around 1km of shacks that are used as shops in the peak season. The climb itself is varied but the gradient generally increases as you move up the mountain. It was hard work but if you take your time it is very doable. No shops were open past the start of the climb. The weather: The weather was awful. We had spent 2 weeks in Galle and Colombo and despite the weather saying rain all day every day we had about 10 minutes of rain up to this point in the trip. It turns out the weather for hill country is spot on. From the minute we arrived until we left 2 nights later it was chucking it down. We were wearing goretex full waterproofs (jacket and trousers) and waterproof walking boots and within the first 30mins-1hr we were completely drenched and had to change at the top. On the way down I wore a poncho and found it was very good at keeping me dry and cool. The summit: A complete waste of time in the off season. We reached the top at around 4:30 and found it was completely deserted. It is a quite built up concrete area with no where to sit or take shelter. The footprint itself is on the very peak and is closed at this time of year, surrounded by a wall. Eventually a man who heard us came out and told us it would be closed until December, but offered tea for 100lkr. We decided to wait until sunrise at 6am, with around 30 European tourists arriving at the top in this time, all very disappointed that it was closed, with some heading straight back down before sunrise. Despite our hopes the rain persisted and all we could see of the sunrise was a blue colour to the clouds. The descent: We heard the descent had the best views, but again due to the weather we saw absolutely nothing until we reached the very bottom, where we had a beautiful view of the valley. Overall, I would suggest not attempting the climb during July or August unless there is a patch of clear weather, as the reward from achieving the climb itself is simply not worth it. The attached photo is our view from the summit at sunrise.

Hands down the BEST experience of my life! It's a hard climb and you need to give yourself enough time if you wanna reach the top by sunset! But, if you're in Sri Lanka you really should consider attempting it! Loved every minute!

I was keen to do the climb despite it being off season. Sadly many Sri Lankan's had frightened me about it saying that wild animals might attack me etc. Thankfully, I didn't see one animal the entire hike! Other than friendly dogs owned by the guides. Being off season it rained the entire hike however I found this quite refreshing! Alas the top was cloudy but I was proud to have completed the climb. Apparently there have been some clear days so it really is just luck! Only takes 2-2.5hrs to the top at this time of year if you have a moderate level of fitness. There were still about 100 of us who completed it for sunrise, it must get very busy at peak season! A guide isn't a necessity as the path is very clear I just got one as a solo traveler. Make sure you take a torch!
Lovely place to travel with a group of people.Has the most amazing view. Definitely you should add to your holiday bucket.

Stayed in Dalhousie for only 1 night with the sole purpose of climbing Adams Peak. Weather was drizzly when we arrived and progressively got worse through the night. We set the alarm for 1.30am and decided if it was very heavy rain we would not do the climb. As luck would have it there was only a fine misty drizzle and off we set at 1.55 am. Didn't  see any one else until after the half way point. This is by no means an easy climb. We are in our early 50's and have  a reasonable standard of fitness .We passed several others who would have been half our age who were having real difficulty .Made it to the top in 2 hrs 35 minutes with lots of short rest stops along the way and would have been in the first 10 to arrive. Only saw one shop open on the way up and the vendor advised us we were at the 3 km mark. The last section of the climb is particularly challenging with very steep steps which seem to go on for ever. I relied heavily on the handrails on each side to haul myself up. Weather steadily got worse and we encountered heavy rain and howling winds. Was very cold at the top and very obvious there would be no amazing sunrise ( only cloud and mist) as a reward for our efforts so we only stayed long enough at the top to get  a few photos and to put a merino clothing layer on. Others seemed quite happy to stay up there. The trip down took far longer than I thought it would - 2 hours 15 even though we hardly stopped. Feeling  the effects 1 day later in the calf muscles but no regrets. My tips would be: 1. Be prepared with a good head torch- we brought them from home. It would have been so much harder to have to hold a hand torch. We saw others just using flashlight function from their iPhone and others foolishly enough with no light. The walk is hard enough without not being able to see where you are going 2.  Wear sensible shoes and carry some thermal layers to put on when you get to the top especially if it is raining 3.  A good rain jacket is essential - the thin rain ponchos others had on were no match for the very windy and wet  conditions. We even saw several carrying umbrellas!! 4. No need to pack heaps of food and water. A few snacks and bananas and just enough water to get you through. We used a litre between the 2 of us. 5 . No need to hire a guide although I wouldn't like to do it on your own 6. Make sure you take the same track down (Hatton Road) otherwise it will add hours to your hike back In summary it is still a must do even for no sunrise  and views purely for the sense of achievement. Completing it in the dark adds to the thrill and adventure. In summary really please

I got to Hatton by train. Then I easily took a bus to Maskeliya. From there, I took a tuk tuk to Dalhousie. Dalhousie is a town full of hotels that most tourists use for the climb. The reason I took the bus to Maskeliya is to decrease the cost. I'm on a budget. The tuk tuk drivers wanted around 1500 rupee from Hatton to Dalhousie. I paid about 500 for just Maskeliya to Dalhousie (half of the trip). It's nice joining the locals on the bus. The bus ride was very fun as the driver furiously rushed up the mountain. I got to my hotel and all the guests were brought together in order for the hotel staff to go over key points about the climb. I'm guessing a lot of hotels do the same thing. Anything you need for the climb can be bought or rented at your hotel. The one thing I really suggest you bring is a strong and long-lasting headlight or flashlight. The one I rented from my hotel was extremely weak. They referred to it as a torch. My iPhone light is much stronger than this rented torch. I got up at 1:40am and started walking out the door at 1:55am. Along the way, I met a group of people who also wanted to reach the top of Adam's peak. In fact, I never felt alone going up even with my weak torch because there were so many people trying to accomplish the same thing as me - to see the sunrise at the top. It was raining, but my hotel loaned me a rain poncho. The hike was hard for me, especially since I'm out of shape. There were closed shops to the top because it's off-season. I made it to the top within 2.5 hours with frequent breaks. It was all clouds and fog when I got to the top. A guy was selling delicious tea at the top for 100 rupee per cup. The temple was closed and nobody was around to open the gate to the temple by sunrise so we all left. Took 2.5 hours getting down, which is much harder as the knees take on a lot of pressure of your weight. Going down felt longer as well because I could see where I'm going as opposed to going up in the dark where I'm focused on each step. Recommendation for a 2am journey: - climb during in-season because off-season does not have favorable odds of seeing a clear view - bring a strong, long-lasting flashlight - be prepared to change into dry clothes at the top because you're sweaty at the top with the clothes you wear and it will get cold once your body cools off from the hike and the wind blows hard up there (feels colder if it's raining) - prep as you would for a hike

Definitely worth doing during your stay in Sri Lanka. Everything we read recommended going up at 2/2:30 am and said it would take roughly three hours to climb. We woke up at this time to find it pouring with rain so left it until the morning and started at 11am. The sky was completely clear by then so we got much better views than the people we spoke to who had gone at night. The climb is very tough so pack a lot of water and snacks. Ask the locals about the forecast because by the time we got to the top the clouds were covering any views. Great sense of achievement though and definitely a must do in Sri Lanka. We stayed at Punsisi rest and found it a great place to stay for the hike.

Some advice for young and fit travelers; Don't bother to start walking 4 hours before sunrise in low season. We reached the top within 2 hours and had to survive the cold wind at the top of the mountain because we started the hike too early. So 2,5 hours is more than enough, if you want to be absolutely sure, start 3 hours before sunrise.

Not an easy climb at all. I admit I totally underestimated the challenge. Most estimates we read were 2-4hrs for the climb, thought we could do it in 2.5 but did 3.5 hrs instead. The descent was no easy task either, the climb took all our legs and left us with little to handle the 2.5hr journey down. It is not a technical climb at all, just thousands of unevenly laid steps. Unless you know for sure your legs are in good shape, please give yourself 3-4 hrs for the climb. Be aware that chances of seeing the sun rise are low during off season, we were surrounded by rain and fog/clouds the whole time up there (see photo attached). Hope you find fulfillment from completing the climb like we did, otherwise you might want to reconsider if all your hopes are on seeing the view from on top.

We went July 17,2017 which we knew was off season. Pros- No crowds to battle, very peaceful hike. Pretty rewarding to conquer a mountain :) Cons- unfortunately we didn't see the sunrise due to the fog layer Tips (from a 30yr old)- > I'm a personal trainer by profession and thought it was challenging. I made it up in 2hrs at a good pace without stopping. I would say the average person will take closer to 3hrs, and I'd budget 4hrs if you do not exercise. > Don't forget to stretch before, during and after! Your body will thank you. >Headlamps are 100% necessary if you're trying to be there for sunrise. >Have a food & water plan! Not much is open at 2-3am during off season so be sure to get water and food the night before and pack it for energy the day of the hike. > Bring layers, the top can be wet, windy and cold. >You have to pass through a temple on the way- they record your name, country of origin, and donation amount. We didn't think to bring cash and felt kind of bad about to that. Average donation appeared to be between 500-1000LKR per person. >Walking sticks are helpful for the way down to reduce impact on the knees.

We made the journey in low season, so didn't know what to expect. The climb was well worth it, especially as we made some great friends along the way. It was a clear run up to the top as there were no pilgrims, but when we reached the summit the clouds didn't part. Despite this we both found the experience worthwhile, although it may be better to climb during the day to give the clouds chance to disperse. The views will definitely be worth it in high season however. We made the climb in 2 hours and I'd say we are both fairly fit (its not overly challenging)

Adams peak is not an easily climb and I would advise a reasonable level of fitness to attempt it. Nevertheless there are plenty of places to rest and as long as you avoid climbing on a poya day (I did this), you will reach the peak in good time. I would advise climbing Adams peak at night so that you arrive when the sun is rising. I've done it and there is no better way to appreciate the views. The footprint at the top is a must see although please make sure to remove your shoes as a mark of respect. The signs for this are not very obvious. I would also advise bringing a light jacket as it does tend to get chilly closer to the top. I cannot stress how beautiful and scenic the views are from above and I would encourage all visitors and locals to climb it at least once.

Even if you have to start the hike at 2 in the morning (in order to get the sunrise) it is clearly worth the effort. 3/4 hours climbing/trekking/walking that really test your innerself but in the end when you get to the top and have the sunrise it is astonishing

Adam’s Peak (Sri Padaya) is a scared pilgrim site specially for Buddhists. They believe imprint of the summit is the footprint of Lord Buddha. Trek is very popular among tourists because of breathtaking views across its surrounding. Site area is a sanctuary. Pilgrimage season starts from December and it lasts until May. Best time to go there is between February and March. Start your climb late night and get down after watching sunrise.

We went out of season. Decided to leave at 3am with another group of 3. It took 3 hours to summit (Age 26 and 27 and in OK shape). We didn't see the sunrise because of fog and rain which of course is pure bad luck. The hike is challenging but a fun exercise. Expect SORE legs! TIPS: Expect a couple of stray dogs to follow you ALL the way to the top! Expect them to get in fight with other stray dogs over who gets to follow you. There is NO open shops so bring your own food and water! There is NO light so bring a reliable flashlight. (Sun up around 5:30) We were warned about fake monks trying to scam you and after 300meters the first fake monks awoke and tried to lure us into their "temple". Our hotel and driver warned us about these people and you can easily take the official road around their temple. Some of our party went into their lairs and were pressured to pay a 1000lkr in donations and get "special" wristbands and write their names in a book. Our hotel said that this has NOTHING to do with buddhism and a donation is never forced and the size of the donation is always up to you. Our guide and the hotel told us that NONE of the money paid here goes to the temple but only into their own pockets. If you want to donate do it at the official boxes. Beware of leeches! 4 out of a 5 party group was bitten and it bled for some hours.

What an experience!!! Make sure you have an early night the night before, I think we were asleep by 8:00pm. We woke up at 2:00am in the pitch black to start the journey. I'm not going to lie, the climb is tough. My partner and I are very fit people and we were huffing and puffing and sweating throughout. Although everyone walks at their own pace and wakes up at a time that will give them enough time to reach the top. We reached the top at 5:00am. There are lots of pit stops and tucker shops along the way to buy water and snacks. Food and drink gets more expensive the higher you get as the locals have to walk all the supplies up the hill themselves.The path is made up of concrete steps and is very well lit the whole way with street lamp style lights. Although the climb may seem hard, it is sooo worth it when you reach the top. The view is incredible. Everyone is silent as you watch the sun rise - I've never experienced anything so sureal. The descent was alot faster than the actual climb. We were down in under 2 hours. Everyone then has a big BIG breakfast - which feels very well deserved. Tips: 1. Bring a backpack with water and sugary snacks for energy. 2. Bring a jacket, beanie and gloves. The higher you get, the colder it gets. Sitting up the top is FREEZING - trust me! 3. People recommend hiring and paying for a guide 'tracker'. I would advise AGAINST this. Its very unnecessary as the path is very clear and well lit throughout. 4. Watch you're legs on the way down - they will be jelly! There are eldery monks and children as young as 5 or 6 that do this climb. Do not let people scare you into doing it. If you take you're time, pace your self and take breaks at the designated rest stops - you will be fine. It is a once in a life time experience and I would highly recommend it. It was one of the highlights of Sri Lanka for me!

Commenced the walk at 2.00am towards the end of April and the night was not unduly cold, so all the rugging up was not really needed. The stairs are a mixture of wide and easy at the start and progressively steeper and more tiring towards the end.  I highly recommend investing around $2 for some walking sticks as they helped a lot. Whilst there was a fairly large number of people doing the trek, it moved fairly steadily.  Different story at the top where there was little room to move, however, the dawn glimpse was lovely.  Took around 3.5 hrs to the top with snack stops and about 2 hrs to get down.  A gruelling but fun climb, but only once.
Do not expect that the steps is ending. You have to just keep climbing and look at the steps in the dark. If the stamina is right, you will reach the top just nice at the sunrise.

Climbed it on 14/6/17 overnight as a couple from a guesthouse in Dalhousie. Despite research, we hadn't realised how much difference it being out of season makes to the climb experience. Firstly, there are no local pilgrims and very few tourists. We saw none at all until the last 2k. Secondly, there are no lights out of season except for at a couple of police points and at the top. There are almost no shops open- we saw two the night we climbed. Thirdly, the temple at the top is locked for the entire six month out of season period (may to December) This means if you are planning to hike it between may and December, you need to take a torch, all food and water and probably a friend as it is a bit creepy being so deserted. The top becomes a bit anticlimactic as you get cold, see sunrise and wait for the temple to open at 6 until the chap who lives at the top and sells you a tea tells you it's closed. It's a great hike, hard work at the top but with stunning views between the clouds. As others have said, coming down is tough and if you have any joint issues walking poles may be sensible. It took us (young and fit-ish, don't routinely exercise other than walking) 2 hours each way. Definitely worth a go!

Join locals as they make their holy pilgrimage to Sri Pada.  A very rewarding and spiritual experience and when you see elderly men and women walking down/up without any shoes on in the middle of the cold night to make this pilgrimage, consider yourself very fortunate to be joining with them and sharing this very special experience. Try to arrive the previous afternoon and book your accommodation for 2 nights if you have the time - that way you don't need to rush down to make your exit out of Dalhousie and can take your time enjoying the views on the way down and put yourself back to bed when you get down for a much needed rest!

Started climbing the mountain around 6:30 pm as we went on a fully crowded day .... knowing it will be bit of a hard hike we stared slowly and move on but as it was bit of a misty day senarice where beautiful.... if you are not use to this kind of a hike better take rest every hours time and go slow to the summit You have lot of shops around to buy foods and all other needs hence carry less to avoid hassle And around 10:30 we where in summit Remember this is a pilgrimage place in Sri Lanka hence if you are not Buddhist please be quiet and enjoy the view breez around you as lot of eldaries treats this as a secret place .... hike is good for your health and build your friendship among others during the journey Worth doing this at least once a life time

Adams Peak is definetly a place to visit during your stay in Sri Lanka. It might be a tough journey up the 6000 steps, but it's all worth it. Great hike, not too many people. We started at 3:15 and made it to the top for the 5:45 sunrise, amazing view.

My boyfriend and I climbed Adams peak a couple of days ago, the morning of 8th May and it was a unique and rewarding experience. Please be aware that the season ends on 10th May, which means that all the lights leading the way will be switched off, so ensure you take a torch or headlamp to find your way up if you are planning a sunrise climb. We set off from our hotel (Hugging clouds - near the start of the route) at 2:30am, and were soon blessed by some friendly monks at the temple near the base of the mountain (we gave a 1000 rupee donation but no pressure is applied so feel free to give as much or little as you wish). There are a couple of forks in the route near the start, however both options always seem to join back together after a few hundred meters. The first hour walk is very enjoyable, sections of steps followed by small sections of flat, there were shops and cafes selling food and drinks so we didn't need to worry about carrying much water with us (not completely sure if these are still open out of season). We travelled quite lightly, just a small backpack with a jumper, extra layers & vegtable rottis. After the first hour the trail gets a little tougher, with longer sections of steeper steps, however there are still some rest points if you need a short break. The route wasn't too crowded when we visited and so we were able to go at our own pace. We reached the top just before 4:30am and entered the temple area (the temple area covers the whole peak, so unless you go into the temple you'll have to descend the mountain slightly to wait for sunrise). You are required to remove your shoes to enter and I would advise to layer up straight away- you quickly get cold at the top once your sweat cools! We waiting for just over an hour and we were able to enjoy a picturesque sunrise, illuminating the clouds over the lake and the nearby valleys. We didn't stay at the top long, but instead started walking down, to see the sunrise at various other secluded parts of the trail. It took around two hours to walk back down and the views were lovely. We tried to do a few stretches when we got back to the hotel, to lessen the ache the next day. If you are relatively fit, then maybe set off around 3am from the base of the mountain, to limit your time in the cold waiting for the sunrise at the top. Alternatively, set off earlier and have a rest or two on the way up. As long as you go at your own steady pace, most people should be able to complete this climb (we saw very elderly people, children & people in jeans and flip flops make it to the top - impressive)! If you are climbing adam's peak for sunrise you will probably want to stay at Dalhousie/Nallathanniya the night before - there are plenty of hotels to chose from near the base of the mountain. To get here from Kandy or Ella you need to catch the train to Hatton (around three hours from either of those starting points), then catch the bus from Hatton to Dalhousie (another hour and a half). Or you should catch a tuktuk or taxi from Hatton if you don't fancy the bus. Try set off earlish if you can, so you can enjoy an early dinner & an early night. Happy climbing :)

We started our hike from hatton and we finished from rathnapura.But remember hatton road is perfect because there were so many shops and washrooms.If you go there on holidays it may be tuff to climb so try to go on week days.

I have only given this 2 stars due to the amazing views with being able to see the shadow of the mountain on the clouds after sunrise, other than that I was SO disappointed. This had been the trip I was most looking forward to prior to coming to Sri Lanka, but ended up being about the worst. The group that had gone up the night before had not made it to the top before sunrise so we left at midnight to ensure we would make it (which I was dubious about, but didn't have a choice). Making your way to the top was an interesting experience. There are so many people to say what time of night it is, with little shops at the beginning and at various points on the way up. The lights towards the top look lovely as you climb, but that is about it for the walk up. As you get closer to the top it gets more and more crowded, to the point where you are being pushed around at times. There are people sleeping everywhere making it difficult to climb at points and you are also dodging running stretcher carriers at times as they career down the mountain with collapsed people. Once at the top, there is a small temple which you literally are crushed by people to get into, then there is nothing else. We arrived at 3am so had to sit on the top of the mountain in the cold for 3 hours waiting for sunrise. The actual sunrise was quite spectacular, but the amount of people detracts from the whole experience to the point where it completely lost its magic. You then need to leave the top immediately to avoid the worst of the crowd, but you are literally crushed trying to get down. Our guide then wanted to rush us down the mountain to avoid the crowds so I had to lag behind to take in the stunning views of being up above the clouds and seeing the peaks shadow on them. On the way down reality really hits with rubbish everywhere and I was left with a feeling of sadness that such a hugely significant religious site could be treated like crap.

This is spoken of as something that every religion has some part in but it is all Buddhist. It is Buddhism everywhere, not necessarily a complaint from me but information. If you do not see value in Buddhism or think of it as idol worship it will be bothersome to you. The route, for being a pilgrimage, is extremely non serene. It is full of vendors all the way up, not meditation stops but normal kades selling tea, soda, rotis. Some are playing radio stations. There is supposed to be no smoking or drinking, signs along the way give the instruction, but it still takes place. There are also signs to keep nature clean, love mother nature and so forth but the place it literally lined with trash and rubbish. There are toilets to use for a small fee along the way, but some decide to use the side of the path, which adds to the smell. I will say I was a bit surprised at the level of defilement in an area that is so often spoken of as a revered site. But I guess each has their idea of reverence. The walk up is 5k. The first 2k are relatively easy with only slight incline. The 3rd and 4th gets a bit more challenging.  The final kilometer is a killer, heading at a very steep incline, but it's only 5k, not too bad. The difficult part is the decent. This whole thing is concrete, mostly steps, over 5000 of them. That is killer on the knees, calves, thights, feet coming down. I would not do this again for a number of reasons.

The day that I did it we had an exceptional sunrise (I've uploaded a photo). Obviously you're not guaranteed that. I'm early 40's and relatively fit - didn't have an issue with the steps. If you don't do any/much exercise you could have issues but I'd say that it shouldn't be an issue for most people. Definitely recommended - hope that you get a lucky clear day.

I am a fit 50 yo travelling with my 23 yo daughter. I was nervous about this climb, even considering abandoning it, and probably did far too much research about it, (some of it unhelpful) but figured we could always turn back if we had to. My advice is to DO IT! We departed our bungalow at 1am for the 1hr drive to Dalhousie. From there we started the walk, gentle at first, before the stairs begin in earnest! The middle section is quite gruelling with long flights of uneven stairs, but then the stairs become less steep for the final 1/3, with the final steep ascent divided by a rail into up and down sections. This section was a little crowded and the pace slows down, which is actually a good thing! It is cold at the top, so be prepared for that. Bright lights mar the sunrise somewhat, but the atmosphere is really exciting. Be sure to check out the west just after sunrise to see the weird pyramid shadow cast by the mountain. This was more spectacular than the sunrise. Don't rush down thinking it will be a bottleneck of people. It wasn't. Just a slow steady walk down; crowded at first but soon easing off beyond the place where you replace your shoes. What to take: A walking pole is such a saviour, but you only need one as there are often rails on one side; a beanie is essential, a fleece for the top and if you have bad knees a dose of anti-inflammatory before you leave. Either the walking pole or the anti inflammatories or both left me with no knee or any other pain during or after this walk, when I have suffered greatly on far easier climbs. Toilets are everywhere and are simple and clean enough for 20R. We took 2 small water bottles which was enough, but you can buy more along the way. Climbing at night means you don't get as thirsty. I would never attempt this during the day. It took us 2 1/2 hrs to get up, we spent 1 1/2 at the top and 2 1/2 to get back down. Ate only a small banana and a biscuit on the climb and returned for a huge breakfast at our accommodation. I can't recommend this highly enough...a surreal experience.

We started the hike about 1.00am and reached the peak at about 4.30am.Its very chilled in the peak so I recommend a jacket to bring with you. You should watch the sunrise from up above its a amazing experience.

We started this walk at 2:15 in order to get to the top for sunrise.  The majority of the walk up (though fairly tough) went smoothly, and we had got 90% of the way up within about 2-2hr30.  This is when we hit the crowds.  The final 10% of the way was just a stationary line of 1000s of people, leading all the way to the top.  We, somewhat cheekily, had to resort to going up the 'down' section of the path (which was empty) to which we were glad we did, else we would never have made it to the top in time for sunrise (we only just made it).  Standing in the queues would have taken at least another 3hrs to reach the top.  If you intend to walk up Adams peak at this time of the year I would recommend starting out even earlier, purely to try and miss all of the crowds.  It was extremely busy at the top, with a lot of pushing and shoving going on, which unfortunately made watching the sunrise a rather unpleasant experience.  The views from the top were beautiful, though sadly tarnished by the the final 10% of the journey.  It is cold at the top/ waiting in queues, so bring warmer clothes to put on at this point.  The views on the way down were great, and we couldn't believe how far we had climbed.

We started walking at 2:20 and we without too many breaks we made it to near enough the top for sunrise. We made it to the edge of the top and saw the crowds and that the view wasn't any better than what we had already seen so we turned around, it wasn't worth the crowds! Coming down was by far in a way the hardest bit so make sure you save some energy. However coming down in the light was much nicer the views are amazing. We climbed Adam's peak on a Friday night which should have been really busy.  However, since it was New Year the week after, everyone must have been climbing then as it wasn't too busy at all. If I was to do it again, I would take more steps as my legs were very sore for a few days after and rather wobbly on the climb down!  The top is a sacred site so make sure your legs and shoulders are covered.  It is also very cold and windy at the top (it is a mountain after all!) so do take warm clothes.  We were stunned by the views and the sunrise and definitely recommend it.

We started our hike up Adam's Peak at 2am on a Saturday night, thinking we would be among only a few "pilgrims" hiking at that hour. Wrong. There were thousands. And I mean thousands of Sri Lankans also make the trek. Unfortunately (or fortunately) we had chosen the last Sunday of the season to see Sri Prada, and many of the country locals were there to worship. We made it to the top by 430am, but only because our guide took us on a short cut that avoided an extraordinarily long line on another path to the top. The crushing crowd at the top made the sunrise a bit difficult to enjoy, but it was very moving to see so many Sri Lankans so determined to practice their faith; many barefooted old women climbed the long narrow stairs to the top to praise Buddha. In retrospect, my wife and I were glad to be a part of the Sri Lankan community on top of the peak, but if you don't have a taste for crowds, best to climb Adam's peak during with week, or in the off season (after March 31), when ONLY tourists make the trek. Wear good walking shoes and be prepared for a good workout! Also, if you do the trip at night, bring a dry piece of clothing to change into, and something warm, because it can get cold waiting for the sun to rise.

Should you climb Adam's Peak? If you like adventure, and a bit of a challenge: YES, it's rewarding and can be fun. If climbing ten flights of stairs leaves you begging for the sweet release of death, this is not the best of ideas. Here are some practical tips for those looking to climb Adam's Peak. WHEN TO CLIMB: In terms of weather, the best time of the year is from December to April. However, this also coincides with the pilgrimage season, which means there will be many people climbing the mountain with you. We climbed in mid-March; while there were quite a few pilgrims, it wasn't too bad. Avoid climbing on weekends, full moon (poya) days, and at the time of the Sinhalese New year (mid-April), as it will be more crowded on these days. If you wish to avoid crowds altogether, climb during the off-season, but be very mindful of the weather. It's probably best not to climb if it's rainy. In terms of time of day, you have two options again. I recommend a night-to-dawn climb, reaching the peak in time for the sunrise. Check sunrise time on the day of the climb, and begin your ascent accordingly, so that you have enough time to get to the top before sunrise. You can also choose to climb during the day, in which case bring along a hat, sunglasses and sunblock, for the sun can be quite strong. WHICH ROUTE TO TAKE: The Ratnapura route is longer. The Dalhousie route is shorter but steeper. We stayed in Maskeliya (a quiet, pretty town), and arranged for a van to pick us up at 2am on the day of the climb, to take us to Dalhousie. WHAT TO TAKE WITH YOU: Travel as light as possible because you'll regret any excess weight. Definitely carry a light jacket, especially if you're climbing before dawn: you may be sweating profusely during the climb, but it can get very windy and chilly at the peak. Consider dressing in layers. Check temperature/weather prediction before your climb, and carry rainwear if necessary. If you're climbing during pilgrimage season, there will be plenty of stalls along the entire route, selling everything from tea to RedBull, from chips to meals (all at a premium, naturally). You will not need a torch because the path will be well lit. There are quite a few small, dirty, pay-and-use toilets (charging anything from LKR 10-40; carry small-denomination notes). Take your camera: once the sun comes up, you'll be treated to some very beautiful views. Sunglasses may also be a good idea. If you're climbing off-season, it might be prudent to carry snacks (energy bars, bananas), water (electrolytes) and a torch. There are plenty of waste-bins along the route (and yet, people still litter the mountain). HOW LONG WILL IT TAKE? (These estimates are for the Dalhousie route.) If you're fit, it might take you 2 hours (inclusive of short breaks). Don't run up the mountain, though: enjoy the journey. If you're not fit, it might take you 3 to 3.5 hours, and your legs will curse you for the next few days. (Don't plan any strenuous activity immediately after the climb.) Climbing down won't be any faster if you're doing this during pilgrimage season because there will be plenty of people descending along with you. Regardless of fitness level, it's not a good idea to rush down a steep mountain: your knees will take a hit, and that will screw up the rest of your Sri Lanka trip. Set aside at least 7 hours in total for the entire trip from the base of the mountain to the top and back to the base. Include some time to relax at the top and reflect on your achievement. If you're climbing from Ratnapura, remember that it will take a bit longer. WHAT ELSE TO EXPECT: Towards the top, it might seem as if the steps never end. Just when you begin to believe you've made it to the peak, the mountain mocks you with the sight of more steps to climb, steeper than before. Don't give up! Pilgrims of all ages climb the 5000+ steps to the top. You'll see elderly people supporting themselves on crutches, trudging on uncomplainingly. You'll see parents holding infants in their arms, singing hymns as they climb. OTHER TIPS: If you want to catch the best view of the sunrise from the very top of the mountain (and take great photos), you'll have to reach the peak with at least 30 minutes to spare, manoeuvre yourself into a good spot facing east (the Dalhousie side, not the Ratnapura side), and wait patiently in the semi-darkness as pilgrims and tourists jostle to greet the sun. The limited space at the top means that it will be very crowded at the peak during pilgrimage season. Once the sun is up, the pilgrims will head for the shrine, offer prayers and start their descent; wait for the crowd to thin a bit. (During off-season, you needn't reach too early.) To walk into the shrine at the very top of the peak, you'll have to take off your shoes. After seeing the sunrise, walk over to the Ratnapura side of the peak. From this spot, you'll be able to see the eerily near-perfect conical shadow cast by Adam's Peak onto the hills over which it towers. (You might need to climb down a few steps for the best view.) There are absolutely no entry fees. When you begin your climb, you may be cajoled into making a donation. If you don't wish to donate money, it's perfectly okay to smile and politely decline: no one will be offended. You will not need a guide: there are steps leading straight up, and any seeming detours lead to the same place eventually. Lastly, if you're not quite fit but still determined to make the climb, go with a friend: you might be quite miserable otherwise. Good luck!

We travelled from Bentota to Siri Padaya with Sumi Tours. Our guide Sumi and driver Prasad couldn't do enough to assist us with our experience. Siri Padaya was amazing a 3 and 1/2 hour climb leaving the base at 2am to catch the sunrise at 6.15am. Thoroughly worth the effort but climb is challenging!!!!

my last trip to Adam's peak was the 5th one.It is really a worthy lifetime experience, the journey and the destination both!. We stayed in a hotel called 'White Elephant'prior to starting climbing at 2 am."White Elephant' is not a place that I would recommend. But the rest of the trip was really great.It took us about 4 hours to climb and 3 hours to come back but can do faster than that. We experienced the breathtaking views of the 'Sunrise' from the top of the mountain

A group of ten of us began climbing at 2am which we were advised to be the best time,  arrived to the top about thirty minutes before sunrise. Perfect timing. Very cold at the top and very busy but even the glimpse I had of the sun rising behind the clouds was worth the 6000+ steps. Legs took a bit of a beating in the days following but I would recommend and it will be the first on my list when I return to Sri Lanka. Simply amazing.

If you want a nice walk / hike up a mountain don't do this walk! We went on a Thursday night / Friday morning and the way up wasn't too bad in terms of how busy it was but the way down was ridiculous, we were getting squashed and shouted at, and there was hardly any space to come down after the sunrise. It didn't feel like a spiritual walk at all. And the path is littered with shops so the views are obscured and the locals are not educated to not throw plastic on the ground so there is a lot of rubbish around too. There isn't really a comfortable view point at the top because of the temple and other buildings they've decided to put there. The walk itself is not easy up or down, or legs were like jelly afterwards, we stretched before and after but couldn't walk properly for 3 days! Take warm clothes for the wait at the top.

I will not talk about religion etc. but only about the climbing experience. Spiritual thing is as you let it to be. We started climbing at 2AM and arrived to the top 5.30AM. We are rather sporty people but at the top we felt the speed we took. The temperature difference is around 15deg Celcius so better take some warm clothes to avoid warming up next to coconuts fire as we did :-) Going up isn't really 'climbing'. There are thousands of steps. The path, despite timing, is crowded. Looking around you will see lots of rubbish. The smell of urine is everywhere. It is just disgusting sometimes. Really bad experience. At the top all you got is waiting for sunrise in the crowd like at Rolling Stones concert. You can't really find any place to contemplate in peace. Crowded mess I'd say. I know this is spiritual place but if you're not so spiritual simply don't go, it isn't worth the effort.

It was a good experience, the exercise was needed after loafing around for some weeks. After reading some reviews I thought it would be much harder, but if you have an average level of fitness then it's just a couple of hours of huffing and puffing. If you are pretty fit you shouldn't start until at least 3am, as you will be waiting at the top cold and twiddling your thumbs. Speaking of the cold it wasn't THAT cold. I bought a thin sweater for 300 Rupees and had a hat, no problems. The sunrise was.....a sunrise!! nothing spectacular, like many others. Thankfully it didn't rain.

In amongst a superb trip to Sri Lanka this was the only low point. Despite the spiritual nature of the area and the wonderful hills the region is blessed with Adams Peak is a scar on the landscape. The path is a concrete highway of steps and mixed pavement. The "magical lighting " is not oil lamps or even full electric lights but neon strip lighting making you feel like you are walking up an urban high street. The entire route is strewn with litter and this UNESCO Nature Reserve is badly polluted by the number of pilgrims who, despite this being a holy place, can't be bothered to carry the bottle of coke they bought at one of the 1000's of stalls that line route back down with them. If you have every been on any kind of mountain/hill top at sunrise, that will be a better experience. Sharing a sunrise with 1000 selfie sticks is not that interesting. Don't waste your time, go hiking elsewhere in the area, I was gutted by how underwhelmed the experience.

Started the climb from our nearby guesthouse at 2am. It was very challenging in parts and very busy (especially at the top) however thoroughly enjoyable especially when you make it to the summit! Sunrise lovely - think we were unlucky as it was a bit misty but the views were still amazing. Definitely would recommend though be prepared for the leg ache afterwards!

Definitely worth the effort. Expect  to have sore calves for a few days..One of the best travel experiences I have ever done..The sunrise and the people  make this journey  worth every step...Don't  pack too much and don't  go too hard too early..I did it in 2 and a half hours and I'm  52 with reasonable fitness..very inspiring  to the variations of people  from the young to the  old completing this walk. So no complaints  abouts sore legs from me..

Climbing Sri Padaya was a fantastic experience. You should absolutely do it.  Here are my tips for a good trip: 1. Avoid the crowds and climb during the week and not on a Poya day. 2. Allow 3 hours. We're pretty fit and it took us a bit less than 3 hours at a leisurely pace. 3. Plan to give yourself 30 mins at the top before sunrise. You can take a look around, ring the bell, have something to eat and position yourself for a good view to the east. 4. You won't need a torch in-season. The track is lit all the way. 5. Take warm pants and a hoodie for the top.  It gets pretty cold up there! 6. Take a spare tshirt. You'll be soaked in sweat by the time you get to the top. 7. Take sunnies for the trip down. 8. Don't plan any serious climbing the days after, your legs will be sore!

One of the Srí Lanka highlights, but consider your visit. Way up take around 2 and half hour, or more. If you are not use to physical activity it could be much longer. At the top its just a half way and your leg will hurt you for nexy couple of days. At the top choose the place not like everybody else, but with a view to thr EAST :-) I like it, but its really crowded and could ruin your plans for next days.

Did the trek this year via Kuruvita trail (Erathna Route), which is approximately 16km one way and the most toughest track to the peak! During the season you have the track lit. Half the distance is without any steps just jumping over the rocks! Expect wildlife too although not much during the season... takes about 12hours to reach the peak. On the Kuruvita trail there are only a very few shops.. but there are many wayside rests (ambalama) on the way You find very few travellers on this jungle route so u can leisurely go unlike via Hatton. Take warm clothes, and edibles as its a long journey. I couldnt use my dslr most of the time as the trek uphill is very tough and risky.specially when going at night.. Started around 2pm and reached the peak at about 3.30am next day. The view of the sunrise is Spectacular!!! Suggest everyone to get down thru Hatton. (FYI Hatton route is about 10km up and down and takes about 6hrs one way.) Very tough journey! but you will enjoy this route! :)

Visited for the third time. It was an amazing experience. We took Rathnapura palabaddara route.  It was little bit exhausting as there were lot of steps. Few tips. Better to climb during night time. If you are planning to  watch the sun rise ("Ira Sewaya") try to reach the summit arround 5am or reach arround 8 - 9pm on the previous day spend night there.. Because in between that, you may have to climb dawn  as there is no enough space at "uda maluwa" ( Summit ). In average from rathnapura side it ll take around 8hrs, from kuruwita side 10 - 12 hrs n from hatton side 4- 5 hrs(Time vary according to the  crew ).  There are enough waters sources  ,no need to carry heavy bottles.  Have some calorie dense food. Most importantly PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT LITTLE.. Have a safe journey..

We went up at night and saw the sunrise from the top. It was a stunning moment when the Sun became visible and we saw the landscape, as we came by night. It was a little crowded sometimes the way up and on the top. Also our legs were hurting the next days we were really happy to be there. Give it a try and go by night. We startet at 1 am, so we were not in a hurry. (Were at the top 1h before sunrise)

We read a lot about Adam' Peak be gute going there. Of course we read that it is exhausting but as we are quite fit we didn't worry. We started at 1 am and were quite quick - it took us 2:50 to go up. The last part I just would not believe that the stairs wouldn't stop. As we finally made it, it was still dark but already crowded up there. We were happy to have another set of clothes with us as it was a bit cold up there and our clothes all sweaty. The sunrise was stunning and the way down was nice, too. But it still took 2:30 and felt even worse than going up. Our legs were hurting for at least two days but it really was worth it!

A scared site, well worth doing mixing with the many mainly Buddhist pilgrims and seeing the views from the top. Take something warm to wear at the top waiting for the sunrise, it is windy and chilly but by Northern European standards not cold.  Decent walking shoes or trainers, torches (the path is unlit in places and the steps vary in steepness and frequency) and we all wore walking trousers for both respect and chill factor.  Avoid the loos if possible but do take on water.  We also had some energy bars that proved useful. Calves will ache for a few days after and a reasonable degree of fitness is required. Four of us (50yrs +) did the Sri Pada climb on 19 Mar 17 setting off from Punsisi Rest House at 01:30.  Our driver had arranged the services of a local guide which we thought may have been unnecessary as essentially it's a set of steps going up and then the same set down again, what could go wrong?  The start was relatively easy, a small amount of people going up and coming down again.  It got busier and busier but we were making good time.  After a few hours our guide stopped, met with his Dad who was guiding a group of German tourists and informed us we were going to take a different route.  Torches to the ready we left the path and plunged into the jungle, scrambling up embankments and through trees and shrubs in the pitch black eventually coming out of a rough stone strewn path which after some time eventually led out onto one of the other longer but less well used paths to the top.  It was still a real effort to the top and became increasingly crowded with a queue of people going up one abreast and a queue coming down, lots of people stopped or sleeping on the path.  Eventually reaching the temple at the top, removing shoes we were amongst hundreds of people, many coming up from the original path we had set out on.  Our guides insisted they knew of a better place to see the sunrise and we started descending to a place just off the peak where we saw the magnificent sunrise.  The queue by this time on the ascent was four or five deep and extended down and up as far as the eye could see.  On our way down (after 06:30) we were asked by a Western couple how far off the top they were, they had started at 01:00 but had been stuck in the queue now for hours and were still probably 3 to 4 hours off the top.  It was only by following our guide 'off piste' that we had managed to reach the peak at all, the amount of people trying to come up the normal path had to be seen to be believed - please AVOID WEEKENDS at all costs.

I am a not sporty person at all. The adam's peak is managable (we did it in 2 1/2 hours) but it is really exhausting please keep that in mind! I think we've been extremely unlucky on our day but i was dissapointed. The whole way there are shops which keep annoying you if you just stop for a second, the top isn't a bit green at all just one temple and everything with concrete. We had bad weather so no nice sunset :( and there was this studpid annoying light! Do not stand at the stairs - the light will blind you the whole time and won't be turned off for the sunset!!! Search for a good place (where the stairs for going down are is the best place I think from where we have seen the sun rising behind the clouds) expected more so i was dissapointed a lot. The path itself (up and down) is really nice (despite the garbage) - PLEASE do not throw your garbage beside the stairs there are enough bins - hate that it looks like that!

The climb was a lot harder than expected! Most of it is stairs, so very hard on the legs. We made good time however, and were up the top with plenty of time to spare. When nearly at the summit, the police call over foreigners, and ask them to remove shoes, cover up, and keep hold of bags. Whilst it seemed a little unnecessary, it was nice that they were keeping an eye out for us. Once at the top, we waited a while for the sunrise. It does get very busy, and once the top is full, it's closed off, so leave plenty of time to get there, and be prepared to wait (in the cold!) for the sunrise to appear. Beautiful views, especially on the way back down. It was a little cloudy, but for us, this didn't detract too much. There are shops and (predictably grim) toilets along the way, so if you don't bring snacks etc, you can pick them up on the way. Most of the locals were in flip-flops, or had no shoes at all, however we saw a snake across the footpath, on the way up, so would recommend shoes.
Great trip had a big experience. Love it, first time we visited adams peak. It was amazing. Difficulty to climb. But  we did. Wish to go again

The Adam's Peak also known as "Sri Pada" is a 2,243 m (7,359 ft) tall conical mountain located in central Sri Lanka, i.e., "sacred footprint", a 1.8 m (5 ft 11 in) rock formation near the summit, which in Buddhist tradition is held to be the footprint of the Buddha, in Hindu tradition that of Shiva and in Islamic and Christian tradition that of Adam, or that of St. Thomas. In my opinion it is useless going there. It takes so many hours till you get to the peak. There are thousands and thousands of steps, it is basically a path to get to the peak till you finally see get to the top as I told you before there is a big rock there which is believed to be the "sacred footprint". And remember you also have to come all the way back! It's so hectic and hard to climb the mountain especially if you are travelling there with your family and kids. Everyone just gets tired.

I'm so glad I decided to climb Adams Peak, it was one of the highlights of my trip and something I'll never forget. I was a solo female traveller and had done lots of research prior to the climb. I can confirm you definitely do NOT need a tour guide for Adams Peak. It's so well lit, and there's thousands of other people climbing it too so you'll never be alone. It was quite tough in parts of the climb and the way down is also hard as your knees are pretty knackered by that point but it's totally worth it! Also, it's definitely a climb for all ages, I saw small children to elderly people the whole way up so you don't have to be super fit! I stayed at Daddy's guest house which was great and easy waking distance to the start. I left Daddy's about 1:45am and began my climb at 2:00am (it's a little walk to the start from all the guest houses). It took me about 3.5 hours to get to the top but it would have been quicker if it wasn't for the crowds and queues during the last 1km. What I wore for the climb: - sports / gym leggings - Trainers (you don't need hiking boots, locals do it barefoot or in flip flops which is pretty mad) - T-shirt - Long sleeved zipper / hoody At different points on the way up I got hot and and then cold but I'd say the majority of the time I had my long sleeve zipper round my waist. However you definitely need it at the top as it's much cooler and quite windy. Also, due to the crowds the climb is much slower closer to the top so you can often find yourself queuing and not moving for 5-10 mins. What to take for the climb: - A small / medium sized rucksack (sports type one) - Drinks & snacks - a bottle of water (I put some berocca in mine) and a coke (you'll need some sugar hits along the way). A packet of sweets & choc bar- I bought the drinks & sweets in the main town before the climb as it's cheaper but you can get drinks and snacks the entire way up, they are just more expensive. - Toilet roll - Phone / camera (obvs!) - A portable phone charger (you don't want your battery running out when you get to the top!) - Hand Sanitiser - Sun glasses & suncream (for the way down) -  A spare top (in case it rains) I was very lucky and saw the sunrise as it was a clear morning and I also had the perfect weather conditions as it didn't rain!  The sunrise & view was absolutely beautiful and I've never seen anything quite like it. I climbed it on a Friday morning which I knew would be busy but it wasn't too bad apart from the last 1km to the top which I did have to queue quite a bit. Try and avoid weekends if your itinerary allows it. I can't recommend doing this climb enough, you don't have to be super fit, you can take your time, there are plenty of stop off points along the way. Definitely one of my favourite parts of my Sri Lanka adventure.

We stayed in Nallathaniya for one night, just to visit Adams Peak. It is a really exhausting way up (over 5000 steps, which are all of different height and length. Some passages are really steep.) but it is definitely doable. We started at 2 am (at our guest house) and were at the top at 4:44am - sunrise was at around 6:20am... We had light rain the whole night. At first we thought we were dressed to warm but when you got near the top it got very cold and windy! (Especially if it is raining a bit). We wore a light jacket and a rain jacket over it. At the top we also wrapped us in the blanket we brought with us and were still freezing (over an hour in wet and windy environment isn't nice -.-). A lot of people were really poorly dressed (some in shorts and tank tops!?) And left before the sunrise since it was simply too cold... It also seems like locals go up there even earlier - with their flip-flops, on socks or even barefoot :-O A lot of them coming down the hill when you were climbing up and some were really really exhausted. In the end it was worth the way up and walking in the cold! The view was stunning even if it wasn't the glowing red sunrise you saw in many pictures (since it was cloudy and a bit rainy). Also to take pictures was hard since you are standing on steps side by side with lots of other tourists and locals - can't use a tripod (which would be useful in the low light) and there's a building which you have to overlook to see the sunrise! We didn't enter the temple since you should take off your shoes as usual - what we didn't wanted to do in that bad weather (even when some tourists and even locals entered with shoes on)... ...So take warm clothes with you (and maybe a fresh shirt to switch at the top!) and enjoy the view! We were there on a Monday. Weekends and on puja days it seem to be very very crowded (and you get stuck in "traffic" in the last hundreds of meters/steps without moving at all) so rather get there during the week. Also it is free of charge. At the bottom they want to tie route you through a small "temple" area where they want to persuade you to donate. Since this seemed to be a bit shady, we didn't donate anything there!
It was amazing experience. I didn't expect to see sunrise due to weather but the top was much more rewarding. It is a holy experience.

Started around 2 am from our hotel and slow paced we made it to the top after 3 hours. Last 30 mins it gets really cold. When we started at 2 am I was wondering why I need gloves, a scarf and additional wind jacket but after getting close to the summit it got really really cold and windy. I had to rent a blanket from the last cafe which was an excellent idea. It was very crowded at the top so I didnt stay long. The weather wasnt great (very cloudy) so I knew it wasnt worth to wait for the full sunrise. Going down was easy and pleasant but I got tired. I wasnt exhousted but it is a bit of a challenge.

We went up today in the morning at 2am and it took us 1h 40 min to get to the peak. We are 2 mid 20 aged men in quite good shape but in our opinion this experience can and should be done by everyone. Even locals go up there with their old grandparents and it's amazing to see how they work together to get to the peak. If you don't feel fit just try it and start early enough you will love it! Definitely a must do in Sri Lanka!
It will take time to climb up there, some people taking 2-3 hours and some 4-5 hours! It really depends on their fitness! Try roti with sambol and their coffee

We climbed Adam's peak 2 days ago, setting off at 2.30 am in the morning. It was cold once we started but we quickly warmed up whilst walking. It's a hard climb, we stopped a couple of times. I didn't enjoy the scenery leading up to the top. There are loads of 'flea market ' stalls all the way to the top taking away the feel of nature. We went on a full moon which is a Buddhist holiday so loads of locals climbed it as well. It was very crowded once we reached the top. We managed to get through the crowd at the top but decided to walk down the stairs a bit to see the sunrise.  It is worth the climb. The view from the top is amazing! You can buy water and food all the way up so no need to get it before you start. The walk down was a lot easier than up! Take dry clothes for the top. It is chilly once you stop climbing and cooled down.

This is one of the most sacred places for Buddhists all over the world. Hy especially at the dawn is breathtaking. It is wise to avoid Poyadays, and long weekend holidays, as this can be heavily crowded during those days. Best time to start climbing is 5-6 hours before dawn if climbing from Nallathanniya, or 12-14 hours before the dawn, if climbing from Ratnapura. Ratnapura trail is highly difficult and will test the physical endurance to the maximum level. It is always better to travel during the season, ie from December to May, unless seeking an adventure.

I climbed Adams Peak with my husband 2 days ago, the day after Poya. I thought it would be slightly easier than it was! The climb was very hard work, we stopped a few times but not for very long. We started the walk at 2am and got to the top at 4.00 am so had a while to wait until sunrise (6.20am) the top got very busy and was extremely cold! - Walking up Adams Peak we were boiling but I would deffinatley recommend bringing warm clothes for the top! We had planned to watch the sunrise from the top but it was so busy it felt like a penn as it's all walled with thick rails on top of the wall, if your standing against them it would be fine but if not it might be hard to see...so we climbed a few steps down and watched it from there & had a fantastic view. There wasn't a lot of clouds around so the sunrise & view was amazing, deffinatley worth climbing up all the steps! The walk down seemed easy at first but after a while of bounding down the stairs my legs and especially my knees were aching! I wouldn't say the way down is harder but it does hurt the knees a quite a bit... It's been a couple of days and the leg wobbles have finally gone but calfs and knees are still quite sore! Still can't walk down stairs that easily at the moment! When we got the village at the bottom of Adams Peak before we started the climb we were very surprised (in a good way) at how busy it was, there are lots of guest houses, restaurants etc and loads of stalls selling everything you need for the climb, rainmacks, jumpers, trousers etc. Overall very hard work, not as fit as I thought but worth it, amazing views and a great experience!
Countless other sunrises to experience on our planet that include less garbage. Less people and more of a challenge.

Do not underestimate the brutality of those steps. My legs felt like the could not hold me by the time I returned to the bottom. There's lots of tea places along the way which are really cute, be sure to add sugar for the extra energy! Bring warm clothes as it gets cold at the top while waiting for sunrise.

I am 62 and 100 kg . It took my wife and I 4and a half hours to climb and 2and a half down with plenty of stops . The path is lit all the way up from November to April when climbing stops due to season. A small torch may be useful for some shadowy steps. There are stalls with water , hot and cold drinks and food at regular intervals all the way up. There are very basic toilets at regular intervals, cafes charge a small fee for use. The path is concrete steps all the way up . It starts wide about 4 metres with flat lengths and occasionally short flights, the second stretch is similar width with continuous steps of differing height, the last part is narrower with metal handrails to the top. We started at 2am in light shower and about 20 degree c . A light polyester base layer and light waterproof is enough. At the top it 10 degrees and a bit windy. I personally did not need another layer as it was like back home in Manchester Uk. There were no leeches as mentioned by another reviewer, you would need to go off the track into bush for this to be considered an issue. The length of climb is 7 kilometres each way plus a bit each way from your hotel . Our guide advised there are 5500 steps plus a vertical ascent of 1000 metres. As he said the village is at 1100 metres altitude, this maybe more like 1100 metres ascent. Don,t worry give it a go. The local pilgrims walking with no shoes or flip flops and singing their way up is inspirational. You will need to take off your shoes at the top and queue to visit the temple and impression of Buddas foot in the rock. The sunrise and mountain top vista are sensational.

It is a special place, really tiring climb but rewarding sight! we started climbing from Nallathaniya around 2am and we reached the summit at 4:45, so waaaay before the sunrise (we went straight to the top, stopped only to make small rests-no tea drinking and eating in the stands). If you avoid the weekend or public holidays it should be enough to start at 2am. SPECIAL ADVICE: bring some insoles that you can put into your socks once you have to remove your shoes at the top. It can get really cold up there and if it is raining (as it was with us), you will thank youself :-) The scenes are breathtaking. The only sad thing is how they treat this holy place (and their nature in general) - a lot of rubbish all around.

Very beautiful sunrise above the sea of clouds. It is a must-visit in Sri Lanka if you are able to climb up 1,000 meters of stairs. Timing is very important to avoid missing the moment (the Sun doesn't wait for us). Recommend to reach the peak before 5:30AM. Both my bf and I are about the age of 30, do regular exercise. We set off from Slightly Chilled (one of the hostels/hotels at Dalhousie) at 2:20AM and reached the peak near 5AM. The way up to the peak is well paved, light-up and stores, so no worries about sturdy hiking boots, torch lights, thirst, hunger and toilets. While we will get a good amount of perspiration on the way up, it's really cold when waiting on top, so do bring enough warm clothings. Also, remember to wear or bring long pants, because it's a temple at the peak.

We started at 2 am. It was raining and cold. But you can buy everything you need up there. Also there is no need to bring food or water, you can buy it along the way. The mountain looks impressive in the dark, like a chain of lights all the way up to the top. I found it an incredible experience to go up in the dark and after sunset to be able to see what is actually around you. The hike is not to difficult. You see singing locals in flip flops :) The view from the top is just fabulous but its crowded and there is not really enough time to enjoy the view and relax because the police sends you back down

You need to start your trip at 2 am to reach there before the sunrise, people are nice and you have many spots to stop and rest with tea and coffee. Defiantly suggest you to go there... Try to get a jacket with you, 5 am its + 10 there

We read a lot of reviews about what to wear/how long it takes etc and there were mixed reports. So, this is our view, we are 2 55 year olds, I am a runner so very fit, my husband is averagely fit. 1. It is worth doing: if you like a challenge it ticks boxes; for the sunset if you are lucky enough to have a clear day, but for me the highlight was walking back down and taking in the scenery and views which were superb. 2. Age related/fitness related: I was fine on the uphill overtaking people far younger, but it does take its toll on the knees, so going down was harder. 3. Whatever fitness you can do it at your pace. Watching the locals, there are people carrying children up, very old men and ladies, so there is no excuse 4. When we climbed it was 60% Sri Lankans: 40% tourists, so that makes you think about the significance of the climb. 5. There are tea shops/toilets on the way, so there is no need to carry much other than a small bottle of water. I advise the Milo, a great treat before the final climb! 6. Clothes, we climbed in February, so cooler, it is warm ascending, it is slightly windy at the top so an extra layer is needed, going down the sun is up, so it is warmer. 7. Time it takes: we left around 2.30 and arrived at the summit about an hour too early for sunset. So with 2 stops, it is about 2.5 to 3 hours. If you are early, stop at the tea room and keep warm for a bit before the final climb. 8. It is busy at the top, if you stay outside the Temple, then get as high as you can on the steps, or stay in front of the temple somewhere on the climb up for a very clear view Consensual sigh as sun came up!!
