It was stunningly beautiful and the journey down was very nice indeed despite being joined by a pack of dogs for the most part. One dog came all the way to the summit just because 😊. Our legs are aching and I would say this is best done by those who are active, if not then I would recommend leaving earlier to allow for breaks! Legs are aching after!

The wheather was amazing,beautiful sunrise.Worth all the steps climbed.I loved it .We climbed in the low season but we was so lucky that we saw the sunrise.We stayed climbing at 2.30 am and reached there at 5.30.It was a nice experience

Me and my friends started climbing the peak at around 1 am in the morning, that's what people usually do so that we can make it to the top by morning to view the sun rise. No need to worry as there are lights and small shops on the way up hill. The climb was worth it, it took us almost 2 hours to reach the top and the view we got to see was magnificent...the sun rise and the mountains covered with clouds, it was like being on top of the world...I was just wishing if i could jump on those fluffy looking clouds covering the mountain just leaving the peaks. And not to forget it is considered a very auspicious place for Lord Buddha personally visited the place and we can see his foot print there. Point to keep in mind, it's very cold up there so it's better if you take some warm clothes or a blanket or two to protect from the cold. And it's usually packed with people.
Worth the visit . Make sure you check the weather forecast and go. If you are an average climber you can get to the top in  3 hours in the off season.

We starten at 2am and we all arrived at the top between 5:10-5:30 The weather was cloudy so we couldn't see anything, but the journey alone was hard but An achievement! Make sure to take dry shirt and sweater with you. Because when you are cold, wet and sweatty, you really hope you would have... the tempel only opens until 6am, then you can ring the Bell. Be aware it is a tempel so no shoes. (Bring your flipflops because the floor is cold.) Tea a monk gives you for 100rs, so bring biscuits 😉 The road seems endless but when you skip Adams peak, you missed an important part of Sri Lanka(and you are just a tourist then 😋)

You should be rewarded of your effort by the stunning view on top, but even if the view isn't there, this climb is totally worth it! We did it off-season so the path was dark and only tourists were doing it.  A certain amount of gear is necessary (good trainers, torch lamp, rain coat, hat...) We happen to do it on one of the worst rainfall as well, leaving at 2.30am, the whole way up was raining hard and got cold, also meaning that the view on top wasn't there. However, despite these conditions, I am so glad I did it because of the achievement that it is! I can only imagine how good it is on a sunny day! Expect all teh guesthouse around it to be pretty basic but fully functional.

This amazing activity is a life time experience, the reward is in the climb it self, and not in the mountain top shrine.  We climbed in the off season, so it was very wet and very windy, and thus depriving us from the view at the top.  Both me and my Friend are overweight, and not quite that young, so it took us a record time of 11 hours for the round trip, we just didn't want to quit, six hours up, and four and a half down, with half an hour at the top for photos.  We started at 2am with every one else, but soon the younger guys passed us on their way down while we were still climbing! The endless stairs take their toll on the knees, specially on the way down.  A walking stick works miracles if you are of a very low fitness level like us.  Is it impossible? No. Difficult? Yes. Even on the fittest.  For people with not so great physical abilities, I would recommend a guid, not to show the way, as it is almost impossible to get lost specially with a flash light handy, but rather for emergencies, like injuries etc.  I would also recommend a sleeping Bag, so you can pace your self and rest if needed.  Leeches were there too.  Other than that, if you are moderately fit, not overweight like us, this will be a four to five our hike to you.  Doing it slow like us, did have some benefits, we saw a herd of Wild Boar, very close maybe 10 feet away, a couple of Snakes, and many birds.  The top was too windy, it could easily move you from your footing, so be careful about that.  All in all, I would definitely do it again.

We spent 4 hours climbing the mountain to finally see a foggy view from the peak. We went in September which isn't the ideal season but the weather is also unpredictable. I recommend stretching well before initiating the journey, having a jacket, and your own light if you're going at dawn to watch sunrise. all the directional signs on the mountain are written in local language so it was difficult for us to know which path to take and ended up taking the longer route. You can enjoy a cup of tea when you reach the top for 100 rupis. In general the place is not well-maintained and is an average hiking destination.
Worth all the steps climbed, all the pain afterwards and all the cold on the top. So worth it!!! Amazing!

You would have already read the reviews about the view, here are a few things that are helpful to know that we weren't aware of before we went... In the peak season the path is well lit and the temple is open constantly. In the off season (the majority of the year) the lights are off and the temple only opens from 6am. Take a torch with you, and don't freak out if you find other people walking suspiciously behind you, they are just borrowing your light. There's no big welcome sign when you get to the top, in fact everyone crowds on the final stair case waiting for the gate to open at 6am. Be mindful here - the rooms that you see are the monks sleeping quarters (no sign to tell you this) so best to keep noise to a minimum. The climb can be pretty tough, take your time and enjoy the experience! Also, I'd recommend taking a guide, the monks and the locals on the climb know them and ours did a great job of then getting us access to tea at 4.30am when we were freezing!

After reading many of these sad reviews I had accepted that the ascent was going to take 2 - 4 hours. However was very surprised when we checked our timer at the top, it only took 1.5 hours! Although it was tough at times, if you are moderately fit it will not take anywhere near a full day like some of the frail people on this page. I recommend starting the climb at 4am. Doing this in daylight would be much tougher as you can see how many stairs are ahead of you! Good luck.

Climbing to the top of Adam's peak was on my "must do" things in Sri Lanka. We came in Nallataniya around 1pm. I was afraid that I couldn't make it to the top and down before dark but I was determined to take my chances. The total walk is around 5km in one way and on various forums people mentioned that by normal walk was 3h up and 2h down. I was able to make it in 3h total which caused me some bad leg pains the next few days :) Nevertheless, the total experience was AMAZING!! The view and nature is astonishing. Unfortunately, the monastery on the very top was surrounded in clouds so I could not see around but it was still worth the effort :)

Like Mt. Fuji to Japan, this is the most important and sacred mountain to Sri Lankans. Climbing season is from December to May. Usually a 4 - 8-hour climb depending on the route you choose. Anybody who has the urge can climb :)

We left early at 2:45, arrived at 5 am thus had to wait one hour until the entrance to the temple on top of it was opened. The guard offered a cup of hot tea for a small donation what was really appreciated. As we climbed up during the rainy season in the hill country, we were in the midst of clouds and mist and couldn't watch sunset. However, at pilgrim season in April it might be not unlikely that the stairs are crowded so we enjoyed our hike regardless.

We did the trek in June which is "off season". If you want to do the trek just for the sunrise you should probably not do it in June as it's very cloudy and the chances to see the sunrise are very small. On the other hand it is a great experience to walk through the clouds, not able to see further than 2 meters. All in all we really enjoyed the trek and it's very rewarding to reach the top. The trek is challenging but doable and not too hard (my girlfriend would maybe see that slightly different ;) ) We startet at 4 am (got up at 2 am for the first time but then it was still raining so we waited) and it took us around 6-7 hours with at least 30min break on the top and some breaks along the way. We stayed in the White House Guesthouse, which was very good as the Manager was very nice and helpful and provided us with a torch, raincoats, water, cookies and bananas for the trek.

We travelled to Delhousie (Nallathanniya) from Kandy. We had done our research and knew there was very little to do in Delhousie so we had some food and an early night ready for the early walk. We started the climb at 2.30am. I would consider myself to be moderately fit but I found the climb a struggle. Once we reached the top there was so much mist that you couldn't see anything so we had a quick look around the shrine and came back down. No sunrise. Having visited Ella since climbing Adam's Peak I would say visiting Ella and climbing Ella Rock and mini Adam's Peak would be a much better use of time. I wouldn't even say that climbing Adam's peak is a must for avid walkers and there is genuinely nothing to see along the way.

Top tourist attranction.. only mountain in the world which has a season to hike..  6 months season time is full of locals, the rest 6 months is quiet..  8-9 tracks to reach the top.. 3 of them are the most popular.. morning sunrise is a must to watch.. start your journey 2am so that you could reach the top before the sunrise..

A lot of people do this walk in the early hours to get up for sunrise but I would suggest that before you get up in the cold and dark you see what the weather is doing because if it's rainy or overcast you will make the climb and see nothing for the last hour of the climb and have to sit there in the cold for sunrise. Due to the weather we left at 12.30pm and made it to the top in 3 hrs. I'm not going to lie, it's tough. The 1st 2 hrs are ok, the 3rd is brutal! The steps are steep, big and uneven. As the weather was overcast we were pretty much in the cloud for a 1/3 of the walk but the scenery before that is beautiful. Fitness wise I would say you need to be reasonably fit however there were elderly people on the climb and even a guy on crutches so don't be put off, might just take a little longer, it's not a race!!

So many fake post claiming that they reach top. You will identify liers if you realy reach the top. First nobody says that you need to walk 4km only to reach stairs. The stairs itself are equal to walk up 600 floors building. We did that in raindy and windy day... There was blood suckers which we had to remove every 15-20 min. Thanks to basic medical kit I took... Going up took 5.5 hours including making pictures and one stop for hot tea (you could see your own breath like in winter). Going back none stop took us 3 hours (stairs + walking back). The video I recorded with storm on top was worth everything... BTW take GPS with you and make stops every 10% of stairs. The last 20% will be the most difficult but also with the best views. There was just 3 other couples who also did climb before us that day (we started 9:30am and finished exactly at 6:00pm)

My daughter and I (52 and 26) climbed the many steps to the top of Adams Peak last March. It was the hardest but most exhilarating thing I have done.  We managed to reach the peak just before sunrise and experienced the amazing triangle shadow which appears as the sun rises.  We should have slept before we set back off down the mountain as we were totally exhausted by the time we reached the bottom. There is a hard and an easy way up/down. We went up the easy path (it was still hard) and came down the hard path (wrong thing to do but very interesting...saw lots of wildlife eg monkeys and porcupines.)  There are little huts for you to buy refreshments and there are very basic toilets. I  wouldn't do it again but I'm so pleased I did it ! It was awe inspiring.

Even in off season it was awesome to teach your goal and to have this amazing challenge with yourself, rainy weather, darkness and pain waiting for miracle that will never happen (you will not see a sunrise during the off season), but you will be still proud on yourself and happy to see all your road in the darkness and in the day light again

Do not climb Adams Peak in the off season! It was raining from the beginning and was getting worse! When we arrived at the top at 5 where we had to wait one hour for the opening of the Temple gate. It was so damn cold and we were soaking wet! Take clothes for change and a good rain cape if you go there!  Then a thunderstorm came up but but they opened the door to let us see the "beautiful" view: just fog!! The way down was the most horrible and really dangerous! The stairs changed litteraly into waterfalls! So funny that the guide and our host told us one day before: "No problem to climb! Weather is good"!

We drove directly after we landed in Colombo to Adam's peak and started the trek at first light. I wish I had slept more since the hike is more difficult than expected. It's easy stairs but very long and the crowd during the procession was crazy. We had to queue fo 2 hours on the top at the temple. I had sore legs for 10 days, which was not very convenient since it was only the beginning of my trip. Maybe do it at the end of the trip if you have extra time.

After the climb, and it is a serious climb even for those in good shape, once reaching the top, there is an amazing exhilaration that was achieved. You realize how small and insignificant you are when you see the landscape around you. It is worth taking a moment and appreciating that this area is meant to be a sanctuary for all ways of thinking and life.

It's a 5500 step 9km round trip with 1km vertical ascent. It's tiring, in July; windy and rainy, but well worth it. We didn't see a sunrise because of the clouds but the gratification we got from doing it was huge. Lovely walk down again out of the mists into the waterfall lined cliffs. Bell ringing is a must for some, we (my partner) just wanted to get out of the crosswinds and get down. Maybe we missed something there, but we can always go back one day. The stalls lining the streets at the bottom steal a little charm but can only be expected at a pilgrimage site of this magnitude.

It's a very historic and culturally significant place so we heard that it would be very crowded in a certain season. Luckily we went there off-season and there weren't much people besides the tourists like us. Unfortunately we were stuck in a heavy rain which soaked up everything we had and the regular raincoats don't help out at all. The walk up the stairs is tough as the height of the steps range from very short to very high within a couple steps so it's a demanding activity. We missed the view from the top as there was a lot of fog that didn't disappear and the sun didn't come out due to the clouded weather. Overall it's a nice climb for active people but I hear there are alternate routes for people that want to climb the hill without the steps, which could be a lot more fun. The sense of vertigo isn't very unusual according to what we heard as there final steps are close to the edge on both sides. The legs feel sore for a few days afterwards and it's not easy to go down the stairs during this period but that shouldn't be a problem for active people.

Adam's Peak, or Sri Pada as known in Sri Lanka, is a mountain 2243m high in the south of the central highlands. The mountain features a rock formation that is considered as the footprint of Buddha for Buddhist, Shiva, for Hindu and Adam for Muslims and Christians. The mountain has a path to the top consisting of several thousands steps, many of different heights and uneven. The ascent takes on average 2-3.5 hours and is particularly steep towards the top, although is quite safe as there are hand rails to hold on. Many Sri Lankans make the climb several times in their lives. The 1400m ascent means a significant difference in temperature as you reach the top, and this is exacerbated by the wind. It is not a hard climb but especially on the way down, leg muscles will be overexerted. The January to March period is particularly busy time to climb. Other months see less traffic, and therefore the many stalls lining the path are not open during the "low" season. So bringing food and especially water is important. Many people attempt the ascent in the early hours of the morning, with the goal of seeing the sunrise, others climb in the afternoon to see the sundown. In either cases, torches are needed to see at night, even with full moon. Travelling in groups is always advisable. At the top the wind is very strong, but the scenery is breathtaking. Clouds lying 500m below hit the mountain and skim over the top, giving a spectacular sight. Similar to other articles on the Central province, getting there is hard due to the bad state of the roads and the sinuous character of the trail. The scenery is beautiful and mostly unspoiled (2012), but hardly compensates for the hardship of travel. There are several guest houses/hotels to spend the night, including "Slightly Chilled" that is very friendly towards climbers.

Great climb, legs were sore for a few days after. If your lucky enough you will get a clear view from the top- worth the effort. I read a couple of reviews that said it was 2500Rs  to climb but when we arrived we found it to only be a donation, average amount was 500Rs. Good luck!

Start the walk to the top at 2am. Just follow all other people. The walk takes about 3hrs and can be exhausting. Take enough clothes to keep you warm, while you’re waiting for the sun to rise. It’s a good idea to reach the temple on the top by 5am. It gets very crowded then. When you’ve visited the temple, you can go down to the highest tea shop, where you can sit and relax. You’ll have an amazing view when the sun rises, without many people, since most people wait at the top. Beware that the way down is just as hard as the way up. You’re legs will be shaking. Overall this was a fantastic experiences. Maybe the nicest thing we did in Sri Lanka.

If you expect a great sunset during off season, don't get your hopes up too fast. We went here in July and could not see more then 6 meters further due to the fog. However climbing the stairs was an awesome experience. Have never felt so swore in my life, but so worth it! Start the climb at 2.45am or 3.00 in order to make sure you don't have to wait in the cold for the sunset too long.

Visited from Kalutara with Select Sri Lanka. A tough climb of 2.5 hours during the night (2.30 a.m. start), not for those with poor fitness. Note the monastery at the top doesn't open until 6 a.m. and sunrise is viewed from outside so don't panic. Amazing views of sunrise if you are lucky with the weather and breathtaking scenery on the way down in the day light, so worth the effort of the climb. Fee stalls open in the low season and can be cold at the top so pack layers as you can go from boring hot to cold and vice versa. A guide is useful though not essential, head torches make life much easier. Make sure you have your camera! Toilets are available along the route but are not for the faint hearted... Definitely the highlight of our visit to Sri Lanka and can't recommend this highly enough. Plenty of places for breakfast and accommodation at the base.

Adams Peak is a very historic, cultural, Religious and Natural and undoubtly  my favourite adventure on earth. I have hiked this peak from all the three main routes and the Kuruwita trail which is the longest and through the dense forest is my favourite. the path is lit up throught the night. I advice to hike this peak in an evening with the fullmoon above you and stay on to see thee very famous sunrise from the peak!! the experience will be the best you  will have.

This was my first long hike and Adam's Peak couldn't have been a better mountain. Aside from the beauty of the place itself, the small inns and guesthouses around the area have all the right facilities and people.

The 7km route to the top of Adam's Peak is shorter, but steeper, than any other route to the summit. " Long and arduous" sums it up. It is best to start in the early hours of the morning and most people climb it with the idea of watching the spectacular sunrise from the top of the mountain. Take your shoes off, enter the temple at the top and ring the bells to celebrate your accomplishment. The knees take a pounding on the way down, but a short rest every now and then helps. If you make good time, you can be back at your hotel in time for breakfast!
In the July season it can rain, and it rained. However every disadvantage brings an advantage. No people, no hassle, and a free path to the top. We enjoyed it.

We started our climb around 1am after a good rest at Daddy's Guest House. We reached the summit 5.00am braving through rain at times really heavy. The climb itself was very steep at certain stretch. Path not very well lighted. Good thing we have headlights. It was very misty and cold at the summit. Spent 1/2 hour there and started our descend. Wow, huge workout on the ankles and knees and arrived at the base around 8.30am.  We were happy we made it all the way to the top and back though we could not see the awesome view and the triangular shadow. What a climb!

The beautiful sunrise makes the climb totally worth it. The climb is pretty rough. We climbed during off season so there was no lights or food to buy. So be sure to have a really good lamp. Take warm clothes with you as it gets pretty chilly up there. We wished there would have been more signs saying how many kilometers are left. We saw only like two.

This is my second visit to Adam's peak. In Srilanka there's a saying that you are a fool when you have never visited the Adam's peak and you'll be fool if you visit more than once. First time I went through ratnapura para (ratnapura road) which is much tough that Hatton route but it's the most beautiful one with all streams and sceneries. The Hatton nalla Thani route is short and you can't enjoy the nature very much, but for short trips this is the good choice.  It took about 6hrs to reach the destination. We went on season time so it was so crowdy and no place to pass the night. But all your hard work will be rewarded by the morning glory the mountain and Dawn. Don't take much heavy bags even water bottles and food you can buy on the way to top, there are so many poor people depends on that income and their price reasonable for their efforts to bring them up.

This is a tough one! We -  four  people in  our 60s - are experienced hikers but we found this hard going. Hard going but definitely worth it to see the sun coming up at dawn. Sore for a few days but glad we made the effort.

While the stairs near the top are a little grueling, the sunset and mountain shadow are well worth it.  A few tips once you arrive at the top: 1) while you do need to remove your shoes, put them in your bag as placing them in the pile will make finding them difficult during the mad scramble on the way down (it is very difficult to leave the summit shortly after sunset as crowds are large). 2) once you have viewed the footprint at the top, head to the rail to secure your spot to view the sunset quickly, as large crowds form and, unless you are very tall, you will have an obstructed view. 3) don't forget to view the unique pyramid shadow after sunset, it is well worth the extra 20 minute wait and will also allow some of the congestion at the top to clear as travelers keen to return will have already begun their descent.

We only had two weeks in Sri Lanka but we made sure we did Adam's Peak whilst there. And I'm so glad we did because it was the highlight of our trip. We left our guesthouse at 2am to start our ascent so that we would be at the top for sunrise. The initial hike is a gradual incline of stairs but they get progressively steeper the higher you go. There are plenty of rest areas along the way so you can relax with some tea or a banana when needed. We made it to the summit at around 4:30am. At the top it was already quite crowded with tourists and locals alike huddled together braving the cold in preparation for the dawn. So we decided to avoid the crowd and not freeze to death and catch the sunrise on the way down. Our legs were so sore for the next couple of days but it was definitely worth it because it was such a magical and spiritual journey.

Started climbing at 7.00pm and it was off season. No lights on the route and no water in taps. By 1.00am we managed to conquer half the length. Spent the night at an ambalama and started the journey to the top again at 6.00am. Reached the top by 1.30pm. The climb was so tough and it was freezing cold at the top. Very much worth it. Recommend to carry extra food. Water bottles could be refilled from the natural springs found throughout the route. Great experience.
one of the best pilgrim sites for all religious and Sri Lankans call it as Sri Pada Adawiya. It is a holy mountain to climb with the mild climate.

Started at 2.45am to climb up. Cold at this time - worth wearing trousers at least! Had all the gear including head torches but actually the path was pretty well lit. Made a donation to the temple at the bottom, a young boy guided us that way but you can actually keep walking up the left fork if you don't want to donate. Lots of steps. Over 5000 I believe, and some are very steep towards to top. Lots of small shops along the way to rest and have refreshment. I think the locals spend the night up there - some were coming down including some very elderly people which is a huge achievement! Got to the top about 5am and it is very cold so bring something warm. Also be aware which way points east (we used google maps on our phone but it is on the right as you come up to the top temple). This will mean you get a prime spot for sunrise because it quickly gets crowded and you'll be stuck behind a lot of people. Getting down was not easy. Very hot now sun is up and so many people up at the top with quite narrow and steep stairs. Very jarring on knees too (we began running down as we found it easier). Should have stretched - was painful walking up and down stairs for the next few days!!

Climbed Adams peak few days ago and it was just lovely. It's a place to relax your mind in a spiritual way. This is a must do attraction in Sri Lanka. Also make sure that you stay and watch the sunrise from the top, will be worth it.

If you’re physically fit and enjoy hiking, this should be the #1 thing you do in Sri Lanka. Alright, alright… maybe #2 behind Sigiriya. The views on the way up are gorgeous (not so much at the top, interestingly enough… there are a lot of fences and guardrails), and by the time I reached the summit, I felt the way Rocky did at the top of those stairs in Philadelphia. We went in the off-season (November), and we started the hike a little before 6am. No matter the season, I wouldn’t start any later than that. It was hot by the time we were heading down. Like, REALLY hot. I wasn’t sure whether hiking Adam’s Peak would be worth it during the off-season and having done it, I actually really enjoyed hiking without a ton of other people on the trail. Having talked with friends who made the trek during pilgrimage season, it sounds like we traded a cool cultural experience walking with worshippers for a much more pleasant hiking experience, if that makes sense. So don’t avoid Adam’s Peak just because you’re hiking “off-season.” You do need to be physically fit to make this climb, and if you’re a couch potato, I’d suggest doing a bit of training in advance (Stair-Master like it’s the 90’s! This hike is a lot of quad). To give you an estimate of how long it will take, our hotel suggested most people took 3.5 hours up and 2 hours down. My husband and I (early 30’s; sorta fit, but mostly just stubborn) took a little over 2 hours up and 1hr45min down. There are outhouses at the base of the hill, and a very basic snack hut on the way up (more options are open during high season). We brought snacks, and I was glad I did-there were quite a few hungry-looking dogs on the trail, and they needed a sandwich a lot more than I did. You’ll need to take off your shoes at the top, as it is a religious site. Also, you won’t need a guide to complete the hike.

We did the climb in daytime because the weather was not very good at night and in the morning (too cold and misty to see anything when the sun rises). We had no rain and a bit of sun. Be sure to bring a warm jacket, enough water and a snack because all shops along the way will be closed off season. We hiked for 3 hours till we reached the top. There is was windy and misty. We didn't had a view from the top, but we had some amazing views on the way up and down. We were almost the only people on the trail. Maybe it's more fun to walk up with other people and when the shops are open, but we liked it anyway.

Before visiting Adams Peak, we had been given various stories aa how difficult it is and what happens etc When we visited, it was an off season. Therefore there were no shops open around. Our own estimation of difficulty and rain level went wrong, it was was windy and full of difficulty. Litches were flying in the air and sucking blood. Few returned half way, few went farther but many against all odd reached to the top of the peak. The way is easily accessible, yet difficult. Best if You travel during winter. We had started in the afternoon. One should start early morning. As early as 3 am to enjoy sunrise and avoid difficulty. Carry hood amount of water, glucose, a good pair of shoes, juices and torch.

What a cool hike! Probably one of my all-time favorites (and I hike a lot!) We climbed in March, when many Buddhists were also climbing for a pilgrimage to the top to see Buddha's footprint. The hike was challenging, so be prepared to walk up a lot of steps! Totally worth it, just try to train on steps a few weeks before hand. Also, it's REALLY cold up there! So even though the weather seems fine, it's not! Bring warm clothes. I highly recommend climbing in the night and seeing the sunrise. And when the locals say run down the steps, do it! It saves a lot of time and pain. It was beautiful and unforgettable. ENJOY :)

This is an amazing place for the travelers who love natural beauty, it is well known for the Sri Pada, i.e., "sacred footprint", a 1.8 m (5 ft 11 in) rock formation near the summit, which in Buddhist tradition is held to be the footprint of the Buddha,It is an important pilgrimage site, especially for Buddhists. Pilgrims walk up the mountain, following a variety of difficult routes up thousands of steps. The journey takes several hours at least. The peak pilgrimage season is in April, and the goal is to be on top of the mountain at sunrise, when the distinctive shape of the mountain casts a triangular shadow on the surrounding plain and can be seen to move quickly downward as the sun rises.

made the climb on the night of a full moon (poya day), along with hundreds and thousands of pilgrims making the climb up the mountain, even tho we were just doing it to see, what is said to be one of the best sunrises in the world we felt part of the rituals. the climb took us way longer than usual as more people climb on poya day for religious reasons, we started the climb at 12:00 am there was such a massive line to reach the top we only reached the summit at 6:30am. the climb was extremely exhausting but worth it as you witness and see people of all ages making the climb. singing and chanting all the way to the top. If you are in Sri Lanka during the season I highly recommend you add this to your itinerary. Tip: If you don't like large crowds of people DO NOT climb on a full moon.

We had an early dinner and went to bed till 12am. The made our way to the peak. I think we started around 1am and It took us 3 hours to climb to the top although some people did it in 2 hours. The last 30 minutes were really tough, but then the locals motivate you and somehow we made it. The sunrise was amazing. We climb on a thursday and there were not many people during the walk. We absolutely loved it. Bring warm cloths as it was freezing at the top. And just a bottle of water as there are plenty of places if you need more drinks. I didn't stretch after the climb and my legs were sore for days. But other guys did and felt much better :-).

It is a tough walk up to the top of Adam's peak, but well worth it, I'm not that fit but if you take it easy and pace yourself you'll get to the top, the route is a concrete path of steps, with shops/tea stops on route!  the guys in the shops didn't seem to mind you stopping and taking a rest.  There is colour and noise at 2 am in the morning, the route can be  busy!!! I walked up mid week, arriving at the bottom at 2am and taking a steady walk up it took 2 hours, there were lots of local making the pilgrimage to the top, very mixed ages and families, old people being supported walking and young kids!    There are steep sections towards the top. Once you get the top there are steps you can sit down on, and have a sleep to the left of the route to Buddha's shrine.  It does get busy at sunrise, but it is well worth it, one tip -once people start leaving, let the crowds go and it can get very hectic coming down - fun but a little nerve racking. All in all one of the my highlights from Sri Lanka, a little tough but enjoyable, with an amazing sunrise at the end of it all.

You have to be quite fit to climb. The stairs are quite steep and there are lots of them! We arrive at the bottom and started our hike at 145 am. Thank God it wasn't pilgrimage season as I don't think I could have coped with waiting in line to go up the steps! It was really hot and we sweated all the way up-and down in the sunlight. It took me four hours to hike up with a few breaks. My friend did it in 3 hours and waited at the top. Some tips: I'm so glad I bought hiking socks, a thirst and shirt that wick all the sweat and moisture away as cotton clothing  will be wet and won't dry quickly. Hiking shoes also helped. Much better than sneakers. Take walking sticks. They will save your knees. A headlight was very useful. Some areas are not well lit at night. Take rehydration salts and some snacks to keep you going. Remind yourself to take pictures. I regretted not taking more, but I was so focused on the steps that I didn't stop to take pics. Your legs will feel like jelly on the way down and will hurt for a few days after. Massages help!

We didn't pick a religious festival to hike so that it was pretty fast, took us 2.5 hours to reach the top and around 1.5 hours go down. It is mostly stairs not trails so going down wasn't very pleasant because my knees hurt. This is more of a cultural and religious experience than a hike. You see buddhist temples on your way. waiting for the sunrise on the top is nice but there are not many spots for you to stay, so give yourself some extra time to look for a perfect view point.

Yes, it's tough climb. Yes, your legs will stay sore 3 days after. But the experience itself, seeing all the locals climbing whatever their conditions, the spiritual feeling up there, the breathtaking sunrise & the stunning views while going down makes it a once in a lifetime experience. It took me 2 hrs & 30 mins to climb & 2 hrs to go down. Always start climbing at 1-2 a.m. to catch the sunrise

It was a harder climb than expected but plenty of places to hydrate and eat along the way even though I suggest eating light. We climbed in 3 1/2 hours and I was surprised by how much rubbish was just thrown down along the way and not cleaned up. Bathrooms charge 20-30lkr but if you really need it then pay it. They re not the cleanest nor do they smell the best either. monks were trying to make foreigners donate but I just signed the book and gave nothing. Sadly no sunrise as we got there it was covered in mists and heavy clouds plus very windy and cold. Bring a jacket and snacks for if you don't want Sri Lankan food and snacks. I am in pretty good shape but I am stile sore two days after the climb but glad i did it. The best time for a clear sunrise is between December- Feb..

It feels like a stairway to heaven specially when you are reaching the peak! The stairs become steep and the steps are becoming higher than usual. Thought we can finish it in 2 hours. We are couple and moderately fit. We started walking at around 2AM and reached the peak at 7am. We made a stop to one of the stores selling bread. And at that time it was one of the delicious breads i ever tasted because im super hungry! The views are amazing when you reached the top. We saw some monks and other people rounding the temple with their offering. It's easy to descend however our knees are in pain so again we took our time. And took lots of pictures! Id do it again if ever get the chance.

Although you spend the night doing this climb, and will be tired the next day and sore for a few days, doing the many steps to the top of Adam's Peak is definitely worth it! You walk during the night, it's dark and you don't really know what's around you, but once you reach the top, and the sun starts rising, you realize that you have arrived at the top of the world. The view is too beautiful for words! And then when you go down all those many steps again, you see the beauty that you walked through in the dark. Amazing! We were a bit unsure of whether it would be possible to go so close to the end of the season, but it was totally fine. It was raining during the evening only. And the best of it: there weren't very many people!

You have to climb nearly 7000 steps and it will take more than 4 hours. A stroll of 8 kilometers and people normally climb at night in between December to April. On the top a foot marknis there which is beleived to be of Lord Budhha by Srilankans and of Lord Shiva by Hindus

All religion people visit this place during seasonal time. two path to reach the peak level. From Nallathanniya or Rathnapura. More than 6 kms to one way traveling. If you able to sun raise this is the best place to stay and check it.

If you aren't a person looking for the spiritual aspect of what Adam's Peak is said to offer, then I can't really recommend or justify this undertaking. It took my wife and I about 9 hours to do this round-trip, which was fine. However, the masses of people who collect there - the shoving, pushing, crowding, etc. coupled with the cold temperature and having to take the shoes off just doesn't make it worth it for me. People push and shove and skip line, as if the footprint is going to just walk off before they get there. Keep in mind, the footprint was covered by a shroud when we made it to the top, too, so the one attraction where you're herded through was unseen. To make things worse, the hotels around the foot of the peak aren't special, and they're quite expensive for what you get. Maybe I'm cynical because I've seen better mountain view sunrises during my treks, but I think it's best to avoid going so far out of the way to do this.

My wife and I set off at 1:30 am as recommended to us by our guesthouse. We managed to complete around 70% of the hike in the first two hours and were optimistic at our chances of seeing the sun rise at the top of Adams Peak. Then we joined the queue of local pilgrims all making their way up to the top. This lasted another 8hrs! We were determined to make it to the top and were undeterred by the continuous stream of foreigners walking down and telling us it was hopeless. We finally reached the peak at 11:30am (10 hrs later). The peak and temple is also overcrowded and you are continually pushed along and are never free from the human conveyor belt. I felt glad that we had accomplished the hike but it is not for the faint hearted!
We went there, but it was raining so much, we decidet not to go up. Anyway we location is beautiful.Go there if you like people. Avoid the weekends or holy days, it is crowdy

The way up to adams peak is mostly steps. The last 15% or so are full with people so you need to be patient. we started at 2 o'clock in the morning and were at the third police station around 4. Just behind there the "traffic jam" started. But there is a secret shortcut:  beween the third policestation and the buddha in the glas box is a way which leads to the stepps o the other side of the hill. The way is also illuminated and around 1 meter wide. You can't get lost. As you reached the steps you can walk up with not so many people. The tempel on the top is not extremly nice but the view over the land and the sunrise is nice. Going down is also chalanging. You have to fight your way down as many people are stuck. At 8.30 we were at the hotel again...with wobbely legs...:-S

Dear travellers, obviously the sunrise is beautiful and also ascending and descending the steps is not as hard as people say. Nonetheless I wouldn't recommend going up Adam's Peak. The first mile or so you walk past tiny stores, one after another. Literally the most commercialised place I've seen on Sri Lanka so far. Then, it was really overcrowded. Although we started at 2 am on a Monday morning, we got stuck for at least three times which took two hours waiting time in total. A lot of push and shove going on. Because of the amount of people, there is waste everywhere. The nature next to the track is completely littered, it breaks your heart. No feeling of pilgrimage whatsoever. If you are anyhow close to authentic backpacking, if you like off the beaten track style travelling and nature, avoid this place!

First off, this is a pilgrimage walk not a mountain climb full of solitude and nature! Over 5,000 steps in each direction, constantly surrounded by people is not something everyone will love but nor something that anyone visiting Sri Lanka should miss. The question everyone asks is about timings: we were climbing the day after a Poya day and left at 2:30am. We made it to the top for sunrise but only because we took the shortcut. There are a number of police posts on the route and just after one of them there is a Buddha in a glass box. Between these two is a signposted path into the jungle. Take it but make sure you have a torch. It will take you to the other side of the mountain and a path that barely anyone uses (the Ratnapura Road). It will save you from queuing to reach the very top and you definitely want to make it for sunrise which was absolutely gorgeous.

I did the walk on weekday, which was Thursday. But there were still so many people. It took us almost 3 hours to get to the top and we arrived at 5:15am, while sunrise was at 6:15. We gotta stand at the small area for an hour to wait for sunrise. As there were so many people. I felt just compacted and not comfortable at all. And you couldn't avoid a picture without a head in front. But the "triangle shadow" was really amazing.

We started 1.30 in the morning. You should wear some long pants and  a jacket /Pullover because it gets pretty chilli during that time. There is no entrance fee, BUT be aware- you will get to a Point with 2 ways... If you go right (and there will propably be a monk Who will tell you, you HAVE TO GO that way) you will get into a "trap" - there will be some other minus telling you to donate money, then you get a wristband. But you can also go the other way- you will end up on the Same way again  ;) IT is pretty Hard to get up there especially if You're in no condition :D unfortunately we didn't make it to the end because too many people were on the way. So we went down some stairs again, to see the sunrise - which was stunning!

It's one of the most challenging climbs I've done mainly due to the stairs (15000) which are of different heights and shaped. We started at midnight and reached the peak around 7am (due to an unexpected influx of people causing a bottleneck close to the peak). The view is breathtaking and well worth the climb. Plenty of small shops to help you hydrate and take mini breaks. The sanitary facilities are bad. What's really disappointing is the amount of litter around! It made me quite upset that nobody is doing anything to protect the environment of this place. P.s the hotels and shops at the base of the peak charge unfair amounts with no value. Avoid those places

I do a lot of hill-walking, both at home in Scotland and further afield. I enjoy the peace, the simple paths and the solitude. Adam's Peak (Sri Pada) has none of those. Please bear in mind my review is based on an ascent during the pilgrimage season. I started - as recommended - at 2am for the climb to the top in time for dawn. There were hundreds - if not thousands - of people doing the climb and approaching from two or three different directions. My ascent from Dalhousie was on concrete steps the whole way - the guidebook suggests there are over 5000, but it certainly felt like more! The route got more and more crowded as I approached the top and finally it was stop-start-shuffle. The whole way is lit with street lamps or similar and there are dozens of small shops/stalls selling over-priced drinks, mementoes, cuddly toys etc. There are also dubious toilets at prices I decided to avoid! (Out of season, I'm told there's no lights and the shops are closed. Probably an improvement!). The top of the hill / mountain is architecturally a cross between a 1970s multi-storey car park and a public toilet. I didn't stay for dawn as I'd made the ascent more quickly than I expected and didn't fancy hanging around for a couple of hours in the cold and being steadily crowded out as more and more people arrived in the limited concreted enclosure at the top. I must admit to not having visited the temple with the footprint. Prior to starting the walk, I heard a tour guide telling a group in my hotel that there's a saying in SL: "If you never go up Sri Pada, you're a fool. If you do it more than once, then you're also a fool." I'm safe!

I really enjoyed the climb. There were a few times when I peered up and thought I'll never get that high without loosing a lung- but fear not- it's doable. I left slightly chilled - my accommodation- at 2.15am when others were leaving. I was alone. My friend was injured. People were friendly on the journey. Many buddist went much earlier it seems and were on the return journey. Some groups were ever so slightly intimidating initially but most were very friendly. There were many stalls with food and drinks along the way. I stopped a few times at the various benches and shops. There were people of all fitness levels doing the climb. Some were going at a very fast pace, many were not. There were lots of resting points. The height of he steps varied in parts. I saw many people following a zig zag pattern  to make the climb a little easier. It's challenging but there are so many elderly people barefoot and many people with walking sticks so very possible to go at your own pace. I arrived to the last rest about 4.10am so waited there until 5.30- about 7/8 mins from the top. Just before the last point the police stopped me and a group of girls to say that it was very busy and to put our backpacks to the front so that we didn't get robbed. When we got to the top it was a much smaller space than I had imagined- I went to the steps- about 10 from the top with the temple. I didn't go inside the temple which required removing shoes. I didn't ha e the energy for removing my shoes and waited on the steps with everyone for the amazing sunrise. It was absolutely stunning- the view was so clear. I did a time lapse on my I phone for about 20 minutes. It was breath taking. There was a great atmosphere and good sense of camaraderie at the top and a great sense of achievement after the huffing and puffing en route. Recommendations- bring water, light snacks, a coat if you tend to get cold - I do and as soon as a I got to the area 10 Mins from the top where I waited for one hour and 20- I and many others got very cold so put on jackets, hats, scarves. Those who didn't bring these extra layers bought fleeces and blankets which were selling very well at the top for 600-800 in local currency. I brought some money and got a banana and Sprite and coffee on the way. After the sunrise I made a dash and jogged a lot of the way down but holding onto the railing for The initial journey down where it is pretty steep stepped. I made it down in one hour and 40 minutes. I took one break on the journey down. I am moderately fit. My calves really hurt for a week afterward!!! So maybe less than moderately fit. Finishing was a great feeling. I was in bed early the following night. As soon as I got back to the hotel I took a shower, ate breakfast and got a local driver to bring us to Hikkaduwa which is a long trip so I slept a lot  of that journey.
Avoid the restaurant around the foothills - a lot of flies and not too hygiene unless u have the strong stomach.

This was one of our trip highlights. The trek is difficult but you can take it at your own pace. There are shops along the way you can get drinks (hot or cold) and food. The little samosa's were amazing!! There were loads of locals making the pilgrimage up the peak with their families young and old. Incredible to see and them and so many were doing it barefoot. The sunrise was worth starting out at 2am. It's a comfortable 3.5 hours up including tea and snack stops. We did it at the end of March and the sun was coming up around 6am at this time of year. I'd recommend taking a small torch. While the path is lit it's still dark. People had said it was cold at the top but we didn't find it cold, around 15 degrees celsius at the top. Take extra clothes in case you need them. I had a selfie stick which was super useful for getting the height I needed to take photos of the sunrise past the fence….not to take selflies :D I found that I needed to go to the bathroom on the way down and was surprised at the standard. While it certainly wasn't the same standard as a hotel it was clean enough. I had to pay the guy a small fee to use the toilets. It seemed it was only the tourists getting charged. Good footwear is essential and make sure you take some cash up so you can buy your drinks and snacks along the way. We didn't see budha's footprint as we couldn't be bothered waiting to get in along with all the locals. Would definitely recommend doing this as part of your Sri Lankan adventure. There's no entrance fee.

I tried to reach the top on Sunday. I left the village at 2:15am and by 4:15 came to a complete stop where lots and lots of people are staying in line. Many people are not trying to advance and are sitting on the stairs. While this was a nice and challenging physical experience - the setting was very unpleasant (see photo) If you add to this the overpriced accommodation in Nallathanniya - avoid at all costs on weekends and holidays.

The way up takes about 2,5 hours with breaks. As a reward you get an amazing view and sunrise, you won't regret. Up on the top it's quite cold so bring some sweater and warm socks, as you can't have have shoes on. It's highly recommended to go during the week days and make sure there is no holiday, otherwise there could be crowds of local people and there is a chance you couldn't even make it to the top,  as the path it really narrow to the end so you could get stuck...

Started the night hike at 2.30 am. Got to the top right on time for the sunset at 6.20 am. We went at a very high pace ascent though! It took much more time to climb to a lot of people who even eventually missed the sunrise even though they left much earlier. Stairs, stairs, stairs... Unfortunately we went during the pilgrimage period so it was extremely CROWDED! All type of crowd tourist but manly locals who were definitely NOT prepared for this hike. It was cold up there (around 8 degrees Celsius, wind chill...) and most of the locals were wearing only t-shirts and were of course extremely cold even some of them suffering!!!  Lots of tea shops & stalls if you need a break. When we finally made it to the top, the sunrise was unbelievable!!! The scenery with all the mountains, the morning mist was a once in a lifetime experience! Couldn't see the footprint, way too crowded! Just don't go during pilgrimage season from December and may in 2016. Check online for the dates before you go! Your experience will be so much more enjoyable!!! There are around 5,500 steep steps on the way to Sri Pada Mountain.The stairs are painful going up but worse going down. Specially with all the crowd you're forced to go slowly. We are fit and we decided to run down on the way back.  It took us about 1 hour, 15 minutes running all the way down. You will sweat! Bring warm clothes and change your "wet" clothes once you get to the top. You will also need water and snacks...Night light was not necessary during season but is when not in season. Looking back on the 7 hour return journey to Adam’s Peak, I’ll honestly say, it’s not for everyone!!! 11.000 stairs! Amazing experience but be ready and think twice before setting off on this trek and if you do, be prepared to pay for it. No matter how fit you are, how often you hike, or run, or hit the gym, your body will be in pain for a couple of days after the hike!!!

We read the reviews and it was indeed mixed. So, we were not really sure what to expect. We did bring necessary headlights (which was not really required), a hoodie and windbreaker which was good as the winds/weather was fairly unpredictable and we were ready to go. Starting at about 2:30am, we gave ourselves sufficient time to have a good pace to be at the summit before 6am for the sunrise. The walk up was chill and nice, only when it became abit steeper, then you will feel the effects of it on your knees. I think it is quite important to have some form of knee-aid or support too. :) the sunrise was awesome! Really worth the climb in the middle of the night and all the efforts. We were there not with the full moon or any holidays, plus it rained the night before, so there was abit less people, although still abit of a crowd at the temple. But, we had a little corner to admire the view, the sunrise and wonderful nature around before setting off for the climb down. It was torturous! The climb down was much more difficult as you feel your knees already from the climb up. I think it was best not to make too many break stops on your way down as you lose some momentum and the legs hurt again. :( But, we made it down in good timing for a nice breakfast and shower before leaving Dalhousie area. Tip : make sure to have 2-3 days of chill holiday days after the climb as you almost wont feel your legs and wont be able to do much.... especially nomore stair-climbing! haha~ :P

We set off at 2 am for the 5200 steps not sure how long it would take to get there. We are quite fit and it took us some 2.5 hours without really stopping - except for some places where we had to slow down for those people being 'helped' up, which meant we arrived an hour before we expected and had to wait around - having a coffee and tea to keep warm since it was (relatively) cold - ensure you take a fleece/warm top with you! When actually up there you have to take your shoes off (religious respect) and position yourself for the viewing of sunrise and the 'shadow' which are both absolutely awe-inspiring and worth the climb, as are the 'pilgrims' that do the whole walk in bare feet - we were passed by a 60+ year-old man walking the lot in bare-feet !! There are also great views on the way back down the stairs that you walked up in the dark (actually lights are on all the stairs on the way up)

Adam's peak is a must if you go to visit Sri Lanka. But avoid to go there on any religious fest (avoid Poya (full moon) whatever the cost) because there are so much people and the stairs at the end are so small that it could be a nightmare !! We did it on a Saturday, 4 days before Poya. So all the Sri Lanka's people where coming which is nice. We did sleep from 5PM to 10PM and go to climb the adam's peak to see the sunrise. But everybody is doing the same thing !!! So we climb 3 hours and then go to the line. The line seems infinite, it's like a psychological torture !! We did one step every 30 mins and wait. It was a nightmare !! We kept going for 6 hours and the summit were still far away. There were still something like 4 hours to wait so we decided when the sunrise arrived to stop the torture. Otherwise it's beautiful, the atmosphere is amazing. People are singing, motivating themselves. But I think if you are not buddhist and you go there on weekend or Poya you will never reach the top.

A painful 14km there and back with only stairs... Once at the top, you get to see the sunrise & the shadow of Adam's peak of you got up early enough. However, the little temple at the top is disappointing. It's very crowded. Though the view is nice, I would not necessarily recommend it unless you're looking for a small challenge. It took us (2 for adults) almost 3hrs to climb up with minimum rest stops.
Adam's peak is one of most sacred place for Sri Lankans. Specially by buddhists. It is a really a great experience to climb this for about 4-7 hours depending on the route you choose.

A very easy, mostly flat walk out to Adams Peak. There are lots of stairs towards the end and the opportunity to do some further exploring after the stairs. A beautiful walk with really fantastic views. The meander through the tea plantations is also very pleasant.

The amount of steps and the steepness of the steps in the last 1 km or so of the hike is an excellent workout for the body.  What make's it even tougher is doing the hike at 2am to see the sunrise.  If you attempt to this hike during the day, prepare for the hot sun and many, many people coming down.  Tip- do the hike for the sunrise, the views are amazing even if it's cloudy or misty. Pack warm as the top can get quite chilly.  Also, don't forget to bring bottles of water.  Another huge tip is to wear long pants and socks or you may find a large number of blood sucking leeches over your legs and feet. The hike is free.  Donations are optional. It's your choice what you want to give or not. Give the hike a go, it's well worth it!

The vast majority of Adam's Peak climbers ascend the mountain to worship the sacred foot at the summit. Depending on your religious background, the foot could belong to Lord Buddha, Lord Shiva, Adam or St. Thomas. However, if you are not religiously inclined and would rather hike to enjoy the breathtaking scenery and the isolation in the middle of nature my firm advise would be to travel during the off-season period. (The season runs from the December full moon day to the Wesak full moon day in May). The downside though is that during the off season the weather conditions can be challenging and the footprint area on the summit is closed. Also there are no shops every few meters during the off season and the paths are not lit up at night, so you would need to carry everything you need up the mountain. During the season, most people prefer to climb at night to avoid the day time heat and mostly to catch a glimpse of the sunrise. However, especially on weekends  you would need to jostle through hoards of crowds so my preference is to leisurely climb during the daylight hours while most of the crowds are descending. Okay, now a little more about Adam's Peak. Adam's Peak is the 5th tallest mountain in Sri Lanka from sea level but if you measure the total elevation gain from base to summit it is one of the tallest if not the tallest. There are a total of 6 routes to ascend the mountain of which the Hatton (Nallathanniya), Ratnapura (Palabaddale) and Kuruwita (Erathna) routes are the most famous. The Nallathanniya route is the shortest and the most popular despite the relatively sharp ascent (there is a closer route through the Murray estate called the Rajamale route but this involves climbing through a footpath in the wilderness). The climb from Nallathanniya starts by meandering through a tea estate and then enters the Adam's Peak forest reserve before starting the steep ascent to the summit. Some of the landmarks encountered on the way are the Makara Thorana (A  dragon arch at the entrance to the forest reserve), Japan Friendship Temple, Seetha Gangula (Translation: Cold Stream) where first time climbers have a bath before continuing the climb, Indikatupana where first timers unroll a ball of thread, Mahagiridamba where the steep climb on the summit rock begins and Ahas Gawwa where you have the most panoramic scenery, the steps are so steep at Ahas Gawwa that you have a floating sensation when turning back and enjoying the scenery. Finally some tips: Nallathanniya is a bustling mini town during the season and there are plenty of shops even on the mountain to get items such as water bottles, tea/coffee, light snacks, etc. During off season though, only a few shops are open at Nallathanniya and none are open on the mountain so make sure you get the essentials before starting the climb. While there are plenty of eateries in the town, I cannot vouch for cleanliness of the food. My advise would be to have meals at the B&B motels situated just before the town. Keep in mind that the mountain is considered sacred to many so respect local traditions when climbing. While not mandatory, it is advisable to be vegetarian at least for the duration of your climb out of respect to the beliefs of all who hold the mountain sacred. Unless you are very fit, Adam's Peak will test your endurance but it is totally achievable as long as you take it at your own pace and enjoy the climb. Of the thousands who climb the mountain daily, you will come across toddlers as well as 70-80 year olds, so if they can do it, there is no reason you cannot.

Bring a compass to find out which direction is East for watching the sunrise. Took us about 2.5 hours for the climb on a weekday. Bring a jumper as it gets cold waiting at the top. Definitely a must visit for every trip to Sri Lanka!

It took us (2 pp of 46yo,14yo and 12yo boys) about 3 hours to reach the peak. I found it much tougher than I expected with some of the stairs being really high. The ascent is hard but the descent is tough on your knees so people should be very aware of their physical condition. I could not give up when you look around and see local elders or adults carrying small children making the pilgrimage. Once at the top, I found the place extremelly crowded especially during the final 30 minutes leading up to the sunrise, however knowing what I know, I would still do it again for the experience. We all felt it was an unique and unforgetable experience and the challenge of the climb is probably a factor. The views are breath-taking. My leg muscles and bones hurt for 3 days afterwards and I needed iboprufen to ease the pain. The boys were totally fine tough.

This is religious place for Locals and great climbing experience for climbers. Season: December Poya to May Poya (but you can always climb any time of the year but you won't find any shops or much of the people and also wild animals and weather changes) Best time to visit: I recommend December (bit cold but less crowd) Avoid Poya and long weekends. Or you can visit during April new year times. Climb : there are few trails and most used one is Hatton, Nallathanniya Start climbing at the night time then you can see the sunrise and Climb lightly Shops: it get bit expensive it the top View: Sunrise and the view is amazing It's worth the effort

the hike is not difficult, but you do need a medium fitness level. The altitude increases quite fast in the second half of the hike, so you will get to feel it. you should have a hoodie or something to cover your ears and head, it can get windy. I was there during high season which means a lot of pilgrims, so at the top you can't really move anymore, the way is blocked. I could see some people getting stuck between the buildings and not beeing able to turn around and watch the sunrise. I left at around 1:30 and was lucky to be 1m away from the summit just in time for the sunrise, but stuck between people, I couldn't really move.

We had a beautiful walk up Adams peak. Unfortunately we didn't make it to the top as the queues were so long. We waited an hour before deciding to take in the sunrise view from a slightly lower point. I'd recommend to try going on weekdays when it may be less busy. The views going down after sunrise are beautiful and worth the hike. However the many many stalls along the way do take away from the natural beauty.

Bear in mind this is a tough walk. I mean, with thousands of steps, if you're not fit enough, you could fail to climb till the top. Enough said... the worst part is coming back down, tired, sweat, and with crunchy legs. I did it till the top, and the view at the sunrise is something that leaves you speechless. Good luck!

I recommend this walk/climb to people who truly love nature and beautiful sunrises. Besides this, there is nothing positive about visiting this site, First of all, the walk up is NO problem for anyone. When walking you will see people of all ages climbing up the trail. The beginning of the trail is very easy and simple, and the further you get the more steep the trail becomes. There are several places to stop on the way if one needs to rest, buy food/water or go to the toilet. Secondly, make sure to start walking at 2am - not because it actually takes time, but because otherwise you will end up being stuck in a long queue of locals trying to reach the top before sunrise. Hence, I cannot emphasize enough, make sure to start before 2am if you want to be sure to reach the top in time.

Definitely worth it!  It's a must trip on Sri Lanka for everyone. Quite tough hiking. The last 1/4 ist the most difficult. And the way down the stairs is tough as well. Climbing up is easy to compare with going down. Take enough water with you. If you are not use to hiking, it will take you approx 3 hours to get up and 2 hours to get down. Afterwards get some feet massage - it will help you to recover.

What an experience! I admit i did it in a good pace and without single stop. Witouth any particular preparation either. Therefore felt my legs still three days after ... But it's worth it, if you like climbing mountains, or climbing stairs ;-)

Wonderful adventure wonderful nature long way up and back, but worth evry moment of it. we climbed on friday. when we were close to the peak, there were a lot of local people that were on weekend vacation, so we stand at the same spot for a long time. wonderful sunrise wonderful viwes

We did the night climb of Adam's Peak. We are pretty fit but it is quite a climb. We did it in one go, taking just over 2 hours. It's pretty impressive seeing young children, pregnant ladies parents carrying young babies and very elderly ladies climbing up the endless steps. The top was pretty crowded so we decided not to wait for sunrise. The descent is pretty hard on your knees as it is steps all the way and it took a couple of days for us to fully recover. I'm not sure whether I would recommend it. I am glad I did it and I might regret being there and not doing it. However if you have to choose between walking up Adam's Peak and walking to World's End over Horton Plains I would recommend the latter.

We started to climb up early (at 2.30 am) to be at the top by sunrise. The first 30-40 minutes have been horrible, because it felt like there are only flashlights and people trying to sell nearly anything. We felt like being on a festival, but not a good one. After leaving all those shops behind it is ok, but sometimes very dark. Own flashlights highly recommend! Unfortunately we did not make it to the top because it was to crowded and after waiting for 1,5 hours at one spot without moving, we watched the sunrise from there and started going down by 7 am. I would recommend not to climb up at the weekend. Besides this the whole way was really dirty. Plastics everywhere and the smell was also horrible. Not a lot to do with an inspiration.

We hiked in the middle of working week, still at the top it was crowded! I would recomend to avoid any kind of hollidays or non working days. To see sunset on 2245m is woth it and would climb  it again for that stunning view. Prepare to climb aprox 5.500 stairs.

I went with trepidation after reviews being so mixed.  My husband and I are fit 45 year olds, but still found it strenuous.  It took us 2 hours to get to the top and I actually wished I'd slowed down a bit.  The problem was once I stopped it was hard to get going again!  The steps towards the top are very steep and really not advisable if you have any health problems.  We met a lady in her 50s who was less fit and she had really struggled doing it in 3 and a half.  Coming down was worse for me, as my knees hurt and legs started to shake.  Took us 1 hour 40 minutes to get down.  We had my very fit 9 year old with us who loved the experience and the challenge. It's a tricky one re the rubbish and sanitation.  This is not a tourist site, it is a pilgrimage, and the locals just don't have the same cultural feeling about litter.  I didn't find it particularly smelly, but the rubbish is strewn along the sides of the path.  All you have to do is look in most hedgerows in Sri Lanka and you will find just the same though. I loved the fact it wasn't for the tourists and on a Sunday night (definitely quieter) a good 95% were Sri Lankan pilgrims.  To see families with grannies, babies and lots of children was lovely and at times they chanted songs to rally them along. I didn't go with high expectation re temple at the top as this is for the pilgrims.  It means an enormous amount to them, but was just an ordinary temple to us.  But that's not the point- it isn't for us! Saying that everyone was really friendly, with lots of smiles and good mornings.  We felt welcomed to join them on this important walk, and to watch the amazing sunset at the top.  As other reviewers said top tip is to see the temple quickly before dawn and  then head 50 yards down past the crowds to watch a beautiful view. We had a guide with us, which of course wasn't necessary but we found informative and helpful.  We got there early and spent a fun couple of hours watching the locals come and go in a little shack before the last bit of the climb.  This was a great idea as out of the very chilly wind.  Again everyone was friendly and we encountered backpackers, Sri Lankan families and the odd tourist all on the same slightly bonkers, but unforgettable journey.  I'm writing this two hours later, still buzzing from the experience.  Go with the right expectations and feeling privileged to join the pilgrims and you will love it.

The climb is hard but the views are well worth the aches going up, jelly legs on the descent and sore calves for two days! I recommend heading off at around 2am and taking it slow and easy up the peak! Take layers as it gets rather cool towards the top.
It's no walk in the park, but it's worth the trek! Get some sleep though cuz if you want  o see sunrise, you gotta start at 2:00 am.

We decided to climb to Adams Peak after being told by many how beautiful it was.  It's true that the view from the top was beautiful, but was it worth the climb?  I certainly wouldn't do it again.  Firstly you need to be really fit.  Some reviews state they made it up in two hours, they must be uber fit.  My husband and I aged between 52 and 61 we are of medium fitness for our age,  took us 4 and half hours!  On the way up, it's very crowded, loads of locals as this is a pilgrimage for them.   We climbed up during the night, started at 2am to get there for sunrise, very busy with people, young, old and some tourists.    It's also filthy, loads of rubbish and plastic all over the place which was really disappointing as this is a world heritage site.  When we got to the top it wasn't idyllic as we expected to be in our naivety but so crowded you could hardly enjoy being up there.  Coming back down took around 3 hours but we did stop to rest a couple of times and younger people seemed to be moving a lot faster, I guess you could make it down in a couple hours if you're young and fit.  Our legs hurt for 3 days after! So if you're only staying in Sri Lanka for a short time and doing other things take that into account.  We met another couple who were roughly our age and their experience was similar.  Also, toilets are disgusting and very dirty on the way, but beggars can't be choosers!! If you're going to go, wear layers as its cold during the night but as you walk up you do get quite hot, once the sun comes up it just gets hotter and hotter.

We were really excited about this, as we love climbing mountains. We thought it would be a romantic experience looking at the stars and watching the sunset. It wasn't!! It is like climbing through garbage with a lot of ugly shops on your left and right. The stairs are made of beton and are us ugly as hell! Spare yourself the misery! Also 300 m from the top everything was jammed so we turned around. Best idea we had. We saw the sunrise from the steps.

We wanted to climb Adams Peak because we had heard so much about it. It is a pilgrimage for the Buddhists of Sri Lanka. For tourists, it is an opportunity  to rub shoulders with this culture.  We were amazed & inspired to see people walking barefoot, fathers carrying babies, mothers breast-feeding on the stairs, grammas & grandpas (who were not in the best of shape!) and then there were the "sherpas". These men were carrying supplies up Adams Peak, on their heads... propane bottles, boxes of stuff and they looked heavy! We started at !:30 am , had a few stops on the way(including a lovely tea), as it is over 5,000 steps and some are extremely steep!  At the top, as stated by others, it was very crowded, so much so, that we opted to go down about 30 metres and watch the sunrise from there. It was definitely well worth the trip! That being said, it would be nice to find another venue to climb and leave Adams Peak to the Sri Lankans to whom it means so much.

A wholly missable experience - essentially a set of steps to a view point. Overcrowded and tacky. It took us 1hour 45 to get to the top as reasonably fit individuals, don't believe the 4 hour Lonely Planet hype. We passed locals in their 80s/90s doing this walk in bare feet... The top was overcrowded and at sunrise, it was almost impossible to get a photograph due to the amount of tourists, selfie sticks, cameras etc. I would recommend stopping just before the 'last 100m sign' and taking photos from there. The sunrise is impressive but unless you're absolutely desperate to see the 'shadow effect' t's really not worth the effort. This takes up 2 days of your holiday as it's a long way on the train/bus. Go to Ella and enjoy Little Adam's Peak/Ella's rock instead.
All together, I'm not sure I would hike Adam's Peak again because of the circumstances
There was garbage everywhere and small shops on both sides of the path almost until the top. I didn't feel comfortable and would no go again. Sunrise was nice thoughp

Climb is approximately 1000 vert metres, took us 2.5hours to climb at a reasonable pace around midnight on a Sunday night.  The temperature was warm and sticky - we climbed in tee shirts.  The queue up the last hundred metres was pretty tedious, and we reached the top around 2:30am.  It was very crowded, dirty and is pretty small, and we didn't fancy waiting for dawn so headed back down again.  Didn't particularly feel like a big bang for the buck.

Adam's peak should be on everyone's bucket list! It was my third time climbing and it was fantastic. Though for most Sri Lankans the climb is purely religious, it was not so for me. I climbed for the view and the challenge of it. Take with you; 1. A torch and extra batteries. the path is lit up during the season (full moon in december to full moon in april) but there are power cuts sometimes and a torch will be a life saver if you are not travelling with a big group. 2. Some salt water or jeevani, a drink you can buy locally if you are prone to cramping. I got some awful cramps at the last stretch called 'mahagiridambe' which is very narrow and doesn't give much space to sit or rest and I had to keep moving so as  not to block the crowds. 3. Something warm to wear up top if you plan to stay and watch the sunrise. It gets quite chilly. A change of clothes are also highly recommended as it gets quite sweaty doing that climb and it is nice to change into fresh clothes once you get to the top. Also, 4. Make the trip on a weekday. friday nights and saturday nights are the worst. Really. You do not want to climb on these days as it gets jam packed. 5. The climb officially takes 3 - 3.5 hours though mine took much longer as i didn't climb continuously (i need to work on my cardio)  my climb took 5.5 hours as we stopped midway and took a few breaks. So plan accordingly if you want to catch the sunrise. There are plenty of little kiosks on the road where they serve hot tea and coffee and also dinner if you feel hungry. Though a heavy diet is not recommended! 6. There are two routes to Adam's peak, we took the route through Nallathanniya, Hatton. I hear the Ratnapura route is very scenic so hopefully another review on that soon. 7. Plenty of small inns and motels in and around Nallathanniya which offer basic facilities.

We made the visit to Adams Peak last night. The overall view and sunrise at daybreak was pretty spectacular, but it was a hell of an ordeal getting to that bit. We stayed in Hatton, which as far as I know, is the closest railway town. It has to go down as one of the worst places I've ever been! There is literally nothing for tourists- no decent restaurants, nothing! Unless you like fried rice, or cold pre cooked samosas which have been sat in a display cabinet since morning! So, I'd say to only use Hatton as a base for getting to Adams Peak- although there are towns closer- I keep reading about Delhousie or Dalhousie, but whenever I do a Map search, it brings up somewhere in India, and nowhere in Sri Lanka. Anyway, we got a tuktuk to Adams Peak, which took about 1.5 hours. We found a great local guy called Peter, who spoke good English, and offered us a very reasonable price! His phone number is (072) 358 503 There were loads of people climbing the hill, even though we purposely went on Sunday night/Monday morning, away from the crazy weekend rush. I assumed there would be a decent view from the top, like a flat area you can sit and watch the sunrise, but there wasn't. There is a small, stepped concrete viewing area, but there were so many people, all crammed into all available space- as well as filling up the entire stairway at the top, that it was impossible to watch from there. We continued climbing to the highest point (in the temple) but it's so crowded, and you are surrounded by big brass railings which spoil any view- as well as the fact you can't see down into the valleys, as they are obscured by buildings.
