We had to climb back down a few 100 metres to where the crowds wernt so thick, to be able to view the magnificent scenery. It was pretty cold at the top- and due to the 3 hours of workout getting there, your clothes, wet from sweat, make you even colder. Be warned, the cost of food, drinks etc is higher, but you can't complain, as some poor guys have to lug all the supplies up there! Coming down took ages, with so many people en masse, flocking to the exit. Stomping down all of those 5000 steps really takes it out of your knees! All in all, it was spectacular, but when I weigh it up, all pros and cons considered, I actually preferred watching Sunset at Little Adam's Peak in Ella.

We visited Adam's Peak March 2016. Started our climbing on 02:15 am and had lots of time to have breaks. Try the Sri Lankan tee with milk and sugar on your way up. It's delicious. Also keep in mind that during poya (full moon) there's lots of crowds there so locals don't recommend to visit there then. Tip: try to be on the top at least 30mins before sunrise, otherwise it can be so crowded that you won't make there. We took a train to Hatton and from there Bus to Dalhousie. Local transportation is very cheap and works well (although they don't always follow schedule). Bus journey is through very beautiful scenery but drivers also drive really fast in the mountains so there's a little scare factor on that. Tip: go early for the bus and hop on from where they start, they tend to get crowded (we saw several tourists waving for bus and it didn't stop).
It takes 7-8 hours up and down to climb - almost all of it on stairs! It was cold at the top and the sunset - although nice - wasn't that spectacular

Whilst quite challenging, the most challenging experiences are always the most rewarding. Be sure to make the trek before the sun rises, as it is extremely hot when climbing. It can be quite busy in April, so make sure you do the best to reach the top as early as you can, this will ensure you have the best area. It can be quite cool while you wait for the sun to rise, but when it does it gets hot real quick.
unbelievable beautiful and inspiring walk. requires some breaks because its really steep. bring a lot of warm cloth for the top

My partner and I have only an average fitness level however couldn't resist setting off at 2am to hike up the mountain to watch the sunrise. There are so many steps and it was pretty exhausting, the hike included a number of quick stops to catch our breathe. We had two minor stops for a tea from one of the hits on the way up, don't carry a lot of food and water as you can get it all the way up through the night/day. We arrived at 5:15 and got a fairly good seat, there were already a number of locals there with the best viewpoint. After sitting down for 10 minutes to wait for the sunrise it did become quite cold so you need a good jumper and scarf or coat. The sunrise was phenomenal and we even caught the triangle shadow on the other side that only appeared for a couple of minutes. The day after our legs aches so much but it was so worth it. It was around 3 hours up and 1.5 down. Loved it!

We walked up Adam's Peak in about 2 hours (we kept quite a fast pace) and although it was not a public holiday etc, the top of the mountain was quite congested and we took a little while to get into the temple area. We managed to see the sunrise but it was a very packed space and the walk back down took a while to break through the throngs. We had a reasonable day - it was cloudy/foggy but we still saw the sunrise and were able to see the shadow of the peak on the west side which was magnificent. I enjoyed the walk, although it is quite challenging but I would be mindful of coming on a religious day as it will be difficult to move on the steps with so many people.

It took us about 2,25 hours to climb if we look away from breaks. The breaks was not that necessary but we had good time as we started 02.15 in the night. It is recommended to sit in the warm in the last tea tent, if you arrive early! We only brought one extra shirt and 1,5 L water for two persons. It was a good hike and not to strenious.

Adam's peak is a place which every Buddhist wants to go at least once in their lifetime as we believe it holds Lord Budda's sacred footprint left behind when Buddha visited Sri Lanka, at the invitation of Buddhist God Saman. So for us it is a pilgrimage rather than a hike/trip. We have inherited culture with it where some will be vegetarian, no smoking and no alcohol before going this pilgrim. People will bless each other while walking with nice verses. First time travelers have some special rituals to do as bringing a needle and thread and keep it in Idikatupana.(you will see this place with lots of white threads)There are lots of people come there with their with families and some even climb with bare foot.Some has even climbed this 20-30 times to invoke blessings. Very old people climb which is so astonishing to see their courage and strength. All we have is belief and trust upon this sacred place. The pilgrimage season begins on poya day in December and runs until Vesak festival in May poya day. If you want to skip the crowd better to avoid Sri Lankan holidays and weekend because it may frustrating to wait hours to climb few steps. We climbed there from Hatton side which is more shorter in length(6km with 5000 steps) and in the season path is well lighted. Food, snacks and water is available through out the journey. Toilets are also there but very unclean and some even without lights. For us it took like 8 hours as we rested in lots of places.But tourists are climbing it more faster. There is a place to sleep on top inside but it may be very crowded so lots of people are waiting outside in freezing cold.So better to bring sweaters,caps to cover your ears.In morning 6 am like you can view the morning sunshine which is breath taking.But the place is so crowded and people push each other. So for a tourist I cannot 100% recommend this place as they are only going this place to see the sun rise.(in cloudy days you won't see it) Definitely your legs will hurt for at least one day so you have to rest. I saw an mid aged tourist who were very painfully climbing which makes me sad because in Sri Lanka it has lots of other places to spend your vacations. If you go there please don't put garbage, pay any disrespect for this sacred place and if possible donate some money to the temple on the top to cover up maintenance cost.

Adam's Peak is probably the most popular tourist destination on the island. It's a 'must'. I've read and heard stories about the unforgettable view and the demanding yet rewarding climb. The reality? Oh boy... First of all, I was there in Februrary which somehow meant that the number of people doing the trip was overwhelming. But we climbed the stairs, passing shop after shop, endless lines of people and so much trash I couldn't believe it. There were toilets along the way but I guess tehre weren't very popular, because the smell that was accompanying us all the way made it clear that people went anywhere and anytime they wanted. The last two hours we spent in a line, waiting for our chance to go to the top. We were lucky, I guess. We got there 5 minutes before sunrise. But it meant nothing, since the peak is a small 'cage' packed with people, pushing one another. You can barely see anything, but what you see is not that astonishing. Don't get me wrong, it's a pretty view, but I'm sure you can find a lot of nicer places in the area to climb or visit at that time of day and have a much better view and experience. Then you have to go down, which was even more frustrating. Don't even think about stopping and enjoying what you see, people behind you won't let you. I don't know, maybe it's different in other months, but for us it was the worst experience of our tour. There were so many other places we could have gone to, but it was Adam's Peak, we felt obligated to go. Now we know better :)

We started at 1am and got to the top at about 4am. The sun started to rise at about 5am and it was amazing. We went with a guide but that's probably not essential if you're looking to save money. With our guide we got to see a tiger in the valley in the dark which was one of the best experiences of our lives. I wore shorts and my knees seized up after walking and then cooling so I'd recommend taking some trousers. It's a pretty tough walk at times but it was easily one of the highlights of the whole trip to Sri Lanka
a thrilling experience. FYI, you have to wake up at 1am if you want to be up to the peak on time for the sunrise. but what a view, what a feeling to see the famous shadow over the tea plantations.
Wonderful mountain, too many humans. i.e. hiking up in rubbish in a crowd, smells like the urinals all along the way

Adam's peak or as locals call it Sri Pada is truly amazing. Just be prepared for second half of going there because it is pretty difficult, so save your breath, bring enough of water and watch your tempo. When you enter temple at the top you need to take your shoes of, so be prepared for that. Also it's a bit windy and cold up there. Remember after all this you will be rewarded by beautiful sunrise. And if you need to go from Adam's peak from Hatton call this number: 077 909 3103. It's a tuk tuk driver who speaks English very good, is very nice and shows you great views along the way for the best price you can get.
A long hike up the mountain but so worth it. The most amazing sunrise you could ever experience. Very crowded though.

Our trip experience: When we have started with my husband, after 10 min we were already like breathing hard, and on that point I realized that I might not have enough strength to reach the top which was like another 4,5 km and from down the top looks so far away!!! I don't do much sports and was not prepared physically at all, so I would recommend to everyone to do a very good stretching. I did not do that, and for next 3 days my legs were having a very bad pain. On the beginning of your journey you will see laying Budda statue, and your long journey here is called "holy way", most of locals who climb this mountain, are not eating meat and do not drink alcohol for 3 days before the climb and for another 3 days after that. On our way, we saw small children and parents holding their toddlers and already going down from the top, it's motivating and inspiring, same as people who actually having only one leg and still climbing, a dog, who had an injured leg and still was running all the way up with us, maybe half of all people were walking barefoot, so I was telling myself shut up and don't complain, keep walking :))) There are places to rest and have some water or tea, and something to chew. About crowd, there were many nationalities, Germans, French, Russians, some Japanese and most of Sri Lankan people of course. Everybody looks different, some Buddhists, wearing orange dressings, some people with crazy hairstyle, others were caring bags like bigger size than themselves (still wondering what did they need to carry) Everybody is friendly and laughing, smiling and it does makes it feel nice on your long way to the top. We have started our journey at 2:10 in the morning and reached just before sunrise,  it was a last resting point and it was like 5:20 we reached it, so as per people (who work in resting places), we had another hour before sunrise ( but still DO reach it earlier) so we had a warm tea (from a glass cup, impressive, I have expected a plastic cup) and walked last hundred metres. Another 10 min, and we could see the beautiful sky with sunrise (that's why I recommend to come up earlier than official sunrise timing) The view was just fantastic, what you see is unbelievable, when you are standing higher than the clouds, and the sky is having these amazing colours. In about 15 more minutes the sky got too foggy and cloudy and there were no view anymore, so we were lucky to take some great photos before it happened. Some people were late for that. Feel sorry for them. About the weather, I am Ukrainian, my husband is Maldivian, as per comments of many people " it will be really cold" it was not cold at all, you will be sweating like crazy and especially on the way back. I was wearing jeans, a shirt, and a sweater + jacket. It was too much clothes, no need a sweater. On the top it was not that cold at all, no need gloves really, same from my husband, it was not THAT cold. What is actually on the top? It's a temple, where people have to stay barefoot and to pray or meditate or what ever you do in your own religion. We witnessed a budism ceremony there. It was lovely. There is a big bell there too, you can ring it, well you deserve it after all!!! So what is this mountain is about, it's a holy place counted as a first place where Adam and Eve stood up when they had to leave the Garden of Eden. There is actually a huge foot print on the top, but it's in the temple which is open like on very special occasions. (we did not see it) Some people have other believes about that foot print. Buddists believe that the footprint belongs to Budda, but why do they all call it ADAM'S Peak than?))) Some people went down after it became foggy, we waited for a while, to have more space, to take some more pictures. Way down takes about 1 hour 30 maybe bit less, we did not take breaks, maybe one was there for few min to buy some juice. Actually did not feel sleepy at all after climbing back down. When to climb Since we were staying in "Grand Adams Peak"  hotel, in hundred meters away from the mountain for 6 days, and we climbed on our 5th day there, we could see people climbing every day, and could watch different weather on the mountain, as it's just in front of our balcony. Better not to go on Friday and Saturday. It was a national Sri Lankan independence day by the way. It was like overcrowded! We climbed on Sunday and it was many people still, so I can't imagine how many it was on Friday and Saturday. Busses with people were coming non stop. What to take with you? - Well, we took 2 raincoats, which we never used. (depends on weather) - Shoes have to be sporty and cozy. - Food (we did not take any and had a healthy breakfast once reached back) - Water yes!!! We had 5 bottles of water, but you can buy it on rest places on the mountain. - Hygienic antibacterial tissues, as you hands will be dirty, face sweaty and you will be happy to feel a normal clean human being. - Toilets are there on the way every 20 min. Charge is 20 rupees. Happy that I did not have to go at any of those during ways up and down. As per my husband it was a disaster. (lol) - Take some cookies to feed dogs on the way, be kind. They are very friendly. I personally admire that fact that many people gather together to climb, respecting the nature, smiling, happy, and having good intentions and dreams, whenever great people like that meet in one place, it makes it already special. True religion is all about having good heart. How to reach Hatton ( we went from Colombo by train around 5-6 hours, and after 1 hour by tuk tuk) if you are used to more luxury travelling, go by van) To buy tickets you can directly at train station. The price is less than usd 10 per person, we took a cab/room for only 2 of us. We went back to Colombo by van (usd 60) and we saw few waterfall on the way.

The sunrise treks/visits were never really my thing - usually crowded with tourists taking selfies, with mediocre views - all different than Adam's peak. It is crowded, sure, but with locals, who treat it rather like pilginage than a trip. The actual buddhist ceremony takes place there, which makes the whole experience real and magical, and it is quite a hike up there, so not everybody decides to go there - good for the ones who do! Practical staff - 3-3,5 hours is definitely enough to get to the top, no need to leave your hotel at 1am. The stairs are lamplit, so no need for the flashlight, huge need for warm clothes though (may be bought in the village) as it gets really, really cold at the top! Your knees will hurt like hell after going down (strech!) but it's definitely worth the effort - the views are stunning. Whole the area is, so if you have time -wander a bit longer in the sourrounding villages!

My girlfriend and I were set to climb Adam's Peak during the January Full Moon. We were told that it would be fine for full moon (Poya) to climb up, however after catching the train from Kandy to Hatton was jam packed. At Hatton we'd spoken to a few people who'd climbed on the Friday full moon and said they didn't make it to the top due to crowds. When we arrived at Dalhousie it was super busy so we decided to wait one night and climb it on the Sunday night / Monday morning. Many of the people we saw who climbed on the Saturday full moon also didn't reach the top and stoop waiting in line for 3 hours before giving up and heading back down. We left at 1am and made a steady pace up the mountain, resting regularly and drinking plenty. We arrived at the top 4am to a fairly busy top. It got fairly cold at he top too despite a very hot a sticky 3 hour climb. Make sure you take some warm clothes. Your sweat cools down very quickly. We waited on the large steps like everyone else looking east for sunrise. Sunrise was spectacular but there were a few cables and bright lights in the way which obstructed the view. It was also very busy. The best view was on the steps leading back down to Dalhousie - that's were I would watch sunrise from if I did it again. The descent was the toughest part. Keep a steady pace to go easier on your knees. But leave quickly to avoid the crowds and the heat as it gets hot quickly.. It was amazing and well worth doing. And I would definitely suggest waiting till after full moon.

My son talked me into this over-night hike! We left the base at 1am and arrived at the peak about 4am.  It's well lit--sidewalks and stairs, a pretty steep climb towards the top. (7500 feet).  Mostly locals, but some foreigners, make this pilgrimage to the top of the mountain where Buddha supposedly stepped down from the heavens.  Or Adam. Take your pick of religion.  The sunrise is fantastic, it was a very beautiful experience.

I decided to hike Adam's Peak to cleanse my seemed-to-be lost soul. I was solo, i decided not to hire a guide and did on off peak season which was a good decision. I could stop and rest whenever I want to. It took me 8 hours all in all. I started 1:45 AM and was able to reach the peak at 5:30, 15 minutes before the sunrise. The sunrise was amazing! And views going down are all worth the leech that went to my tummy (yes, leeches everywhere, SO BRING A BANDAGE JUST IN CASE), and body ache!

This was very tough as we had just hiked up lions rock the day before! It was helped by stopping off for tea as we climbed. The one thing I didn't realise is the whole way up there are steps, and lights so you don't need a torch. Once we climbed to the top it was cold so take a jumper and take your time getting there- once we reached the crowd was huge and we could not get through so we stayed at the front to catch sunrise... Which is stunning! The walk back down will turn your legs to jelly but it's much quicker than the way up! One thing I would say is people tend to stand at the entrance to get the best picture.

Adam's Peak/Sri Pada is incredibly important to the Sri Lankans, but as a tourist I wouldn't do it again.  Here's why: 1. For us, it was not a spiritual experience.  I certainly wasn't expecting it to mean the same thing to me that it does to the Sinhalese, but I definitely had a different picture in my mind of "climbing through the night alongside pilgrims, under the stars", as I read somewhere.  The temple at the top isn't very big, and there was a lot of pushing to get to see the actual "footprint", which in reality is a super decorated altar like you see in a lot of other places.  And the pushing, really...it's not like you get a chance to stop and soak in ambiance or anything. 2. The climb is very strenuous, but it's also completely on irregularly sized cement steps.  In some places it's both steep and twisty, so difficult to keep your balance as well.  We started early and it was still very crowded, but I know that if we had started later, the last sections would have been absolutely packed with people pushing. Definitely skip it if you have joint issues...I'm young and active, and my knees were still killing me for days afterwards (not to mention my muscles!).  And since my knees were hurting, I found coming back down just as bad as the climb up.  Seems like it will never end... 3.  There are lots of beautiful views in Sri Lanka, so the view alone isn't enough reason to do it.  Sunrise might be gorgeous, or it might just be meh.  And if you spare your muscles/joints this climb, you'll be more able to do some of the others. If you want to do the climb, I'd definitely suggest considering a daytime/sunset climb instead of the through-the-night sunrise.  Crowds will be better, and you won't slow yourself down by skipping a night's sleep like we did.  But really.....just skip it.

We had gone there reading the review and following the reviews of our tour guide who had climbed 14 times. But however our timing wasnt right which made it the worst decision of our trip. it is a max 2.5 hour up and down the mountain, however it took us 12 hours as it was new year time at Srilanka and people of all ages went there to worship, which made it really crowded. Stairs got steeper and the way up was scarier, however the way down way very dangerous. However the Sunrise, the purpose, happened on the way up & it was beautiful. Possibly worth the 12 hours but not worth costing the trip. Note: Do take along heat sprays and gel if you are not working out.
Climbing this mountain is a great challenge, for people who are not to experienced with climbing like me. Beautiful scenery, and amazing sunrise!

I took 11am Hatton train from Kandy and reached there by 2pm. Connecting bus is there which takes an hour to an hour ten minutes journey to the foot of Adam's peak. Had my lunch from there for 130/- SLR (Rice meal with egg and yogurt) and started my hiking at 4pm. But by the time I think the first police control room, (1 km hike) I was exhausted with 10kg backpack. Total trip is a 6km hike where the last three km are more steeper. While starting my journey somebody suggested me to buy a sweet candy roll made of rice floor and jaggery... That helped me a lot. An 1 inch bite gave me enough energy with in 5 minutes sufficient to hike for 10 min. That was wonderful. Finally I could finish my up journey in  three hours and down journey in one and half hour. The last bus to Hatton leaves by  9:30pm. But some local students from there gave me lift to Hatton in their car. I missed the sun rise view. That I will try next time. After 4 and half km hike, you will be hiking through clouds. So you may need thermals. At the peak, there was full chilling cold wind... Some times you may need some support to walk steadily. There was no entry fee in the temple. It is a strict rule that you must pay homage to the god of you enter the temple. There is a huge Bell at one corner of the temple. February March is the season for pilgrims. So locals are arranging new shops and sitting places on either side of the path. The route is well light... There are toilets for every half km. Drinking water tanks are also arranged. But they were empty. So you may need to carry water. Hike time is 2 hrs quickest. 3 hrs moderate. 4-6 hrs with with kids. Usually people go for sun rise view starting at 2am. Temple closes at 9pm. Opens at 6 or 7am. Toys are being sold on either side of the hike.  But prices are a bit high. There are no high temperatures but sun tanning is there. So one may need sun screen lotions...  In rainy seasons it may not be opened for visitors due to slippery steps.

Long journey up, which personally I did not mind. The sweat and tears were worth it once I’ve seen the Sun rise above the clouds. Amazing experience as we got to witness a Buddhist Women pilgrimage on our way up. It is not an easy climb. Not for people who are out of shape and most definitely not for those who have previous issues with knees ( old injuries become new injuries very quickly). It is the climb down that puts a lot of pressure on the knees and ankles. Despite being in quite a good shape I thought I will not make it down purely due to my knees hurting so badly. Worth doing but for me I shall not brave it again  

My cousins and I have been planning on this hike for well over 2 years now since its a popular local attraction. As you all know Adams Peak (or Sripadha in Sinhalese) is a religious pilgrimage common to many faiths due to the many myths associated with the footprint at the summit. Due to this during the peak season there could be massive crowds taking part in the hike so a little bit of standing in line is expected. Since we left to Adams Peak from Kandy it took us around 2 hours to get there and another 3.5-4 hours to get up to the summit. Along the way you are constantly reminded that it's an arduous task and not an easy one, but you know how they say ''no pain no gain?'' that's exactly what it is! But more on that later. Since I was a first timer (or Kodukaraya in Sinhalese) I was entitled to take part in an ongoing tradition where I was to make an offering of a needle and thread. Even though I'm not aware of how the tradition first took place and why it is done, I took part in them with full enthusiasm. After all its little things like this that make hikes like this interesting and special. Little by little, one cup of coffee at a time we reached the summit where the view was mesmerizing. Jaw dropping even. You are instantly reminded that you are 7,359ft above sea level when you see the clouds below you. All your senses awaken once you smell the burning oil lamps, hear the ringing of bells and the humble prayers of the pilgrims, taste the frosty air and see that surreal view. It is then that it hit me, all that I went through while on the hike up to the summit was well worth it. Things to bring, -A well insulated jacket and long pants. -A beanie or a hat to cover up your ears. -A camera and maybe a pair of binoculars. -WATER! (It could be very humid).

It is long way up and maybe even longer way down, but you can really nicely test what your body can handle. The views are really nice, unfortunately the weakest point of the whole journey is the top - it just does not look nice - buildings are covering the view. I thing it is maybe better for the locals. btw we did Little Adams Peak the next day and views were maybe better - but it depends on weather ;)

Here is where you will witness the true strength of the mind body and spirit. All ages from all around come to do this climb whether it be for religious reasons or your own personal achievements it is worth the push. There were even a couple of one legged beggars half way up the peak. There are plenty of food and drink stalls along the way so you can take your time. As a couple in our prime we still struggled, mainly at the beginning of the climb, where the steps were much bigger and having only just woke up from half a nights sleep. By halfway the steps got smaller and handrails were available, also getting caught behind slower climbers made it a little easier. We started the climb at around 1.45am and got stuck in a queue about 200 steps from the top at around 5am. This was peak season on a Monday morning. It was much colder at the top and standing in a queue made it worse. I recommend a hat and gloves for sure. The top was a little overcrowded but is monitored by the police. As a religious peak you are asked to remove shoes and headgear whilst viewing the footprint. The Stars were a highlight and the sunrise was beautiful to watch as we descended.

We left at 2:30 am and reached the summit by around 5-5:30. I'm not in great shape but managed it fine. First hour is through shops and is mildly hilly, then the steps begin. Buy drinks or snacks lower down as they get more expensive as you climb. Many people wear gloves as the metal railing can be quite cold to grip. When we almost reached the summit, a friendly police officer took us aside and warned us to put our bags on our fronts and to be careful as the site would soon become crowded and dangerous. We then walked the last few staircases to the top, where we found it was indeed packed with pilgrims and a few tourists. We decided to rest for 10 mins and then start the descent, as we could see the view on the way down anyway. The way down was (for me) much more challenging as my legs had turned to jello. It took around 2 hours in total. We left our hostel (Grand Adam's Peak) at 2:30 and returned by 8 am. It was mentally and physically very demanding for me (my partner wasn't too bothered as he is in better shape than I am) but you are driven by seeing all the old ladies persevering and the people carrying their children up the mountain. It's definitely a worthwhile experience and one of the highlights of the trip.

It's about a 3 hour hike up. But during peak season and poya weekend it will take you over 12 hours. Very unorganized. Lots of fights, yelling, and pushing. Who wants to stand in a queue for 9 hours freezing their butt off. Views are amazing yes, but no better then climbing any other mountain. Do yourself a favor and skip this.

I can't express how great of a hike this was. Leaving at 2am (1:30 if you are slow, 2:30 if you are fast) for a 6am sunrise was an amazing experience. If you walk very fast you can get up in 2 hours, but most people take closer to 3 or 4. It's 2.2k vertical along the 7k path. The path is well lit and paved, with small stops every 20 minutes selling fresh roti and bananas. There will be hundreds of others walking up with you including family bringing their children to pray, so you have nothing to worry about except pick pocketers (especially at the top). Getting there for sunrise (or I imagine sunset) was truly an amazing experience. Locals and tourists alike stand there just watching, taking it in. Even though it was cloudy, the sunrise above them with the ringing bells from the monastery is unforgettable. Wear long pants and bring a jacket – the top is cold as you wait. Oh and the surrounding area is picturesque too.

Adam's footprint at the top of the mountain. Never underestimate the climb and the mountain can be brutal if you are not prepared well enough for the journey. Make sure you are physically fit and take a light jumper to wear when you are reaching the top. Make sure you are not scared of heights. Lots of walking to do around 10,000 steps up and down (apart from the walking) Make sure you are used to climbing stairs and walking for long periods or your feet would just give up. Carry a small water bottle or some cash. Water and other supplies are available at the shops through out the clim but gets expensive when going up. Max 100/= local money for a small bottle at the top. Best time is to go early in the morning 2-3am in time to catch the sunrise. Then start the journey down the mountain. All in all great experience and everyone should have done it at least once in a life time. But only once is enough :).

Trekking up Adams Peak is not for the faint hearted!  The steps are deep, so if you have little legs this makes it all the more difficult.  Take plenty of clothes to put on as you get quite sweaty whilst climbing and then when you are queuing you get very chilly.  I wouldn't climb on a weekend day in the season as the crowds are nothing like we've ever seen before and the pushing, elbowing and close quarters are a little off putting.  Sadly we just didn't make it to the top due to crowds but we waited for the sun to come over the mountain and the views are spectacular!

This is also known as Samanala kanda/butterfly mountain.This can be reached via Hatton or Rathnapura.If you,re going via hatton you can reach this place by bus or train too.But Rathnapura Kuruvita road you have to go buy bus or own vehicles.My first experience was via Hatton.From Hatton you need to go by a bus to Nallathanniya.it was nearly half an hour.Its better if you can rest in Nallathanniya before climbing.We started climbing around 12 mid night.We had 6 first timers and we manged to reach the top by 5.30am which is the ideal time if you are interested in watching the sunrise.we started descending with the day light for an amazing view.And we came back around 10.30am.On the way back we went to the siddhalepa spa to get our body relaxed.they did a good job.Foot massage costs rs.450 per head.Since it was the season we found small shops everywhere to have snacks ,hot and cold drinks.the season starts from December Poya day and continues till Poya day of May.If you're travelling in off season you wont be able to find any shops.So you will have to carry everything by yourself.And it's important to make your back pack light which will make you easy to climb.Meantime you need to have your ears and neck properly covered and a sweater to keep you warm on the top.This is what i collected from my first visit.

This was one of my favourite place/things to do whilst in Sri Lanka, although my calves did hurt for 3 days afterwards!! Ouch! The climb is fine - all paved steps and hand rails where the steps get vertical. We set off at 2:30am and made to the top about an hour before first light and then sunrise 20 mins later. We didn't really stop for tea or a break, which in hindsight might have been better (or setting off at 3am) as it gets very cold and windy at the top in the dark. Highly recommend it - the views are amazing

Really nice hike over the night (not easy! But if you take your time it is normally fine). Took us about 3 hours from the very start of the Peak to the top. No need to carry a lot of water with you since it is possible to buy some on the way (prices are increasing at the same time as you are going up). The top is a bit crowded, especially when the sun rises, but we could still reach it. Important to stretch your body when you reach the top as well as when you get down. Do not forget a jacket to protect yourself against the wind as it might be cold at the top and it might be helpful to have another t-shirt to wear after sweating during the hike. The view above the clouds is amazing and it absolutely worth it in my opinion. Do not plan too much the next day(s) :)

Adam’s Peak in English, but ‘Sri Pada’ popularly known in Sinhalese in Sri Lanka is the most sacred mountain among the Buddhists in Sri Lanka. According to popular belief, Lord Buddha has once visited the top of this mountain and planted a holly footprint (Sri Pada) there in response to an invitation made by the god Sumana Saman (the regional god of the Samanala mountain range). Today, more than a million Sri Lankan Buddhists visit this location for blessings during the pilgrim season falling from December to May. Apart from being a pilgrim destination for Buddhists, it’s a major attraction among foreign tourists to the country. As a Buddhist, climbing Sri Pada involves a lot of cultural and religious rituals which are worth studying in detail. It’s not a matter of how scientific these beliefs are, but we have to value those traditions as historic and cultural heritage of Sri Lanka. For me, it was more about the climb! Yes, I respect the religious value of the Sri Pada, but I climbed the mountain for the sole experience of the beautiful trail to the top. If you are planning to visit this attraction, make sure to choose February of March. This is the season when it is least predicted for rain. And start the climb after 6.00pm. Route from Hatton-Nallathandi is well lit up and you would be able to find the trail without any difficulty. There are many other pilgrims who would support you whenever you need help, and there are plenty of small boutiques for small grocery items and short food. We started the climb at 1am and managed to get to the top by the dawn, just in time to catch the Sunrise from the top. Be mindful not to pollute the area with plastic bags and bottles. Travel with minimum baggage, and make sure to bring back literally everything you take up, without becoming a burden to the Mother Nature.

I thoroughly loved Adams Peak. The surrounding villages are stunning, all tea plantations and fir trees. We stayed at the Blue Sky Lodge which was great, situated right at the bottom of the walk in Delhousie. We started the trek at 2:30 am. It was hard work, some of the steps are almost completely vertical but it's definitely doable. Really not as killer as others have made out, the views on the way down are beautiful. My legs hurt abit for a few days but nothing major. To get there you can take the train to Hatton, then take the bus from outside the station to Delhousie. It's 70/lkr so no need to fork out 3000lkr on a tuk tuk. It takes about 1-1.5 hours on the bus. It gets pretty cold on top but you'd be fine with a jumper and maybe a rain coat, our accommodation gave us some lovely yellow ones. There's lots of tea shops on the way up and toilets (squats, they're not that bad!) All in all it's an amazing experience, you really must do it!

This is a tough climb, but satisfying when you reach the top. If you reach the top... For all the right reasons you should do this climb, however it is not the spiritual awakening I was hoping for. There is no sense of crowd control and it took us over an hour to climb the last 300 steps (we climbed to that point in just over 2 hours) as the climb bottlenecks and the queue was terrible. At the top there are shoes everywhere and it feels chaotic. We didn't get in the monastery as the queue was horrendous, so we found a small space by the steps to watch the sunrise. All the way up there are stalls and toilets, which is helpful on one hand, but tarnishes the majesty of the event. The litter is terrible. I think we were unlucky with the crowds (it was a Monday morning), and without them it would have been much better. However, there are better climbs in the world.

I was a little unprepared for what the hike up Adam's Peak had in store. Let me be clear: if you are not a seasoned hiker, then you need to do some stairs training. My fitness levels were pretty good, but it did get to a point where I thought that my legs were going to give way! All that being said, the experience was amazing. Ringing the bell in the temple, watching the incredible sunrise....it was disappointing that there were a number of concrete slab buildings up there that made it hard to rest and capture the incredible sunrise.
We start climb around 9 pm and we made to peak by 6 am. In Feb it's bit crowded. Don't forget to bring jackets, caps, gloves since it's really cold towards to the peak.

3 stars for the walk itself, 5 stars for cultural value and atmosphere. We climbed Adam's Peak in mid Feb on a Sunday night / Monday morning. We left Dalhousie around 1:50am and reached the 300m to top Mark around 1.5hrs later, the next hour was spent behind slower older age people and the crowded thinner stairs until we reached the top. I'm glad we walked fast as many of the people we passed on the way up we saw on our way down stuck on the stairs with a huge wait to the top temple. It's worth beating the crowds. As we had quite a wait until the sunrise at the top, we walked back down and we're better off for it - we found three amazing spots with a brilliant view just as good as at the top yet minus the crowds.

Adam's peak or Sri Pada(as the Buddhists call it) is the fourth highest mountain in Sri Lanka and it is one of the most sacred places in Sri Lanka because on the summit you can see the footprint of the Lord Buddha. Locals climb the mountain only between the poya days of December and April of the next year and this period is known as the season. There will be hardly any people climbing the mountain off the season. The only way to go up there is on foot. There are two routes to climb the mountain one route is from Maskeliya and the other one is from Ratnapura. The way from Maskeliya is much more easier to climb than the other way and many pilgrims choose the way from Maskeliya as it takes less time and is less tiring. If you choose to start climbing from Maskeliya, you can go upto Nallathanniya by vehicle, from there you have to go on foot and the path is very scenic along the route and will take at least 4 hours to climb. You should take a jersey with you if you are climbing in the morning because it might be very cold during the morning. You can visit the Japanese Peace Pagoda, which looks like a Japanese temple and not like any other normal Sri Lankan temple. Halfway up the mountain, you will see the entire surrounding area including the Maussakele reservoir, which is situated in Maskeliya. There are many places along the way where you can stop and have a snack. The last part of the climb is the steepest part. Once you reach the summit, you can visit the shrine, which houses the footprint of the Lord Buddha, and a temple of the God Saman. The view from the summit is really spectacular because  Sri Pada is the highest mountain in the area. When you are having a glance from the top, there is a huge chance that, once in a while, the whole view would get covered by the mist. Climbing down the mountain takes less times and is less tiring. Climbing up, visiting the places on the top and climbing down will take you at least 8 hours but the place is a must-visit in Sri Lanka.

It's very tough climbing more than 5000 stairs. But I feel it's worth when I watch sunrise. It's sacred and amazing. After sunrise, go to another side of the peak. The shadow of Adam's Peak is like pyramid standing on the mist. Don't forget to bring your coat.

The climb up Sri Lanka's fourth highest mountain is not one to miss! You don't need to be a mountaineer to conquer this one, just determined. 5,400 steps assist, along with lighting and tea houses. Get up very early and join the many local pilgrims hiking up for their visit to One of Sri Lanka's most sacred sites. If you time it right you will also be treated to a magnificent sunrise, and as you return to breakfast in Dalhousie, drink in the amazing landscape around the peak.

If you are climbing Adam's peak for the first time,  these tips will come in handy. -Arrival : Hatton is the nearest Railway station,  easily accessible from Colombo/Kandy. From Hatton,  either take a bus to Dalhousie (Rs. 70,  leaves every half hour,  fully packed with people standing very uncomfortably,  luggage space in the rear,  takes 1hr 15 mins) or a Tuktuk (Charges Rs. 1300 to 1500,  you need to bargain,  takes 1hour,  but you can stop on the way to take pics).  Tuktuk definitely is the far more comfy option. Try arriving late afternoon. The ride from Hatton station to Dalhousie is very scenic and you wudnt want to miss it. Also this way you will get some sleep before the climb starts at 2am. - Stay : Several budget hotels to crash down for few hours when you arrive. Like Blue sky or Adams peak inn. These are really close to where the climb starts. But they will be overbooked during weekends. This hike is very famous with the locals as well. Book in advance. - The aim is to see the sunrise from the peak. To do that,  start at (Very important!! ) 1 am on weekends /holidays and 2am other times if rush is low. The hike covers more than 5000 neverending steps,  and they get steeper as u reach the top. It will take you at least 4 hours to climb with stops. However,  on weekends the last part of the climb is so crowded that you wont get to reach the top. I started at 2 and got stuck few hundred metres from the top in thick crowd queue,  which was standstill for upto 30 mins. Sun rose beyond the valleys and I missed it. - Take water,  but you will also get it in stores all along,  also carry dry clothes to change sweaty ones,  winter wear for the chilly summit and walking stick. Of course a good camera is a must too. -  The view from atop is mesmerizing. The peak is the highest in the vicinity and looks down on others around it. Dreamy clouds below and smaller hills rising up,  a beautiful lake make a picturesque landscape. The sunrise of course is the icing on the cake. - Coming down takes 2 to 3 hours at leisure,  and your knes will be shaking. This is when you will thank me for the walkin stick idea.  It saves your knees from becoming gelo.

I would highly recommend doing this if you're up for it.  It would be difficult even for the fittest, but well worth it. Plenty of opportunities to stop along the way which we did. We started our climb at midnight and it took us 5 hours to get up ( we rested along the way for quite a while each time) We waited til 6am for sunrise which was a great view. I would r comm me getting to the top earlier than sunrise to claim a good spot, as it did get pretty crowded by 6am with tourists. Definitely take a jacket as it's quite cold at the top. My husband and I were sore for 2 days after. Overall really worth it.

We took off at 2:45 from del house and arrived to the top one hour before sunrise so we had to wait. Be aware that it is very cold up there and you will be sweaty so take some quick drying and warm clothes. If you go slowly and take small breaks it is not that bad, worse is the way down when it's even more crowded as everyone is descending and your legs shake. It was cloudy so we didnt see the 'proper' sunrise but it is still very magical how the tops of mountains appear from the total darkness. Worth going.
What good shoes and watch out for toilet adventures by less discerning travellers.Is the view worth 45 minutes walk in 35 degree heat? If you've been to the Lake District its debatable!

We set out for the climb at 2am as we had been recommended - but if you are fit and active I think it would be better to start at more like 3am. It only takes 2 and a bit hours to climb, and with first light from 5:40am you don't want to get up there too early. It gets very busy so you need to get there a little before sunrise.

- It's not easy to get to. We left Negombo at 9pm and arrived at 2:45 using a driver/car from Negombo that said he's been there a few times. - The climb up is going to have you wanting to give up. Seeing the old people, cripples and people carrying other people going up with you won't let you quit. - It stinks pretty much all the way up. - A lot of people, very crowded. - Lots of shops that sell neon teddy bears, candy and other crap. There is however a massage place near the bottom that was only 400-500 rupees. And they sold pretty awesome balm for only 100 rupees (we regretted not getting more, it worked great!) - The path is entirely lit so there's almost nowhere to see the night sky. - The bathrooms that cost 20 rupees are really gross and nowhere to wash your hands. - You're going to carry a lot of water which is heavy, and probably a camera. If you want to buy anything along the way its 3-4x the normal price at sea level. - It's 7km each way, and a 1150m ascent. The peak is 2243m, you can use your iPhone's built in altimeter to let you know how close you are - It helped encourage us to keep going when we knew how far/close we were. - You have to bring spare clothes to change into on the way down. You will be very sweaty from the climb and cold because it's really windy up there and about 6-9 degrees. celsius. - About a 100m from the top you will reach a line of people waiting to reach the peak. You will now go down (or wait in line) and find the best spot to see the sunrise, providing you make it on time. It rises around 6:00am. It's stunning! - The sunrise is
Be warned this is not an easy walk. It takes 3-4 hours, all uphill. 5,000 steps. Buddhist Pilgrim? Then do it.

It was amazing to see people making the pilgrimage carry the elderly on their shoulders and walking barefoot. If you want to catch the sunrise you need to give yourself at least 3 hours just to be safe.  The stairs start off quite shallow but quickly  get quite steep.  There are stops with snacks and drink that become more frequent the higher you get. The path we took was well lit but take a small torch just in case.  We made it in a little over 2 hours and arrived about 15 minutes before sunrise. We didn't encounter any crowds on the way up.  Try to use the bathroom before leave your hotel because the ones on the mountain are not very nice at all.  Don't think you'll be alone there will be plenty of people up there waiting also.  The earlier you get to the top the better spot you can get.  The viewing best spot is all the way to the left to the side of the building or on the top by the temple.  Avoid standing next to the speaker since its big and just annoying.  Wear layers since you'll most likely sweat on the way up but be cold at the top from the wind. Once you're at the top and found a spot you'll see some spectacular colors of the sunrise.  We stayed late enough to witness a ceremony procession.  I don't know if this takes place everyday. Going down sucks WAY more than going up.  Very hard on the knees.  Stop at the first or second restaurant on the way down.  Had the best cabbage rotis on our entire time in Sri Lanka.  Spicy and crunchy goodness.  The tea was pretty good as well.  You will see amazing views of the countryside you missed on the way up in the darkness.  Expect another 3 or so hours to go down depending on how tired you are and the crowds. Very good attraction that you must do if you like to challenge yourself.  Just make sure you give yourself a day to recover after.

After a 2.5hr climb starting at 2:00am the last 100m took another 2 hrs as it was Independence Day in SriLanka( public holiday) and  it was packed with local Sri Lankans making there pilgrimage. A challenging climb and not for the faint hearted. If your are fit it will take 2-2.5hrs if not so allow 3-3.5hrs. Try to get there around sunrise but take warm clothes and something to cut the wind as its freezing once you reach the top.The climb will have you sweating and peeling off layers of clothes.It is very rewarding and a magical view and you will have sore legs the next couple of days.

A genuinely unique experience. We travelled to Dalhousie for Kandy and started the walk at midnight. A weekend, so busy as predicted and we had to queue the last 250 metres at the top for an hour. A truly  atmospheric, special feeling though at the summit, surrounded by the crowds of pilgrims. We caught the sunrise en route down to avoid the traffic, which was still spectacular. One if those experiences you'll never forget.

The climb is hard work and even more so the decent. I would not have minded if the top was excellent but, unfortunately, it's really grimey and one side you have to look over the men's urinals and showers. Imagine a super congested dirty bus station on an Indian highway. It's also very busy at sunrise and so the chances of actually getting a space to see the sunrise is very low. The walk upwards is far from endearing either as it's lit by neon lights most the way and the majority of the path is flanked by stalls selling naff tourist garb. I would really recommend skipping Adams Peak and spending more time in one of the other beautiful places in Sri Lanka.

Adamspeak was really good place to visit. And we climb month of February 2 (srilankans independent day) oh my god very crowded this place. Really good view on top. And see sun rise also. When we start to climb it's okay for climate. But some places dirty. If some body climb Adamspeak I recommend off season period. But probably not crowd.

We started walking already at 1.30AM since we wanted to make sure to reach the top before sunrise. What a mistake! It  took us less than 2 hours to reach the top and then we had to sit there and wait for two ours in below 10 degrees as the places filled up with people. Yes, we are young and reasonably fit and both kids and elderly make this journey as well but do not expect it to take four ours unless you will be stopping to have a tea at every food stand (there are plenty). Yes, the view is beautiful and so was the sunrise but I wish that I would have brought a jug of tea or soup, triple socks, a blanket and a winter jacket. It was still a beautiful experience though and I can highly recommend it even if it is purely 5500 stairs and not really a natural experience, more of a spiritual one, if you are interested in these things.

We, not experienced hikers, decided to do the climb based on what we have read about the amazing views from the top at sunrise. We left our guest house at 2.10am and walked ca. 10 minutes to the starting point. Although the hike was daunting and tough at times, we managed to reach the top in 3 hours, which included a few stops for water and tea/coffee at the many tea stalls all along the route. When we got to the summit, we were hot and sweaty, but it was also very cold up there. The view of the sunrise was amazing and well worth it. Be aware that it is very crowded up there, due to the mix of travellers and locals making their pilgrimage. We made it back down in just over an hour, which was also very hard on the legs. All in all, a very rewarding experience, but you will feel the pain in your legs for a few days.

Though a little nervous about the climb up Adam's Peak, it was not as difficult as we had feared, and was well worth the effort, and the pain of sore quads for the next 2 days. We started early to avoid the rush, and it was lovely to have some time walking in the dark without too many people. We stopped at a tea kiosk for an hour with just 20 minutes left to climb, so we arrived a little before the lovely sunrise. We also stayed once the crowd had dispersed to watch the incredible arrival of the shadow. I had not expected that would be such a beautiful sight. I was dismayed to see some tourists making the climb wearing inappropriate clothing - short skirts or shorts, singlets or shirtless. People also entered the temple area wearing shoes; climbed all over sacred areas; fought over the best spot for that photo of the sunrise. This is one of the most sacred places in Sri Lanka, and if people can't show some respect, they really should consider going somewhere else to see a sunrise.

Go up to the peak starting around 4am will be a good timing. It took me 2 hours and 1 minutes to reach to the peak. You will still have the time to rest a while before you can catch the magnificent sun rise.
If you love for walking and enjoy the scenic beauties you must visit the Adams Peak via Rathnapura trail.

I was a little apprehensive about tackling the climb on our honeymoon trip to Sri Lanka - when you see it from the roadside it looks huge and I hadn't done any training to prepare for it. We set off at 2am and climbed at a good pace making it to the last tea shop for around 5am where we were able to have a proper rest break and chat to others making the trek! We reached the top just before sunset, visiting the temple, ringing the bell and finding a good spot for photos (it gets very busy very quickly at the top and can be hard to see). It was magical and we were able to see the famous 'shadow of the peak' on the other side after sunrise - the best part of the experience. It is a tough climb - very steep in parts - but well worth it. If anything coming back down is worse - my calfs ached for days! But would do it again if I got the chance!

It is great hike. we started @3pm and reach to summit @6.30 pm. There are many shops along the way but don't expect much more. If you want to take some photos around the way, its better you start your journey in the morning(before 9a.m). but you have to face heavy sunlight. but most of people choose the night. If you need to watch sun rise you should start @ night. but remember to bring some sweaters. because its very cold when you reach to summit. There are two buses @5 a.m from Nallathanniya to Hatton and Colombo via avissawella. There are buses for every train from Hatton Railway station to Nallathanniya.

My husband arose at 2.30am and joined the throng to climb Adam's Peak from Slightly Chilled Hotel, Dalhousie.  He hasn't stopped talking about it since (and that was two weeks ago!).  I was a bit surprised it was higher and more awesome than I thought it would be, and if it had not been so hot I would have liked to walk up during the day.  Maybe next time!

I have been here twice and this place is exceptionally amazing and stunning.  The climb was moderate and you have to climb 5000 steps in steep. but trust me, when the summit is reached you will feel all the pain is no longer matter. Make sure you go in weekdays (during season) to avoid crowed, so it hive the feeling you’re in the heaven. Tip: o	Start your climb during late evening, so you can target for the perfect sunrise, also to avoid sunburn. o	Toilets available every 500m (approx.) o	Avoid carrying many items o	Don’t forget to take your camera o	Very cold at the top hence take a thermal/jacket with you. o	Avoid eating east rotti while climbing. o	Wear proper dress (highly recommended), as you entering to a spiritual place

Amazing views and the hike is well worth it. Make sure you have a good fitness level before the hike. Took me about 3.5 hours to the top. Plenty of shops along the way so you don't have to carry too much water and ect. However prices increase as you go further. It can get wet and cold towards the top so better to be prepared for it. The only disappointment is it's next to impossible to find a decent toilet.

Was definitely worth the climb, we had a stunning sunrise and the views were amazing. There are plenty of places to stay at the bottom to get a few hours sleep however our hotel was foul! Luckily the walk made up for it!

It's hard. I walked funny for four days after! when you are at the top, your sweaty, wet face gets cold, very cold. And after sunrise you should hurry down before it gets too hot. I loved it. Everyone can do it. There where little children and ladies as old as my grandma when I climbed. Just take your time and have lots of tea-stops!

Climbed Sri Pada in January 2014 and then again in 2015 (after swearing I would never do it again!). The sunrise is worth all the pain and the stupid walk you will endure during the days after. I wouldn't call myself 'fit' so, the trek was tough but, climbing up is a lot easier to bear than the descent. It was PAINFUL! I looked like a cross between a crab, a flightless bird and a penguin... you get the idea :) Not to put anyone off this adventure, though. The views at the top are spectacular on a clear day and the scenery along the way is breathtaking. Worth it and the pain does go away, and is almost forgotten. During peak season, there are tiny shops selling food and tea and water is abundant from free flowing taps. I was thankful that I didn't have to carry too many snacks, heavy bottles of water etc. If you have to wait for a few hours to see the sunrise, bring a warm jacket (keep it light weight) and perhaps gloves as its cold at the summit. Cannot emphasize enough to keep everything light weight because, carrying a load both ways is not funny after the first 2 or 3 hours. Climbing and descending on the Hatton route was the easiest for me. We started at MN, tolerated the people crush for about 2 hours to see the sunrise and were back on the ground before 10am. The Ratnapura route is longer, much longer. The trek can be peaceful and relaxing but, this is depends on each person.

We started the climb in Dalhousie at 3:30 and arrived just before 6 am to see the sunrise. The climb had a very special atmosphere as we were walking in the dark with just small lights from kiosks selling tea and refreshments along the way. It wasn't so cold so we were walking just in a T-shirt, but it's gets colder on the summit, so it's good to take some warm sweatshirt and a light jacket. It's also a good idea to take an extra T-shirt because you get quite sweaty during the climb. Although we weren't lucky and it was quite cloudy, the sunrise was worth the effort.

It was hard to climb the over 5000 steps, but well worth. During the climbing all sort of people greet you, encourages you or viceversa wait for your smile to push them up. Once in the top you wait for the marvellous sunrise and after you enjoy the sight at over 2000 meters high and it is breath taking. Unfortunately we did not listen to our guide and began to descend on the right side, even if he told us to go down in the left one ( we thought it was only one way up and down). We ended up descending a much longer way with a much higher number of steps until my knees were in a very bad pain. Our fault, nothing to blame to anyone. Just a suggestion: go there, it's well worth and, most important, take the same way down you took to go up.

Need so much stamina to climb the mountain. Took me 4 hours to reach the top.and 3 hours to cme back. But the sunrise frm above the cloud is just amazing. Totally worth the pain. Tips : should start at 12 midnight so u can take break in the middle. Bring water and snacks with you. Don't wait so much aftr the sunrise cz its going to be hot soon. U must need any muscle pain spray or cream later so keep one.

Adams peak is ... interesting. As a couple of other reviewers have said, be sure to know why you are going... If it's to tick boxes in Sri Lanka and say you've done it, you'll probably be a bit disappointed - it's an a small mission to get there, and there really is nothing to do in the town, or see aside from the views of the mountains (which you can get in alot of other places) and climb/see Adams peak. Accommodation and the town is rough, I'd guess 95% literally there to see and climb and shops are temporary for the 'on' season, so don't expect much. The climb itself was much harder than I expected. Even when i felt fine on the way up, by the town you get half way down your legs are screaming and you can't wait for it to be over - and I'd say we are fitness freaks and still felt it. I admire all the older generations who were trekking up - unbelievable. The sunset and peak itself is beautiful, however I'd say you need to be in touch with the sacred part of this mountain to truly appreciate it - otherwise you get up, and just want to get the heck down again (and with about 20 thousand others... that makes that part rather difficult). Goodluck!
Climbed this New Year's Day, well worth a visit , lovely views and good exercise , Hatton is a nicer place to stay in and get a Tuk Tuk to the peak in the morning

First of all why it is worth visiting Adam's Peak: 1. Great exercise for sportsmen and sportswomen. 2. to admire a great landscapes while climbing up. 3. To see / observe a sunrise and a beautiful sky. 5. To see hundreds (sometimes thousends) of local people climbing up the mountain for religious purpose. 6. See a hole shrine on the top. Why not to go there: 1. If you're weak - skip this since you are not going to make it. Climbingc up requires a lot of stamina. Stairs are with different hight and you will go up and up and up ... 2. Hotel/lodging offers in a remote town are less than good so if you like high class hotels - skip this trip. Remember - on the Adam's Peak area and all the remote towns it is stricktly forbidden to drinking alcohol, including beer. Tip - if you book via booking.com check the pictures and descriptions of your hotel/dormitory since there are some unfair people offering you a 2 m x 2 m room with a bucket saying this is what you booked. I will write more about this very venu in my next review.

The climb up to Adms Peak is fenomenal! It starts out pretty soft in Dalhousie, and gets steeper and steeper, ending with thousands of steps towards the top! We started walking at about 2:30, and its lit all the way up. The view is just amazing as you ascend, and even more so as you descend, after sunrise! The only negative thing about the climb, must be the vendors and small "shops" playing terrible music very loudly on your way up, even though music supposedly is forbidden.. The summit however was a dreadful sight! Dont get me wrong, the view is just amazing, and when the sun rise above the mountain tops, the atmosphere is just magical! Howerver, the top itself is totally ruined by people! The entire top is covered in tacky, horrible buildings and concrete, theres not a single place to just sit on rock anywhere! The buddhists have "decorated" the whole area with plastic crap, making it look more like a typical Sri Lankan highway stop, that a so called holy spot! In other countries, these kind of alterations would be strictly prohibited, as to maintain the nature as intended. This obviously has no meaning to the Sri Lankans - unfortunately. I just have to say, I cant see the spirituality of badly painted concrete, decorated with flashing lights, neon coloured plastic flowers, gold and glitter plastic remesies everywhere, and loadspeakers shouting buddhist prayers so load your ears will pop! Not to mention the music played by some local boys from 5-6:30. Three unaynchronized drum players, and a whizzle so sharp it felt like it was cutting into my brain! No dont let all my negativity stop you from going, the trip itself, as mentioned, is just awesome! But dobt expect any spiritual or godly awakenings when you reach the top - expect quite the opposite..

I climbed Adam's Peak in January 2016: this is an experience that I will not forget in my life - simply amazing!! I arrived on Delhousie the night before and started the climb at half past two in the morning. The temperature was not too cold (it was possible to walk in a T-shirt) in the beginning, but make sure you bring some warm sweater and / or jacket with you, because it will be really cold at the top! (If you did not bring any warm clothes from home, you can buy warm sweaters for 400 Rupies in Delhousie - also gloves etc.) The climb is not easy, but I think everyone can do it (even old Sri Lankan grandmothers make it to the top -  barefoot!). It is about 5200 stairs till the top, and in the last part they are really steep... But it is worth the effort!! You can look for a hiking stick which makes the climb and descent easier... Once you reach the top you pass a sign which says to take your shoes off - so make sure you wear socks!! Otherwise your feet will be frozen... I saw some people that had walked with their hiking shoes through the sacred area - this is not nice nor does it show any respect towards the locals who are on their pilgrimage to the footprint... I watched the footprint at about 5 o'clock (it took me about 2,5 hours to hike up) and then looked for a nice place to watch  the sunrise. The best place is the steps at the entrance area (where the first sign asks you to take shoes off) - you have excellent views there - and can wear your shoes! :) Once the sun rose up, many people started to rush down again, however, no the best time for pictures starts! The light is amazing! Hope you guys will also have good luck with the weather! Have fun!!

Exciting trekking, amazing view from the top, an healthy and inspirated start of new year. 3 h walking paths, really challenging if you are not in exercise. It's difficult to describe all the emotion you feel, it's something to try.

Fantastic. If you come to Sri Lanka, Adams peak it is a must do. It's a magnificent walk with the most spectacular views. We have been in Sri Lanka for a surf trip and made ourselves go to Adams peak and it was without a doubt the best day of the trip. We left at 2.15am and smashed the walk out in an hour and a half. We were stuffed at the end tho. This left us freezing until the sun come up after 6. Make sure you have some warm clothes to pop on at the top. It's a really hard walk. Super steep. Worth the pain. It's a free which is a bonus as well compared to worlds end which costs $$25 odd dollars. When you get there make sure you know the location of the sun rise. If you want the best photo you need a good spot. We didn't. Just go!!! We paid 15,000rp for a taxi from Adams peak back down to matara. Expensive but it took 6 hours.

We started at 2am and it took us 2 hours to climb, so we had to wait a long time to see the sunrise from the top. Lots of Buddhist pilgrims. Temple guards nicely advise you to avoid burglars and make you take off the shoes in the temple although it is really cold (!) up there. Many shops selling local souvenirs and cafes with vegetarian food and tea on your way (in my hotel the say the water is taken from the river, I felt sick after drinking one but most of people seem to be ok). Be sure to check the weather forecast - the view is a key here, you don't want to miss it because of rain or clouds.

6 of us started the climb at 1 am on a cold winter night on 26th December 2015. 4 of us made it to the top and 2 had to return to the warm bed of our hotel. Even though we felt a sense of accomplishment after making it to the peak, we slightly envied the quitters as we shivered in the misty breeze that engulfed us. It took around 3 hours for the climb and it has certain stages which will make you consider quitting. But if you fight that off then the climb gets easier. The path itself is quiet well lit and you will be accompanied by several pilgrims. Some of them quite old to make the climb, and I found myself garnering my strength looking at their resolve. You will find several tea shops serving some snacks in case you need to re-energize yourself and give your legs a little rest. Once on the peak, there is a temple with the deity's feet in it. The temple and its surroundings is pretty small so it cannot accomodate a lot of people. It would be advisable to do this on a weekday or a not so auspicious occasion since the crowd mar the experience. We were unfortunate to not see the sunrise as there was a dense cloud and fog cover. Do it for the thrill and if you are lucky, you might be treated to a beautiful sunrise.

We started walking around 2 am, as we heard someone tell us it took approx 4 hours to reach the summit. We were going down on the Rathnapura side of the mountain, so we had to bring our luggage as well. This made the climb a bit heavier, but we had still no problem getting to the top before sunrise at 6 am. It's around 5000 steps to the top, and the entire route is covered by street lights. There's also kiosks along the way for resting. Great feeling to reach the top! The trip is kinda popular, so the place was pretty crowded. Still nice to sit with equally excited strangers, anticipating something as spectacular as a sunrise on top of a mountain. We were unlucky enough to get there one day before they opened the temple, but we could still wander around the building. The descending on the other side was longer than the trip up, but totally worth it. Around 12 000 steps down made this the less popular route, and we had the entire descend for ourselves (lucky us). The views on the way down was beautiful, as we descended through jungles, entered small villages, and ascended more summits on the 5 hour walk down. When we arrived the bottom of the stairs, the villagers was happy to help us order a tuktuk who drove us to Rathnapura. I will definitely recommend this great experience, but  pack light..

The trekking is not so bad, it is quite enjoyable, if you find your pace. The view from the top is great. Unfortunately, it is very crowded and also not so spiritual as I read before; there are shops on the entire route, which is pleasant because there are many tourists with witch you can talk with, share experiences etc.

Adam’s Peak, or Sri Pada as known in Sri Lanka, is a mountain (2243 m) located in the south of the central highlands. The mountain features a rock formation that is considered as the footprint of Buddha for Buddhist, Shiva, for Hindu and Adam for Muslims and Christians. The 1400 m ascent means a significant difference in temperature as you reach the top, and this is exacerbated by the wind. It is not a hard climb but especially on the way down, leg muscles will be overexerted. The Jan – March period is particularly busy time to climb. Other months see less traffic, and therefore the many stalls lining the path are not open during the “low” season. So bringing food and especially water is important. Many people attempt the ascent in the early hours of the morning, with the goal of seeing the sunrise, others climb in the afternoon to see the sundown. In either cases, torches are needed to see at night, even with full moon. Travelling in groups is always advisable.

After 3 hours of hiking and walking stairs in complete darkness, you are finally up there! Too many people, the top was packed!! No chance to enjoy the sunrise unless you reserved your 'seat' and stayed there for about an hour freezing your... off. No chance to walk around, just too many people at a too tiny place... What a pity as it could be nice!

This time I climbed from Rathnapura side which is about above 10km hike and ascending to top about 2 km from the 1st step. This route has a lot of ups and downs and during this hike you climb 2-3 few mountain peaks as well. When you get to last peak out of those small mountain peak you could see the adams peak which stay half a km above and 4 km away. This route is 10 times hard than Hatton route, which is about 600 - 800 m climb, but more fun. Hikers would love it..!

After visiting Sri Lanka on several occasions climbing Sri Pada has always been on my to do list, so this time we planned our trip around it. Knowing it was peak season we knew to avoid the weekends and Poya days, so we organised our ascent on a Friday. We also booked accommodation in Dalhousie so we didn't have to travel to get to the base of the mountain. When we arrived on Thursday afternoon you cannot help but be impressed by this holy mountain. Then at night you can see the sparkling ribbon of lights that mark the trail to the top. Like many other tourists we wanted to see the dawn of the new day from its peak, so we set out just after 2am. The path is well marked out and lit. As our legs are older than a lot of others we went at a slow and steady pace, with plenty of breathers along the way. It took us over 3.5hrs to get to the summit but the view & the feeling when you get there is so exhilarating. We arrived about 15mins before dawn and there was already quite a crowd of people at the top - which meant vantage points were at a premium. We weren't able to watch the shadow of Adam's Peak fall across the valley below but were able to watch the sunrise from the east. Despite the size of the crowd we were all able to disperse fairly quickly back down the mountain. The total climb and descent was over 17.5km (6,500 steps) - it was exhausting but totally worth it.

First at all I have to say , don't believe everything you read. This trekking is not that hard as people (other tourists) say. I am pregnant (5 mnd), haven't trained the last 4 mnd at all. Before that I used to train 2-3 times a week. We started 2:30 am, at very slow pace, I didnt want to lose my breath. With some pauses for pictures. I just needed a break twice. The secret is Don't go fast. You have enough time to reach the top. I could talk all the way up because i kept a very slow pace. We used 2:40 min up to the summit. I recommend to use training clothes so you dont get to swety. i didnt need to change my tshirt as others reviewers wrote but i did use a lightweigh jacket at the summit. When you start to get down you dont need it anymore. We used 2:10 min down and it was not that hard. It is better if you try to keep a good pace otherwise you knees will feel it.

Amazing experience of The Adam’s Peak with my son in Dec 2015, a gruesome challenge for the physically fit travelers. Pilgrims, visitors and tourists climb The Adams Peak during the season of December to April every year. Generally they plan the night trail to reach the 2,243 meter pinnacle and see the beautiful sunrise around 5.30 AM. The temple at the top houses the sacred footprint venerated by many religions. Buddhists believe it is the footprint of Lord Buddha. Christians and Muslims believe the footprint belongs to Adam, while some Hindus believe it to be that of Lord Shiva. We reached the site from Hatton – Maskeliya route via and over the Maussakele Dam site and arrived at Nallathanniya, where the climb starts. Good budget accommodation with restaurants are available at Dalhousie and Nallathanniya for the visitors and tourists to spend the night. During the climbing season the night trail is well lit and has many food stalls and tea & coffee kiosks and police assistance to help the climbing public. The off season climb is not favoured as the wind is too strong for the steep ascent safely and only few roadside facilities, assistance and lighting may be available. For the pilgrims it is a solemn, arduous and fulfillment journey. For seasoned travelers it offers an epic adventure and test of stamina. However the amazing views of sunrise and the 360 degree panoramic views overlooking the surrounding hills and valleys with lush greenery of rain-forests and nearby reservoirs are memories of a lifetime experience.

I'm in moderate shape and found my 3 hour hike challenging. Started at 2:30 AM.  The pitch of stairs and number of them can be quite overwhelming. The tea stops along the way are a gift. Sri Pada (SL name) is a huge domestic pilgrimage site and there's good traffic. Went on an early weekday and it was jammed at the top. Be careful if it's a Poya Day or weekend as the crowds up top could be crushing. We had clouds so missed a glorious sunrise. But it was spiritual and rewarding in its way and should be hiked by those that are able--just be honest about your level of fitness.

We made the trek up Adams peak during our two weeks in Sri Lanka, it was definitely worth the 6000 steps. We left at 2 am from our hostel which was a 15 minute walk to the start and ended up at the top at 4:30. In hindsight, it is freezing at the top so we might have wanted to slow down a bit, but we didn't want to get stuck behind loads of slow stair walkers. The sunrise was ok on the day we went but the most amazing part was the views from the top that you can see during the day that were hidden at night. Definitely bring a jumper and some snacks and water!

What an experience!! I don't know what to say , it was very spiritual for me , I was thinking of God all way up !! Something I don't do very often ... and the fact that I did it just before the new year made me think of my goals and resolution for 2016 , me and my other 2 friends was never that focused , we just had one goal in mind , and that is to reach the peak , unfortunately we didn't think of going back down which was the real challenge! It just seemed endless. So here we go : -I suggest you only go half way and wait for the sunrise at a stop point cause the peak is too crowded and u can hardly see anything. -sleep well before you start , u mush go at night , the stars are beautiful up there. -take a thermos of tea or hot chocolate, we didn't buy food or tea from there , not so clean . But canned food is fine . -it gets hot while climbing and u sweat , but once you reach or rest it gets cold ... Freezing. -cover all your body just in case of blood suckers. -takes lots of wet wipes. -red bull or any energy drink and carbs.
