Definitely do this if you can fit it in to your Sri Lanka itinerary. It's an incredible experience climbing with the locals - and the sunrise and views at the top are spectacular. We climbed Mount Batur in Bali and Mount Rinjani in Lombok last year and compared to those this is a walk in the park. Don't be put off by the reviews saying how hard it is. It's a lot of steps, yes, but they are easy to manage with hundreds of rest stops all the way up. Just give yourselves plenty of time if you're worried. My husband put his back out the day before and we still managed it in 3 hours with two or three rest stops on the way. We both had stiff calves the next day or two, but nothing that a bit of stretching wouldn't solve. The top is hideously busy and you can probably give the temple a miss if you aren't doing it for religious reasons. We got to the top at 5 a.m. and it was already very full. We found a great seat just before you get to the top where there is a building with ledges you can climb onto and a little balcony bit the other side. It was pretty empty when we got there but rapidly filled up. The people who arrived after 5.30/5.45 found it harder to find a good spot, but there is plenty of space if you're willing to squeeze. The people who say don't bother and that you can see better sunrises elsewhere are very cynical, in my opinion. The sunrise was great and the views are breathtaking, but that's not what it's all about. It's a very unique, sociable experience and you will climb with far more locals than tourists. They are really friendly (possibly less so in the temple scrum at the top) and it's a pilgrimage for them so you see a lot of old people and people carrying very small babies. A lot of Sri Lankan people were coming down as we were climbing and they all said hello, good morning, enjoy the climb, etc. I'm really glad we did this and the drive through the hills the next morning was also incredible.

Let's be honest: waking up at 2 am to see the sunrise after a 3 hr plus walk through the stairs, full of people, crowded, with no place to eat decently, and having to go down through the same stairs another 3hr plus with hundreds of people...with dirt all over the place...honestly, the place is fraud. You can see better or equal sunrises in lots of places around Europe, America, the Caribbean...and in a much better environment. To make it worst, when you go down and arrive at the "camp base", there are just 2 things you can eat: 1) packed noodles 2) buiscuits and sweets. No real food anywhere. Maybe for some people from SriLanka it has a meaning (we saw a lot of elderly people barefoot goin up and down, sufffering) but for someone from abroad that expects a beautiful place...just avoid it and go to a good hotel. You'll see a better sunrise and at least you will be able to be a bit comfortable.

I went there with a friend of mine and we took the Rathnapura route to visit Adam's peak(Sri Paada). There is a season to visit AP that is from December to May (Till Vesak poya) and the off season from May to December (The monthly dates of starting the season and off season might differ annually depending on Poya days) . You can visit even in the off season too using Hatton route but you have to go to the peak and come before evening comes . There are three routes to visit adams peak 01.Hatton route (the easiest-5500 steps) . Lot of shops in the season and will take around 3 hours to climb up. Here you have to come to Hatton and take a bus to Nallathanniya . 02.Rathnapura route.(12700 steps there are steps from the begining to the end-fairly difficult but safe) Here you have to go to Rathnapura bus station and take a bus to Sri Paagama / Palabaddala. 03. Rathnapura Kuruwita route- Not much steps you can walk in the forest. From Rathnapura you have to take a bus to Kuruwita bus standand from there you have to take the Erathna bus. Then we started climbing using and it took close to 10 hours to reach the top in the Rathnapura route and make sure you go in the day time because the beauty of the natural environment is only visible when there is good day light. At around 5 the sun rise can be seen and that is what you should not miss but for that you should be bit lucky the environment should not be full of mist. We got down from the hatton route and it will take only 1.5 hours for us to climb down. You don't wanna take many things with you but it's really cold at the top so if you are planning to stay at the peak make sure you take a sweater with you.

You can't go to Sri Lanka high country and not do Adam's Peak. It's sunrise is hard to describe. I never seen anything like it before. You can't tell which way it up and which way is down. There is a cloud layer at dawn and the reflections are amazing and up and down are hard to distinguish besides your feet are on the ground. HERE ARE SOME HELPFUL TIPS - It takes three hours to hike but if the path is busy, it might slow you down and take longer. Depends also on your condition. - I got to the top by 5:30 and there wasn't any good sunrise viewing seats left. So I went down the steps 50 meters and had great views and way less people and easier to leave and beat people down. - Bring enough water for the hike. They charge up to 300 rupees on the hike for 1 liter of water. - Go on weekdays as this is free for all, even the Sinhalese and there is a temple on top they go to. They walk slow. There were even plenty of Sinhalese on the weekday when I went. I would be afraid of seeing what the weekend looks like. - Bring warm clothes for the top. I hiked in shorts and a t-shirt but needed a hoodie and long pants and wished I brought a blanket for the top.

We met 'Master' at the bus terminal. After an offer of help and a polite decline Master left us with his card. Soon after we called. He turned out to be a very friendly guy and extremely informative. He helped us find accommodation which proved to be a struggle as everywhere had closed for Sri Lankan New Year. We would highly recommend Master to anyone who wants a knowledgable friendly guide around Ratnapura (and his english is perfect!). Master's contact details are 071 130 1952. We found a place, got introduced to one of the nicest Tuk Tuk drivers (Kumara 077 845 3522) and got organised for Adam's Peak. It takes around and hour and a half to get to the start of the climb in a tuk tuk and cost us 2500r.. Usually there are buses running but as it was the night before new years and everything had stopped. This also meant that the infinite stairway, 11kms in total, was completely empty aside from us. We carried our packs, about 10kg each and it took us 6 hours to summit. Just in time for sunrise! The view from the top of Adams Peak is pretty spectacular. Pilgrims are chanting and there's all sorts of sights to see. Unfortunately the infrastructure is very poorly designed with a big ugly building obscuring a lovely view of the sunrise. You need to clamber up between a million other people trying to watch the sunrise over the top of the building and if you're lucky you won't have an iPad screen in between you and the view. We then walked down the Hatton side which was really cool. But we were forlorn and battered from our 6 hour ascent and stepping down is surprising hard on the legs. It took us 5 hours to get to the bottom. Once we reached Dalhousie we ate and slept and recovered. Unfortunately, we didn't find Ratnapura to be a remarkable town AND I was heckled at several times from random guys on the street which was bizarre. One gave me the finger, another told me to go home. We suspect this was something to do with my girlfriend being Sri Lankan and me being a white boy.. but who knows. Having said this, we certainly didn't get a chance to explore the town fully.

Hiking up the Adam's peak is definitely something you should do at least once in your life. We got up around 2am and it took us exactly 2h and 48minutes to get to the top. It was hard, but worth it. It was the biggest Hindu and Buddhist "bank holiday" so the place was packed with people going up and down all the time, but like I said, worth it. The views are stunning. Just take some warm clothes because it does get quite cold on the top, especially when they ask you to take your shoes off. The wind was a bit bitter too. But I would go AGAIN!!

First I'll tell you about how I reached adam's peak base or starting point: I've started from Dambulla at 7:30am, Took bus to kandy (Cost me SLR 100) then kandy to hutton bus (Cost SLR 95) then Hutton to Nallathanniya bus (SLR 70) Reached Dalhousie / Nallathanniya / Adam's peak starting point around 2 pm. I took 2 night room at cheap hotel, started climbing sripada (adam's peak) at 3:15 am on next day morning on 26th march 2015. Reached top at 5:30 am. It was painful climb for me, in between i almost felt like it's impossible by me to continue. But as i reached top, i felt like i reached heaven! Wow! All pain gone. Watched sunrise &  visited Sripada Maluwa. There is no entry fee. Started coming down at 7 am. Reached back down at around 9 am. Pain is back, i was almost unable to walk. Tips: It's better to take 2 night hotel room & rest for a night. Do not take any bags, water, food when you climb up. You will get everything on the way until you reach top. Taking bags with those stuff will make you more hard to climb up. Next morning at 4:15 am i took direct bus to colombo [Cost LKR 218 ]. Reached colombo around 11 am. There is only 2 direct bus to colombo. one is at 4:30am (starts before that) another is at night 9 pm or so. Hope those information helps you.

It is a hard climb, up lots of steps, but take it slow and you will get There! It took us just over 3 hours to get to the top, with a couple of tea stops along the way. The steps aren't even, and at sometimes very steep, but to see the view (and the sunrise!) its all worth it in the end! Seeing the locals on their pilgrimage with no shoes on and carrying infants wrapped up warm, and the older ladies - keeps you inspired to just keep moving on. If they can do it - so can you! When we got to the top, they warn you about looking after your belongings, which is good, however a shame that they feel that they must. Because we got us there just before 5am (we set off at 130 - I was nervous that I would take forever to get up there!) we were talking to one of the policemen up there, who pointed us to a great view point from which to watch - there was no one in front of us! - As soon as you get up the stairs, before entering where you need to go to see the footprint, turn back and you will see the donation building, close to the stairs is a fenced area that runs along side the building. There is nothing in front of you here, so if you can get there - AMAZING Views! Make sure you have something warm to wear for the wait and remember to take a snack for the wait as well - helps pass the time and provides sustenance for the trip down. The walk down was the killer for me (I have bad knees) but I was so elated by what we had achieved I didn't let it stop me or spoil it. The walk down is like a completely different walk, as you didn't get to see any of it in the daylight, seeing the views is amazing... I did however, keep turning round and reminding my hubby - "Look where we were!!!" There were bathrooms on the way up... although I stopped once, and very quickly changed my mind about needing to go! Ive never seen a toilet so disgusting!!! Its no walk in the park, but a memory that will stay with me forever!

We came to conquer Adam's Peak, and we did.  Our schedule changed and we had to go on a Saturday instead of Monday, which was unfortunate.  On the weekends there are bus loads of people, tourists and locals arriving to make the climb. So we set out at 01:30.  We made great time until the last approximately 700m.  There the line came to a complete stop and it took us 4 hours moving one step every 5 minutes. This made our total 2-way trip 10 hours.  Very frustrating. When we got to the top, they were ushering people in single file and one at a time to see the "footprint" in the temple.  They really should split the line at the top for those who just want to reach to summit and take photos, and those who want to see the temple.  If we would have known that was the case, we would have jumped the queue like several others (run up the "down" stairs).  Many have indicated that this disrespects the locals who are waiting in line. I disagree since I would only want to get to the top to see the sunrise and take pictures, not see the temple. So, it would not delay anyone from seeing the temple, in fact it would speed it up.  We managed to get photos of the sunrise while on the stairs, but it was tricky over all the people. Now, a comment about the people.  Sri Lankan people are the nicest people anywhere.  Our whole time there we were treated so well.  However, get them on a mountain climbing to a sacred temple and many transform into pushy rude people.  We had to really stand our ground on the narrow steps at the end or else we would get rudely pushed aside.  At times, it was actually quite dangerous. As many have mentioned, the bathrooms are not nice. Still, if you have to go, you have to go, and there is a minimal charge.  I never used them but my wife did.  She managed to find a "better" one than most near the top.  As for the comments about paying more for water etc the higher you climb, we are OK with that.  It's still cheap by our standards, and they do have to haul it up the mountain.  I'm OK paying extra for that.  We saw the guys bringing bags of supplies up the mountain on our way down and they deserve extra pay for that! They really need to fix up the top as well.  I know it's a religious site, but the reality is a lot of tourists go up there. They need a better viewing area where you can take better photos etc (and I already mentioned how they should split the line up). In all it was a rewarding experience.  Would I do it again?  Maybe if we were with others, but definitely not on a weekend.  A real sense of accomplishment having a beer after looking back up at the mountain.  If you are there, your should at least try it!

About a third of the way I was convinced I wouldn't make it to the top, as my legs were killing me about an hour into the continuous steps. But I did, and it was well worth the effort and several days' hamstring ache. The sunrise was bliss and the view on the way down is breathtaking. My boyfriend and I climbed on a Thursday night/ Friday morning and it was relatively quiet on the way up. We left Dalhousie at 2.50am and took 2.5 hours to reach the summit, with a stop of 10 mins (and many many brief stops as the steps got steeper and steeper!), and I'm not particularly fit. It really is hard work on the legs coming down - if you have weak knees in the slightest then I highly recommend using a stick to soften the impact on some sections of steps....or try running instead! But anyway, the views are so lovely that you may end up taking longer on the way down to stop and take in the view. When you see the very elderly and frail being guided up and down the mountain by relatives you realise you have no excuse not to make it!

Hard experience. The going is VERY long. Avoid the high season, we did our way with at least one thousand peregrines and it's the worst time because even if you can be on the top within 2/3 hours, you have to stop and wait for an extra hour almost on the top (because there is more people going up that people coming down, so you can't go further if the people on the top don't leave). Take very warm clothes if you're thinking at the sunrise on the top.

We started at 2:00 AM and took us 4 hours to get up. First hour the track is surrounded by different refreshment places, and then it is just steps and steps. No easy as the steps have different sizes. Also the way back is not so easy. Sun rice is OK, but honestly you can see sunset not just here….and budha footprint place is also OK, it is up to you if you really need to see it. For us it was something we could easily skip in our itinerary. Up the hill was not so cold, pullover and t-shirt was fine (climbed in middle March).

I won't lie & say that this was a walk in the park. This was by far the hardest thing I've ever done physically! Myself & my Boyfriend climbed this in 2hrs 15min, making it to the top for around 4:30am. The climb was extremely tiring, but once you see 90 year old ladies being carried up by their loved ones, you complain a little less & get stuck in! There are tea shops literally every 100m up the mountain, so don't worry about not being able to take breaks. The last tea shop is around 300 steps from the top. When you actually get up there, it's absolutely freezing, so it's best to take up a blanket or a few layers of warm clothes for the wait! The sunrise is absolutely beautiful, although the donation buildings do ruin the view a little. Getting back down is a real test on the knees, but once you're at the bottom, turning around & seeing what you have just achieved it a feeling like no other!

Adam's Peak is a must for hikers in Central Sri Lanka, however, while the mountain offers a good climb because of its towering size, the entire journey is really through a flight of stairs and that is really not what hikers like as it can really destroy your knees. And it did mine. Nevertheless, climbing an iconic mountain still offers the rewards at the top: seeing the footprint of Adam or Buddha or Shiva dependent on whose religion you're listening to, and the experience of climbing with the pilgrims is also quite nice as you feel you are one with the locals. Be warned though that the wait for the sunrise isn't the most comfortable and even finding a good vantage point to take photos would be difficult. The view going down is much more spectacular than the cramped summit. Plus points to the Sri Lankan police who gives a short orientation to tourists as you near the peak. There are also endless stalls for refreshments and resting stops along the way and climbing at 2am need not require a head lamp or flashlight as the entire route is lighted well. We also met a very nice Swedish couple going down the mountain and that is great because talking with them distracted us from our knees shaking and breaking every step.

THe views from Adam's Peak are what you imagine Paradise to look like. It was beautiful with the clouds and lakes, the sunrise was great. The ascent was a killer, I think it was more difficult than climbing to Everest Base Camp at 5300 metres. Also the descent was the worst though, you destroy the back of your legs, and ache for days after. If you want to take a bus back to Colombo from Hospet I would advise against it, try and work your trip around another way by going somewhere else, because the Hospet to Colombo Bus is not fun, given its windy roads along steep mountainsides and relatively small seats for westerners.

Don't be fooled, this climb is all steps it's a hard core climb! The steps are proper steps though and the path is clear and there is a handrail all the way up. I loved the sun rise though - just perfect.

The climb of Adams Peak was, for me, a once in a lifetime experience. It was hard and my muscles still hurted 5 days later but it was well worth it. I loved the climb more then I loved the view/being on the top. It's cold, crowded and you really have to fight for an okay-spot to see the sunrise. Other then that, the experience of climbing up a mountain in the middle of the night was magical.
Another must visited (only to worship and to feel the beauty of nature) site @ Sri Lanka

We started the climb on a Sunday morning around 7am, as we were not keen on seeing the sunset. It was very busy with endless streams of people coming down. The walk up is tiresome but okay if you're in a good condition. It took us 3 hrs to get up. Arriving at the top I was disappointed as the view from the peak is obstructed by the temple and safety fences. The view of the area is better on the way down. It took us around 2 hrs to get down. Other tourists we met at the top had reached the top around the same time as us but they had started at 2am! Apparently it was a lot of queuing to reach the top for them! We had taken a shortcut, at a junction at a water and toilet station we took a quieter road up, for a while it wasn't concrete steps anymore, but apparently saves you a lot of time to reach the top! I believe the shortcu brings you to the other side of the mountain which also has a track going up, but a lot more quiter than the main track!

Left around 2am to start the hike / steps. Made it up with enough to time to stop for breaks and time to spare at the top. Pretty cold at the top but didn't bother me that much. Seems longer on the way down for some reason, but worth it for the views.

Definitely one of the hardest things I have done. Great climb great views. Need warm clothes for the summit,  very cold. My legs took 3 days to recover. Adam apparently went there after he left the garden of Eden.  Adam's foot print is there. If you are a Christian believer. Do not go on the full moon, way too crowded. We commenced the climb at 2.15 am to allow enough time not to miss the sun rise. Three hours up and 2.5 hours down.

this was probably the hardest thing thing Ive ever done but was truly amazing. Started the climb at 2am to make sure I got to see the sunrise at 6am. the walk is approx 7km we managed it in 2hrs 35mins. There is approx 2000 steps of various sizes. I would say its only for the physically fit however there were children and older folk doing the climb too. I couldnt walk for nearly 2 days after. The views at the top are stunning and it was worth all the pain. plenty of places to stop and many shops to rehydrate at. the shops at the bottom are cheaper and progressively get more expensive but still reasonable. Only let down on this trip is there is quite a lot of rubbish around but efforts were being made to keep it clear. my tip would be if you had the time, book into one of the local guest houses and rest before and after, when you get back down also have a leg massage for approx £2.    toilets leave a lot to be desired.

I like looking at mountains but loathe climbing them. I'm physically not that fit and walking up hill for even a few minutes make me curse at myself, as I did much of the time I spent climbing Adam's Peak. And yet it was the highlight of my time in Sri Lanka. People start climbing it around 2am to see the sunrise at the top. The norm is 4 hours, but I started little after 12am for I knew I'm slow and not good at climbing mountains. It took me more than 6 hours to get to the top. It is much harder hike than you'd think. They're very steep steps up to the top and if you're not fit or don't enjoy trekking much, be prepared for a long and tiring night. But when you reach the top the view will be breathtaking, and it just feels good to share that feeling of accomplishment with other pilgrims around you. I know people say you should avoid weekend, for there are more people. But I picked the weekend intentionally because I wanted to be among locals. Sure it's pretty busy on the path and when I got to the top it was hard to find a spot to see sunrise due to so many people being on the top at the same time. But yet it felt more authentic and memorable because I was around all these local Sri Lankans who climbed it up to experience it like I did. It sure is a hard walk, and you will be kicking yourself saying why the hell I said I'll do this. But trust me when you get to the top, it will be the most memorable Sri Lankan moment for you as well.

Don't go in to this thinking it's going to be easy!! Having said that when we climbed to the top we were accompanied by young children and elderly people who were climbing either barefoot or in flip flops. It's achievable but it's tough especially if like me you are not a sporty/active person! I climbed it in 3 hours, plenty of rest stops and tea shops. Take snacks with you and if you can, water too as the price of a bottle doubles when your climbing! I didn't find the peak as cold as everyone else but the I was suffering with a mild fever!

Climbing the Adams Peak was an incredible experience. Although we climbed it during one of the poya days (a holiday) with many other people, we enjoyed the sunrise to be never forgotten. We stayed directly in Delhousie (Nallathaniya) which was a great thing because we could get some hours of sleep before taking off at 2 AM. The weather in the village in kind of strange, because when we arrived the previous day, it was pouring rain. However, at eight PM the rain stopped and it was cloudless in the morning. The next day, aroung four PM the raining again started, but the next morning was cloudless again. So do not worry if it is raining when you arrive in the afternoon. We definitely recommend staying in Delhousie two nights, so you can rest after the climb. After those numerous steps, you will be exhausted and your legs will hurt also the days to come. But the sunrise was just worth it!

As described by other reviewers, this is a hard climb, in the dark and could be exciting, but the number of people on the same pilgrimage detracted from any enjoyment. I was assured it was not so busy during the week but on aFriday night it was well nigh unbearable. The closer one gets to the top, the slower the progress and therefore the colder one gets. Once the summit is reached the wind is bitter and quite frankly I had no need to see the footprint. I found a corner, facing east, in which to huddle, waiting for dawn and sunrise. I could not wait to start the descent but sadly, due to the sheer numbers of people, this was also painfully slow. The views  were not out of the ordinary and so the main benefit was a sense of achievement.

Whether or not you're there for religious reasons (nearly every major religion seemed to have a claim to significance) or just for a hike with beautiful scenery, it's a trek worth taking. You'll encounter such a wide variety of people (children on their first climb crying because their legs hurt and elderly people with canes who show such determination climbing for their 30th time) along the trail.  Wonderfully lined with tea houses (and lighted) much of the way if you want to stop to grab a drink, some roti or other carb-based snack.  There are toilets advertised, but it's not going to be anything enclosed or anytthing near Western standards of a toilet (read: find a place away from the path and go in the bushes) The sunrise from the summit affords you a vibrant display of colors, though it's best to get there a bit before sunrise as the top gets quite crowded.  You can't stay in the temple area and the police do their best to ensure that people aren't blocking the stairways so there's quite limited areas to sit down (the path that leads to Ratnapura Rd seemed to have a bit wider space to allow for seating than the Hatton Rd path). The hard part is going down as you spend all of your energy and muscular exertion stopping yourself from falling forward.  Make sure you're fed and hydrated or else you'll end up with some cramps in your calf like I did and have to hobble down the rest of the way.

My girlfriend and I climbed it on a Monday night during pilgrimage season which was great as it wasn't as busy as we heard it could be on the weekends. We were told that it was about a 4 hour hike to the top so we wanted to be there for sunrise and left at 2am. I'm definitely not the fittest person but we made it up in 2.5 hours. The first 3/4 of the way up was quite warm and we were working up quite a sweat but the last 1/4 of the way up it starts to get pretty cold. Right at the top of the peak it is absolutely freezing so I would recommend taking a few extra layers to put on when you get to the top or even a blanket/sleeping bag (especially if you're like us and get up there early and have to wait for 1.5 hours for the sunrise). The best spot for photos is along the wall where the stairs for the exit are. The view is fantastic from the top but to be honest you can take photos just as good going down the stairs within 200 metres from the top as there are less obstructions and people blocking your view. One thing that we did not expect was the foul stench emanating from the so called 'toilets' all the way up the mountain. Because the toilets are terrible a lot of people (mainly locals) decide to relieve themselves just off the side of the path which adds to the disgusting smell. Overall it was a good experience though especially watching the elderly and families with small children and even babies making the trek which gave more meaning to the pilgrimage but I probably wouldn't do it again if I had the chance. I wouldn't recommend spending any more than 1 night here as there is really nothing else to do. The bus from Hatton train station takes about 75 minutes and runs in time with the train schedule. From memory it was about 65 rupees for the bus. Find a place to stay in Delhousie (they are all pretty average so don't expect much) hike the mountain that night and then leave the next morning. The buses leave for Hatton quite frequently.

It all seems so easy when you arrive at 02:00AM in the morning, looking at the top of the peak thinking to yourself "oh it doesn't look that hard". But it is so worth it, after climbing what felt like an endless amount of stairs we reached the top just after 2 hours of climbing. It was beautiful climbing up as the mist was surrounding the mounting, the full moon shining so bright and the stars so beautiful. On the way too the top there must probably be 100 little shop that sell drinks and snacks. The toilets are disgusting so i would advise you to clear everything out before starting the hike. Reaching the top you are advised by the local police to keep you valuables save and not too journey to any alleys as it may be unsafe. So just go straight to the top and stay there. It gets REALLLLLLY COLD!!! Make sure you take atleast 2 pears of socks as you need to remove your shoe when entering the temple area. Long pants, a warm jacket, beany some gloves and a blanket if you tend to freeze easily or you can be smart like one guy we met and take a sleeping bag :). Seing the sunrise is truly majestic! After that, most of the tourists start making their way down, so if you plan to do the same, try and get a spot close to the exit. Overall and amazing journey with an amazing view, truly rewarding.

How long can you stay on a 'Cross-trainer'? Do you undertake 'back-to-back' step classes? Try twelve hours of continuous stairs. If you want to come face to face with physical suffering, then climb Adams Peak (Sri Pada) during pilgrimage season. Approaching the site in the middle of the night on a jam packed bus, in the distance; I could see the sparkling stairway path, twinkling all the way up to the top of the mountain, glowing incandescently at the summit. Lightening cracks brilliantly behind the mountain and at every flash, reveals the silhouette of Adams Peak. Spectacular. Dracula eat your heart out. An image you would see in a film like ‘Frankenstein’. Sri Pada during pilgrim season is not for the faint of heart. Sri Pada during pilgrim season is not for the weak of mind. The Itinerary... * 12 hours to reach the summit. * 3 hours to get back down. * 15 hours of continuous exertion. * 30 hours without sleep. ... I was utterly distraught! I remember falling in and out of consciousness, in the crush (at the summit) as people kept slapping my cheeks, to see whether or not I was breathing. You see stretcher bearers, definitely. At one point on the way up, traffic came to a complete deadlock for quite a while... crushed together on the mountainside like sardines; I speculated that should one person faint or trip, then like dominoes we would fall. There are Tea Shops at various intervals, all the way up the Mountain and prices are relative to altitude. The higher you go, the more you pay. The physiological impact that I experienced; *Exposure *Dehydration *Sunburn *Third degree lactic burn to 100% of my body. I was dribbling, dizzy, disorientated and had extreme difficulty forming speech. Non compos mentis. Pilgrimage festivals are notorious (Worldwide) for accidents and fatalities. Adams Peak during Pilgrim season, was very dangerous in terms of crowd management. ... there wasn't any... It was a self managed, free formed, Buddhist approach to crowd control which is '' Just love each other and be kind ''. Sadly, Adams Peak is a human tragedy, waiting to happen.

Started the trek at 2am. It's a bit nippy so you'll need trousers and a jumper to start. This is an intense climb up several thousand steps, taking about 3hrs45mins with a few pit stops. (Toilets are few and grim by the way) I'm a relatively fit 30 year old and I found it physically tough on the legs getting to the top. Was amazed to see elderly people getting up and down! Faith must be strong. Every couple of hundred metres or so there's cafes/shacks selling snacks and hot drinks as well as other tat. It's packed when you get to the top. We got there about 5.45am and sunrise was at 6.30ish. It was difficult to get a good view due to the crowds, high fences and man made obstructions. Take a selfie stick to get a decent photo. The decent down the mountain was not any easier and two days later I am still hobbling around.
Great!  - but don't climb in the weekend! & don't be a jerk tourist and skip the queue at the top!

This is one way to do Adams Peak. A must see in Sri Lanka. Take the train to Hatton from Kandy, Ella or where ever you stay in SR. Book a room at Punsisi Rest in Dalhouse and they will have a driver waiting for you at the Hatton station with your name on a board. The Pick up is free and the driver will take you the 30 km to Dalhouse and the hotel. The hotel is a few hundred meters away from the starting point for Adams Peak climb. Check in at the hotel and have dinner and a sleep before you get up at 3 am in the morning to walk your way up to the Adams Peak. We are age 56 and is relatively fit. It took us 2 hours and 14 minutes from the official starting point at the Japanes freindship portal. If you start at 3 am you should have plenty of time to reach the summit before the breathtaking sunrice. I do warn you, it is NOT only an easy walk in a park. The many steps are in some places high and your knees will be sore. Do NOT visit Adams Peak on sundays or at fuld moon. The place Will be crowded and you May not  reach the summit. Bring warm clothes. It is very cold before sunrice at the peak. The walk down is worse the the walk up, I Think. My knees was a shaky and sore. When you reach the hotel, you can have a hot shower and a really good breakfast before you check out and go back to your train in Hatton. There are local buses to Hatton, if you want to save the 1500 rupees, but be sure to reach your train in time. My reason for posting this way to do Adams Peak, is that we found that Dalhouse and Adams Peak was remote and NOT easy to reach by public transport. We almost skipped it. That would have been a shame. Even though it is a circus, with all the small shops and cafees all the Way up, it was a very good experience to do the Adams Peak. And you know what? It is free  of charge, unless you donate some money. If you found my posting usefull, please hit the usefull button 😃

We started the climb at 2 am to see the sunrise. Took me 3:40 hours and i am definitely not athletic, on the contrary! Take your time, rest if needed, take water and a snack (banana or chocolate bar) and warm clothes.  Beware of pickpocketers.  View is very beautiful.

Read my other reviews as they come on line Think carefully about your Jo Upney here, the roads are very difficult if approached from the south, try and come from the north and avoid a white road. We arrived in the evening and could see the peak lit up, an instant feeling of awe. Setting off at 0130 one of our party had joint issues so progress was slow. This is an achievable walk if you are averagely fit and can do steps. There were pilgrims asleep on the steps all the way and very few westerners. The start of this walk is like Romford market on speed selling plastic toys, cuddly toys, inflatable toys and sweet things, don't expect any  quality souvenirs. We didn't make it to the top because of he queues and there were warnings of pick pockets which was a shame. This is more of a cultural experience for Sri lankans than a tourist destination, our Sri Lankan friend felt real spiritual contentment. It was worth the visit to see him so happy

An amazing sacred site seated on the peak on above 7000 ft above sea level. Be sure to be impressed by many Sri Lanka could make it to the peak by all walks of life, women, children, parents carrying kids, elders; most of all, even barefooted, slight handicapped, it's such a phenomenal. Another attraction would be sunrise, you need to start your journey around 2am to reach the peak at 5pm, to secure a good place to catch the breathtaking sunrise! Guide cum helper is avaiable for around Rs2000 per guide.

We enjoyed the view of sun rising more on our way down. At the top there are literally hundreds of tourists and locals which takes away from the whole experience of beauty and tranquility. Massive spotlights ruin the epic sunrise... if you even lucky enough to see anything over all the people and their cameras. My advice: appreciate the sun rising and views as you climb up. Once you at the top it should be light where you can appreciate the 360degree view. One last thing: don't expect a very authentic experience. There are stalls selling all sorts of stuff all the way to the top, even at 3am. And things aren't cheap (to be fair they do have to haul everything up the mountain).

Adam's peak - 5000 more stairs journey begins in the middle of the night and ends at the crack of dawn. Long and difficult journey to the top, requires strength and stamina but worth every second! Reaching the top at dawn is breathtaking and spiritually powerful! Don't miss out on a once in a life experience

A holy mountains climbed daily by thousands of local pilgrims, a must-do during your trip in Sri Lanka if you have the legs and the patience for it! Basically if it's during the weekend, you will need to leave a little bit earlier because of the high number of pilgrims. I did it in the night between Friday and Saturday, left my hotel at 1am and I reached the top just right before the sunrise at 5.45am. But it is not five hours of constant climbing. I climbed maybe 2.5 hours and the remaining time is just queuing during the last kilometer where I advanced one step per minute on average. It was really crowded at the top, it is believed that 20000 pilgrims climb it twice a weekend. So if it is during the week, you can probably leave your hotel at 1.30am, if it is during thr weekend, I would even recommend 12.30 to be sure you can enjoy the sunrise on time. Do take some warm clothes!! It is freezing up there at night, especially when you are stuck in the crowd queuing! And there is some wind as well so you will regret if you didn't take anything. There are plenty of food stores in the first half of the climb, and some stores serve hot tea in the second half as well, when it gets really cold. The whole trail is 8km about so it will be 16km in total and expect to reach your hotel again at around 9 or 9.30am. The sunrise was just wonderful at the end and believe me, it was really worth it! On the second day, go enjoy an ayurvedic body massage, you will need it!

Yes it's tough, but not the toughest hike I've done by far. Now, looking at the mountain from Dalhousie, I wonder how we ever made it, it seems so high and the top so far away. But in fact, it only took 3 hours up at a fairly leisurely pace, having time for shopping downtown for snacks and gear and making several stops on the way up. Even grannies and mom's carrying small babies do it. Back down took us the same time as we felt bored with the never ending steps and had some longer breaks. What helps you most is doing it on a regular work day as you may walk at your own pace, weekend and festival times being very crowded. Also, starting at 2 or 2.30 depending on where you stay in D, you can walk in the cool night air and not the in scorching sun. Also wearing good gear helps a lot (not too hot as you really do sweat! It doesn't get cold until the very last couple of hundred meters). A good idea is also to carry an extra shirt to change into at the top so you don't need to freeze in a wet shirt at the cold and windy summit). I prefer a merino wool shirt as you won't freeze in it even though it gets wet and it's lightweight. Comfy (and hilarious looking) beenies are also sold both downtown D and along the way for 100 rupees, all the locals seem to wear them. As for shoes, you won't need anything special. The path is made of concrete steps all the way until the end. 99% of the locals wear flip flops. Water and snacks are sold every couple of hundreds of meters all the way until the top, so I wouldn't bother carrying too much, water costing 100-200 rupees for a 0,5 liter bottle. Tasty snack such as samosas, dal vadi, biscuits and bananas in every stall. All in all, a good walk, a good workout but by no means impossible if you're a normal healthy person. Coming down and watching the locals do the same walk up carrying 20kg bags of rice and flour and heavy loads of d drinks to sell in the stalls will make you appreciate the effort they make and easily pay the "extra price" for the water. Only thing I wish is, the donation money paid at the start would be used for cleaning up the area. The path up is stinky and the rubbish piles keep growing...

This is a really challenging lifting upstairs, but it is available nearly for everyone: there is a normal stair everywhere (not like on top of Moses peak in Egypt), frequent stops to take a drink, snacks and take a rest. You don't need to be a sportsmen, but should be patient: lift up will take 2 h for sportsmen, 3 h for well-fit and 4-5 for normal fit. Upstairs you will find a tiny temple with Buddha footprint (only outside photo is possible) and several buildings of locals. On top you have to be barefooted - don't forget second socks! View is excellent if it is not cloudy and misty. Many people lift at night to meet sunrise upstairs. Well, good idea, but I reco to take weather as a top 1 term of lifting time choice: picturesque view is better. Reco to stop in one of hotels at the lift start, however be prepared for simple conditions. Better not to prebook, but select being there to check out them instantly. Shops: there are only warm clothes (it may be cold on top), some gifts, drinks and snacks: you won't find such things as medicines, hair dryers etc, that you may need. Considering eating, there are small local cafes, but with very simple food. I reco food-court in a big 4 or 5 floors hotel in a middle of a valley (don't remember it's name, but that's an only big building there).

We had recently been trekking to 5200 metres in Tibet, but this walk up Adam's Peak was at least as difficult, if not more so.  Beginning at 2.00am we made our way to the start and began the climb, which is unrelenting.  Such pilgrimages are the great levellers, elderly Sri Lankans making perhaps their last pilgrimage rub shoulders with young international backpackers and everyone in between.  We are in our sixties [traveling with two daughters in their 20s] and not super fit, but reasonably fit - we found it hard. We arrived about 30 minutes before sunrise, the small area at the top of the peak was already fairly crowded but we did manage to find a place off to one side to await the sunrise.  When it came it was quite spectacular, but I think was eclipsed by the feeling of utter euphoria and relief at having made it to the top.   The walk up is marked by lots of tea shops and small souvenir shops [the last thing on your mind when you are exhausted], and is very picturesque.  It would be best to avoid full moon days or any kind of holy day as we heard that the crowds can become so huge that it completely reduces the experience. We were warned that the walk down was more difficult, I had mentally dismissed this as nonsense - it;s not!  The walk down is very difficult, especially on the knees and ankles.  All this makes it sound like an ordeal, it wasn;t, it was actually a highlight of the trip, it just calls for determination and a bit of fortitude.  My resolve was strengthened on the way down when we passed and elderly Sri Lankan lady, obviously in poor health, being assisted to make the climb by her two grandsons.  Suddenly there was nothing more to complain about!

Your legs will be so sore after this! Don't go on a sunday morning to climb, it is packed with the thousands and therefore many didn't make it to the top because the top got full and no more could get up....

The walk to the top of Adam`s Peak is extremely boring. The stairs seem never ending. But the atmosphere at the top while sunrise is amazing. Multicultural crowd wait for the moment when first ray of sunshine wil touch gently the temple. Prayers begin. The triangle-shaped shadow of the mountain is extraordinary. Worth to climb all the way to experience it.

We used the train to reach there.  We left Colombo Fort at about 12pm and reached Hatton around 7pm and from Hatton we hired a taxi which was about an hours drive to Dalhousie. We reached around 8.30 pm and had dinner at Adams Peak. We decided not to hire a room and passed time by sitting at cafe and playing cards. We started the hike at 1.30am and reached the top at about 5 am. It was a beautiful place ans saw the foot imprints. We started the climb down and reached about 8.30am . I feel one needs to be fit to climb this up and down and it was very tough. In the end with the climb down our legs were like Jelly. The view is great going up at night and climbing down in the morning. On our way going up and down were many little tea and food stalls and toilets (pit latrines) every 20 minutes. The climb is worth it, we didn't see the sunrise from the top but while we were going down which was beautiful. After having breakfast we went straight to Colombo and didn't see the need to hire rooms.

An absolute must-do in Sri Lanka: probably the best experience in our 4 weeks of traveling around the country. It took us 2 hours to get to the top, in a slow comfortable pace it usually takes people 3-4. The path is very comfortable, with tea shops, snacks, food and toilets at literally every 20 minutes. Which is both a big plus - but also quite a disadvantage, as it takes away the romance of the climb. People are many, and especially at the top at sunrise it might be difficult to fully enjoy as you have to almost fight for a spot. That being said, the view is stunning - and well worth the climb. Don't worry too much about carrying much stuff - you can buy most of what you need during your climb (sweaters, scarfs, water, etc included). The way back is quite picturesque too - in the morning you can enjoy the view if tea plantations and locals gathering tea, which in itself is a nice sight. Highly recommended experience
Get up early avoid holy days and climb the thousands of steps, stop off for tea and snacks. Hope for a decent sunrise although the views are magnificent without. Tiring but unique pilgrim experience.

I climbed it three times in a month. It's so amazing. You start the hike around 2am, and it takes in between two and three hours, plus breaks if you need (plenty of tea and snacks shops along the way). As you climb you can look down and see the lights of the trail, or look all around and see the stars. The atmosphere is fantastic, since it's challenging, everyone supports everyone all the way, the energy is so good. Then you reach the top, with its beautiful temple and people, and wait for the sunrise. And what a sunrise. If the weather is good, it will leave you speechless. And you go down with this beautiful morning light surrounding everything. Truly magical experience. Warning though, even if full moon (poya) is indeed even better to see, it gets absolutely crowded at this time of the month, which makes the climb not enjoyable at all, it can take up to ten hours to reach the top! Not worth it.

We mistakenly climbed on poya day during independence week. WOW it was chockers... We got up at 1am and ran for the first hour to get ahead of the crowds.. People were sleeping on the path as we ran past them... We got to the last bit of the summit where we hit  a jam. IT took us 3 hours to get up the stairs for the last bit but we unbelievably made the sunrise... On the way down it was so packed that we could hardly get past the queue going the other way.... What an experience. So happy we made it but probably better to go during the downtime.

This is a must visit place if you are traveling to Sri Lanka. Make sure you book a place to stay before you arrive.If you are using the public transport you can take the train from Colombo Fort station (you can even pre book a seat) to Hatton station and from Hatton take a bus to Nallathanniya. Or even you can take a bus from Colombo Fort - Hatton. Its a clod place so bring your warm cloths.Make sure you reach the peak by morning 6.00 you must see the amazing sunrise....!!!!Try to bring some biscuits and drinking water with you.Don't eat any rotty on your way to the peak.Maggi noodles are the only fresh thing you can get. Try to avoid weekends and public holidays as its going to be so crowded. enjoy your hike.this is a nice place to visit.

Definitely a must-do whilst in Sri Lanka. It's hard work, there's no doubt, but well worth the views & the sense of achievement when you finish! As two reasonably fit 30 year olds it took us 3.5hrs including a dosa & tea stop near the top. We didn't leave until about 3am and got there in plenty of time for sun rise, but recommend getting up a bit earlier if you can so you get a good spot to watch the sun rise from. Definitely take lots of warm clothes too as it's chilly at the top!

If you have enough of heat during the day it is a good oportunity to refresh yourself on the top at 5.00am :) And it's worthy. Nice view. We did it in exactly 2h with small breakes. If you are not a good hiker or you likes to walk very slow you have to count 2.5-3h. Better pack warm clothes to the backpack cause on the top in the morning is cold and windy. Lot of people (also locals) write about leeches. We were there (february) just after heavy rain and didn't see them but better to be prepared :) Have fun!
Good viewpoint and free entry holy place. In weekend very crowded, use western way - eastern way have long queue (see Google map).

Reading the guide book before I came to Sri Lanka, I knew this was a complete must to do. And it was pilgrimage season, so to do at night they said would be best. They were right. We started the climb from a little village called Dalhousie at 2am and made our way up the 7km route/5,300 steps to the top. The path was illuminated and there were regular stalls on the way selling food, tea (the nicest tea ever!) and bits and bobs. The walk was tough. Very tough, but we made it to the top for 6am, as the sun was rising! It was unreal! So amazing! Spent some time at the top, in the temple grounds and then made our way back down. This was a totally different experience again - we could see all the stunning scenery that we were unaware of in the dark! Hills, mountains, rivers, mini waterfalls, tea plantations, Monkeys! Again - this walk was not the easiest, and as a person who suffers with knee problem, I was in pain for a couple of days after. But even knowing that I would 10000% do it for the amazing views and how it made you feel on top of the world! One other point - I would highly recommend The White House accommodation in the village of Dalhousie. It is in both the Rough Guides and Lonely Planet travel guide books but I couldn't find it on here. The accommodation was lovely, lovely grounds and river you chill by. Food - buffet dinner and lots for breakfast, was delicious! And super cheap too. Staff couldn't do enough for you. :) Fantastic weekend! And great surrounding area - great for tea plantation/factory visits!

Pain in our legs lasted for a week after! BUT....so worth it. Make sure to get a massage afterwards to ease the aching muscles. Most amazing sight are all the elder and handicapped people taking on this huge challenge.

We just finished our trek up to Adams peak and absolutely loved it! Stunning views- even though we didn't make it quite to the top because it was so busy! If you can, try to avoid climbing at the weekend as it gets sooo busy and It made the experience a little uncomfortable towards the end. We queued for 3 hours to get to the top and got 5 meters from the temple and had to turn back as it was just gridlocked! We were told by two french girls on the way down that the view from where we were standing was actually better than from the peak anyway! It's a demanding climb but well worth it for the view! we started at 2am and without queues would have made it in plenty of time to the temple for sunrise - and I consider myself a v. slow walker! Bring good walking shoes and water/snacks. There are toilets but only use them if you are absolutely desperate...It took us 6 hours in total with queuing time! next time we will climb on a week day!

This hike is longer than the two other popular routes and harder to find the trail head.The trail is lit almost the entire way, but a small flashlight will help you get through the small portions of the trail that may have lost light. We rarerly went more than 100 meters between burnt out light bulbs. The route is challenging and would recommend taking two days as there are plenty of places to take refuge on the trail. We pushed it to the extreme and did the whole trip inside 24 hours, a big mistake as we did not get enough or any down time to properly rest and were physically beat up by the descent. Not too many foreigners take this trail due to their time constraints but if you are up for it, it is a spectacular hike even at night! I can not wait to do it again in order to the sunset spend the night and see the sunrise! I have spent at least 12 months of my time in Sri Lanka over a 7 year period and this is an absolute must do trip!
Pain in our legs lasted for a wk after! BUT....so worth it. Amazing amazing amazing- photos don't do it justice!

Adams Peak is simple and stunning. Stay in a local hotel, climb the peak in the early hours and watch the sunrise over the mountains, it is peaceful and beautiful. A few things to note: You need not stay in the area more than one night, there is little else to do. Also, bring warm clothing in a bag to put on at the top of the mountain, although it is hot walking up and down the mountain, once you stop walking it does get very cold whilst you await the sunrise. You most definitely do not need a guide for this trip the route is very obvious. It's takes around 2.5 hours at a normal walking pace and the sun rises between 5:45-6:15 so get up and go, there are plenty of little stalls selling snacks, hot meals, tea, coffee and water for the duration of the walk. If you can fit this into your trip as a couple or a group of friends it is a lovely experience and shouldn't be missed.

This climb was tough but totally worth it. We left the bottom at about 2am and got up there around 4:30am. The sunrise was one of the best I've seen! Certainly a must do, be prepared for lots of stairs though, take warm clothes for the top as it gets cold!

Start your hike just after 2am or a bit later if you are confident that you are fit. The hike is 14km return and proved to be quite difficult to hike up and back down. You will no doubt feel the joints of your knee wobble as you make your way down. The view of the sun rising behind mountains of the Sri Lanka is one of the most scenic things I've seen in my life. As you walk around the temple situated at the top, you will get different views of the sunrise. Make sure you pack some snacks or buy them at the bottom. Once you're near the top, the local vendors hijacks the price i.e 150 rupees for one banana.

Only do it, if you have a long enough stay in Sri Lanka. In mid-January my girlfriend and I climbed to the top a cold morning. The sunrise was beautiful, I'll give people that - but it wasn't worth the trip up and down the mountain. We left our bungalow - which was situated about an hour's drive away - at 01 a.m. We arrived an hour later and reached the top around 04.45. It seemed a bit early, but at 05.25 the best seats were taken. The sun rose around 06 am. and we left the peak around half an hour later. The climb down took two hours. The sunrise was beautiful, but the noise and setting during the sunrise ruined much of the experience. And due to the fact that we lost a great amount of sleep - affecting both the evening before and the day afterwards I'll recommend it, only if you have time enough. /Peter (&Anne) PS. Remember warm clothes for the waiting at the top - a blanket would also be a good idea - and toiletpaper.

After a long bumpy winding 4 hr drive to our hotel. Then a short night of sleep and another 1 hour drive at 1am we made it to Adams Peak. We are in our late thirties and in great shape and this was still a trek that made the legs sore! The trek from the bottom starts out pretty mild but in the second half gets pretty Crazy hard with straight steps at a very steep pitch. Make sure to wear socks as you have to take your shoes off at the top and your feet get very cold. Also wear layers! We took everything off on the way up as we were pretty sweaty even at night temperatures, when you get to the top and have to wait an hour for the sun you will put them all back on. Women also must have their legs covered. Once the sun came up it got fairly cloudy and we only got brief peaks at the sun but on the trek back down we were able to get beautiful pics. It feels like a great accomplishment when you finish and you won't regret it. The only downside it getting there ( we came from Unawatuna) one of the worst drives ever - if you get car sick easy this is not a trip for you!)

The climb starts at 2:30-3 am after a short nights sleep, and the first steps up the pilgrimage path begins easily for us. As we approach halfway and the steps gets steeper and steeper, the going is also slower and slower and the touts selling tea and a samosa or banana becomes a nice addition to the climb instead of a bother. The sunrise is totally worth the climb - but you actually see it better standing in the stairs just below the monastery than if you go to the obscured viewing platform. Enjoy!

Well I was told I would be able to do this climb easy, that was so not the case. I am 54 years of age, and whilst I play golf, nothing could compare to this. My son had previously done the climb in 2 hours, and that was with a wait at the top. So I think he expected 2.5 hours for the two of us. Well it happened to be 3 hours, and a lot of coaching from my son. Did I want to give up, yes most definitely. Thank goodness I didnt. The sunrise was amazing, and the budders footprint was also great. Yes it is cold at the top, so sit in the last shop and have some tea, also put on extra layers. I was a little bit disappointed by the wiring system at the top, talk about obscuring ones view. Then it's the coming down, it is relentless, wobbly legs, but as you have to get down, somehow it's fine. Didn't take too long at all. Now for the legs after, I have not ever been in so much pain. 1 week later and things are back to normal.

Having completed Adams Peak twice, I have yet to see the shadow of the mountains, despite this I have not regretted it once! The views from the top are breath-taking and it's probably the best achievement possible in Sri Lanka!! Please ignore the negative comments and make sure you do your research and follow these steps: 1) DONT LEAVE TOO EARLY! It's bloody freezing at the top and it takes an average person (I'm not an avid walker) about 3 hours to climb. 2) take toilet roll 3) take a thick blanket for the top if you do get there early 4) we bought ponchos at the bottom due to rain! Best decision EVER 5) take snacks, not only for your but for the cheeky Sri Lankan kids who have camped over night at the top And most importantly DO NOT ATTEMPT THIS ON POYA DAY!! It is comical to read some of the negative reviews of ques and being very busy. To us it was almost common sense not to climb when every Buddhist in Sri lanka will be climbing too! Both times I have climbed we have had pretty much the whole climb to ourselves, only slight ques walking down! Lesson of the day is don't climb Adams peak on poya!!

Adam's Peak is a must do in Sri Lanka for those who are fit and enjoy hiking and the outdoors. The path is wide, well marked and well lit. The path is predominantly stairs and gets steep towards the top. There are stalls along the way but the path is not overcrowded with salespeople (like the Great Wall can be). The scenery is pleasant - there are many waterfalls in nearby mountains. The walk is difficult. It took us about two hours and twenty minutes. When we walked it drizzled or rained the whole way and there was low cloud. Hence there was no sunrise or view from the top. We knew the forecast so we began the walk at 530 am rather than the traditional 2 or 3 am start. This meant we had the path to ourselves and we weren't too tired later in the day. There is very little else to do in Dalhouise so don't bother spending much time there unless you want to stay a few days to wait for the perfect time/day to climb.

One of the highlights of our holidays. I was a bit unsure of doing this at first. The thought of 6000 steps, a 2am start and me not being all that fit (!) was not appealing. However I am sooooo glad I did it. Starting at 2am is really worthwhile. The climb is much cooler than during the day and the steps are well illuminated (but only during the pilgrimage season). There are plenty of tea houses along the way to stop and have refreshments and the paths are wide enough to stop regularly to catch your breathe and let others past you. I took my time and there was no pressure to speed up- in fact it was comforting to see everyone else around me trying to catch their breathe too! - so it took me 3 1/2 hrs, which got us there in plenty of time before the sunrise. It was cold up there though so definitely take extra clothes, gloves, hats, scarves (maybe even a blanket!) to put on. The  sunrise, temple and views from the top are spectacular and our favourite photos from the holiday. On the way down enjoyed seeing the sites in the daylight and found the beautiful Japanese peace pagoda a great spot as well.

Definitely the highlight of my holiday in Sri Lanka! Yes, it is a hard and long climb, especially if you are not fit, but it's worth every step. I started at 2 am and it took me a bit less than three hours, stopping every now and then to catch my breath. I went on season, so I didn't need to get a guide even if I was on my own. You'll find plenty of people on the way. The last hour of the climb was really tough, but I made it. I felt a great sense of achievement when I got to the top and the sunrise was stunning.

do not miss Adams peak! after a great drive alongside tee plantation and a beautiful lake, we arrived at the hotel, we had planed to go op at night but since the rain was not going to lrt up decided to start at ~15.00 we made the track up the 7000 steps in just over 2 h. (there where not a lot of pilgrims on the way up, so no traffic jams )  be aware the the top can be verry windy , so bring a good jacket! as for the footwear we did used good flip flops.

Wake at 2 am and start your hike in the dark. I promised myself I would not write anything to ruin ones own experience. Yes, dress in layers and bring water and snacks. It is a long climb but very enjoyable. 3 hours up, perhaps. We took our time to enjoy each moment and catch our breath. For me, the best part was hearing the other languages on the way and watching families and seeing the young kids bound down the steps with ease. At one point we saw 2 young boys ( late teen age perhaps)  helping -whom appeared to be their Grandfather-on the climb.They had apparently assisted him, practically carrying him, both up and down this mountain. That, for me, was the most touching part of the trip.Famiy. It is the journey, each step, each voice, each breath. For some it is about reaching the top, or being first, or wanting to say they did it. For others, it is a deep spiritual experience that they have waited years to earn. Each body handles it differently. Each precious soul that we passed was my joy in this trip. From silly boys starting up conversation to the very old man that makes this a special place. I was amused that you could get soda, tea and cheeto puffs on the trail. The steps are wide until the end and then the rail helps assist you. Go for your own experience. My daughter took a photo of 3 birds 1/2 way down that took the prize photo upon our return. Adams Peak birds, just like the 2 boys and their Grandfather. This is a magical and special place. Upon coming down we saw lots of monkeys and almost took the wrong turn and a little boy, about 4, told us with a bright smile, which was to go. He is etched into my heart. What a magical place. Go in good health. Enjoy! USA

Im not fit and have bad knees but managed to do this - so if I can than you can! We got a guide as were a group of girls and when we set out it was pitch black with no-one around. I would suggest a guide, it is cheap espec if you are a group and divide between yourselves. It took us 3-4 hours to climb up but we took a long rest before the last climb as were ahead of schedule. It's really cold at the top so bring an extra jumper and hat. Walking sticks help. Our guide helped carry our bags when we were tired and updated us each km we completed as there are no signs telling you how much further to go! Also he got us a special balm (smelt like tiger balm) to protect against leeches. The view is amazing. Took us 3 hours to go back down and it gets warm during the daytime and its nice to see the views you missed at night. Many shops along the way selling snacks, drinks, tea, sweets so no need to take much. Definitely worth it!

We started the climb at 2.30am, knowing very well we would not see the sunrise given the cloud and rainy weather but decided to do it as we are trail enthusiast and we loved the idea of sharing spiritual path with the pilgrimage across religious (see the history, quite interesting about how each religions value the 'sri pada'). As we did it during the beginning of the season, the crowd is not yet there and the path was pretty much for us at our pace. We exercise regularly and finished ascending to the top by 2 hrs,  our parent (60 y.o. +) finished 2.5 hr (they regular trek as well). Steps were well made and challenging but not dangerous with the steel hand rail along the side. There were lights all the way up which made it extra beautiful looking down the trail. The temple was worth the visit  despite exposing your cold feet as shoes were not allowed inside. The locals, walking up in slippers and praying, will make you more determined to reach the peak. Descending took almost same time, a lot of pause for breathtaking view. It was really a pleasant journey. If you can carry a backpack, bring some clothes to change or put on top as your sweat will make you super cold at the top especially if you were waiting for the sunrise. There were hops all along for water and snacks. Stop by at the tea shop to keep yourself warm. The last stop before the temple generously offered free curry rice to any visitors. Good spiritual and physical activity.

Adam's peak is located in south central Highlands of Sri Lanka, in the Ratnapura District and Nuwaraeliya district of the Sabaragamuwa Province and central province. T/4 nearly half of the year (06 months) is close for pilgrimages due to heavy rainfall during May to December of every year. Season start from December full moon day with cultural activities up to Full moon day of May, and it's call "Vesak full moon day" by Buddhists. Since major crowed is visiting Adam's peak in high season and Climbing Adam's peak in low season is a bit of risk due to lack of safety and no service providers are available.

Adam's Peak is the number one most brutal physical undertaking in 10 months of active travel. This is not a hike for the casual.  In fact it isn't even a hike.  It's a climb up thousands of steps with very little variation in composition.  After the first 1/5 of the journey or so there are never flat spots, never down hill parts and it's never on a slope.  It's a non-stop climb and unlike the theoretical ideal of let's say climbing the empire state building stairs - there are almost no landings.   The steps are in decent condition - IE - they aren't falling apart, but they are also not consistent in height - some are smaller than a western step but really most are taller than a western step.  The only thing you can count on is that the height changes. Does this sound like heaven or hell?   I am not the person to consider it to sound like heaven but on the flip side the payoff can be glorious.   The view from the top is absolutely stunning.   the feeling of accomplishment is excellent and the comraderie can be wonderful .... as long as you can actually see - which we were lucky enough to do. Here are some pieces of advice - #1 - research what the Sri Lankan crowd will be at the time you are visiting.   We went "Off season".   This means only international tourists.  From what we were told about "On season" when the Sri Lankans flock here for annual pilgrimages it sounds as if it could be an absolute nightmare.   We were told by a trusted local that sometimes it takes several minutes to make a single step up the stairs.  This would be an absolute nightmare.  Horrible.  Can't even imagine it.   I am guessing the "terrible" reviews all visited in this period. Again - ask about what the local traffic will be like while you are there and do NOT go when it's peak. #2 - If you are going 'off season' and there is cloud cover or you can't see the peak when you plan to go at 2:00 DO NOT GO.  We spoke to people that made the climb and saw nothing and I simply couldn't imagine that feeling.   It would be horrible to make this ascent and see nothing.   The weather pattern works like this - if it's cloudy at 2AM it will most likely be cloudy at sunrise - don't let your tuk tuk driver or hotelier tell you otherwise.  Wait until you can see the stars at 2:00AM - if you can see them then you have the best chance of making sunrise. #3 - although I stated it before - this isn't for the weak legged.  Your legs are going to hurt and if you aren't in excellent shape you more than likely will not make the climb.  Don't take this warning lightly.   This will be the most challenging climb in years unless you are a sheer face rock climber and even then it's totally different.  No one - I mean no one - climbs up constant stairs like this in any venue. Be ready with this information and you can have a glorious, exhilarating experience.    Ignore the advice and you will just be sorry and mad at yourself.

Climbing up Adam's Peak is very very challenging. Those who are planning to climb up the mountain, are advised to start the journey as early as possible. frequent breaks really help to restore your stamina. Don't forget to carry sufficient water, chocolates, and food items with you. Water keeps you hydrated while chocolates keep your sugar and energy levels high. You can't find any food or beverages on the top so plan your trip well prior to start journey. The weather is unpredictable, so don't forget to carry an umbrella with you. If it rains, be aware of leeches, the rubber shoes are a recommended practice if the sole is not slippery. Overall, it is a hard job and physically very challenging. When you reach at the top, you can enjoy the spectacular scene of the surroundings and the sun rise scene is of particular interest. Good luck!

It was one of my must "to dos" while planning the trip to Sri Lanka due to positive reviews. Must say it was worth it. Started my walk at 2 in the morning with a guide. We were told that sunrise will not be visible, but we had a pretty amazing time and excellent views. Nature is unpredictable, so I'd say take your chances. Strongly recommend a guide if going during the off season as it is pretty deserted and the number of other travelers may be scanty. Took me and my guide approx. 2.5 hours to reach the top, but folks with lesser climbing experience took about 3-3.5 hours. I understand that doing this in peak season may take more than 4-5 hours due to huge crowd. The downside of climbing during the off season is that the main temple compound is closed for public viewing, so you can't see the "foot". But other wise, the sunrise is amazing and you can have a 360 degree view of the surroundings. It gets very very windy at the top at night and so, must carry a shawl/ windcheater.

I undertook this climb as I’d never had the chance before & also as a “must see” attraction for an Australian friend who accompanied us to Sri Lanka.  We actually travelled over one year ago but I feel I must add some comments about my experience. In the early hours one morning, we drove as far as we were allowed to & then started our 7km journey to the peak in the dark.  Soon realising that my pace was too slow, I urged my companion to go ahead without me.  With hindsight, this was a bad idea.  The uphill trek in darkness became a mentally draining & lonely exercise.  Physically too it proved very difficult & I felt my legs quivering. I stopped many times for breaks & reached the top later than anticipated thereby missing the sunrise.  Though I absorbed the beauty of the landscape from the summit, I spiralled into what I can only call a deep depression.  Try as I might, I couldn’t even recall a prayer:-( I’m aware that climbing this sacred mountain (hallowed to many religions), it is ‘bad form’ to express this negativity.  Now looking back, I appreciate the achievement & I’m glad I made the effort.  For this reason, I rate it 4 stars. My advice to others contemplating this climb is as follows: 1)  you need to have got your fitness levels up 2)  keep hydrating yourself along the way 3)  carry some sweets with you for an occasional sugar hit 3)  if you’re a slow climber, keep more time for the ascent 4)  NEVER CLIMB ALONE!

I'm not going to lie physically very challenging but it's mind over matter! Left Clovefield Villa Laxapana via tuk tuk about an hours drive at 2am began the climb... You come across two Buddhist minks at different points who put bands on your wrists for a 'donation' of around 1000 pp. (most common amount) and they wish you luck which you will need. It's a tough climb in pitch black - pack a torch or head lamps - mozzies bring aerogard - and leeches are everywhere pack some salt! It poured rain on us but we kept going 2.5hrs later reached the top to be told we were half way bahaa not so funny at the time! It's cold up there but mid during the climb so pack extra layers. Can big tea at the top off peeps who live up there temple opens at 6am - only in season. 6 months not open which is when we went. No sunrise due to the cloud cover but a total achievement and glad we did it. The trip down hurts the legs too but at least you can see the scenery which is breathtaking and totally worth the blood sweat and tears in the way up - Adams Peak would only do it once and glad we did ;) Carly & Breyton Coogee

Climbing Adam's peak is certainly a challenge, but can be fun if you have good company. As other reviewers said, it's better not to go during rainy season. It can be too wet and slippery. There is a path to follow, so it's not too rough. Just bring good, waterproof hiking boots, maybe a walking stick, food and water. The view from the top is amazing. I'm really glad I did it! If you are adventurous and are happy to take your time climbing up, you'll like it.

I did this in the off season which was great as there were many less people but it did mean you couldn't go into the monastery at the top. This wasn't a problem as you get to the top anyway and you get to see all the views anyway. High season can be extremely busy with the steps becoming a bit like a long queue at the top. There are steps all the way up so you don't need any experience just a relative fitness level. Going up is relatively easy but the decent is surprisingly hard, especially at the end. We left at 5am so didn't see sunrise but that was fine as you then saw all the views on the way up which were stunning. No need to get a guide as you can't get lost and there was no entry fee which was nice.

Please be prepare before you start. its quite challenging but worth to it. I would like to suggest not to go to here if you are in rushing because you will miss the feel of the mountain and forest here. the best about this place is Adam;s footprint it self which is only one in the world!!! and also the view from the top of it.

Sure enough that we have read a lot of reviews and received so many local advices about climbing Adam's Peak during off season or not. Well, locals, as a habit, visit the place during season, and thus they will definitely recommend not to visit it during off season as it rains heavily and all the shops are closed etc etc. All these points are so true: it rains heavily, and no shop is open..This makes us question the safety! After arriving the place around 9 pm, we have decided not to climb at night (well, tradition is to start it by 2.30 am to see the sunrise). In the end, we have started to climb around 11 am after a good night sleep: very important as you will need a lot of endurance during the climb. In brief, it proved to be the right decision: very challenging but well worthy experience.. No safety issue but it does not mean that you will not check around as few tourists are there to climb..no matter how safe you feel, just pay attention to your surroundings. Ok, here is the nice part : The climb starts with gentle walk paths and some steps. After an hour, you enjoy a break of ten minutes near a Budist Temple. Second stage starts with steep steps that burns your muscles. After the second hour ends, during the break, you are in between continuing or giving up. When you continue the final stage, which is the third hour, you can be sure that you will not forget this wet, extreme, in some sense enjoyable experience with lots of impressive sightseeing in your life. The walking path is quite ok, you are not walking on a muddy ground, they are in fact concrete steps..but at the last stage, wind and rain impact you a lot and you need to be more cautious..last point: Adam's Peak-the holy place- is closed and also the sky is sooo misty during off season, and what you do is totally physical challenge, forget about the bird eye view of Sri Lanka. All in all, here is the reco: do not climb at night and get a good raincoat and an extra tshirt to change. Enjoy :)

Initially we were slightly anxious regarding the weather, having read several negative reviews of rain and fog. However we set off at 2.20am for the top spot in high spirits.
