We walked at a steady pace with many comfort breaks and I must say we made pretty good time arriving at the peak at 4:50am, I anything a little early in fact for the 6am sunrise. But let me just say what a magnificent view Adam bestowed upon us. We could see for miles and miles and treated ourselves to a cup of sweet tea to warm our weary bones. The only one negative was that it being low season the viewing platform was closed, however we knew this in advance. And this did at least mean that there were not very many people~30 at the top. Would thoroughly recommend this to fellow adventurers and sunrise seekers.

I recommend booking a guide for 2500 from a hotel near by and go out of season, the climb is amazing, such a nice challenge and it was exciting to do it in pitch black. Take a torch. It may be a bit rainy so take water proofs. At the top it is freezing, take warm clothing. Cover up skin as much as you can because leeches are about. Although I didn't get a single one. We set off at 2am and Made it up to the top in 2 hours, although I do a fair bit of walking and excessive already. My friend who is a heavy smoker and not a regular walker did it in 3 and a half. Check when sunrise is. Gets very cold waiting for the sunrise once you are at the top. The top of the mountain is built up as it is a temple and the foot print thing. But the view is breathtakingly beautiful. The climb down us difficult, takes less time the views make up for the joints giving way! Steps all the way. Right as the top there are railings to help if needs be. Food I recommend. You can buy black very sugary tea at the top for 150. Oh and only pay what you want if you choose to be blessed by the monk. We only gave them 500. Don't feel obliged to give any more than that. Enjoy!! Ps. I'm keen for nature and exercise. Oh and the stars you will see are vast and amazing. Just do it!

October 2014 Ok so after completing Adams Peak I thought I would look at reviews. /couldn't help but look at the 1 star reviews to see what the bad stories were. Basically after reading all I can say is thank god we did it out of season! Sounds absolutely horrible!! It took us 2.5 hours up (started at 3 AM) and pretty much the same on the way down (its pretty hard on the knees on the way down). Plenty of space on top at this time of year to walk around and take pics. Only tourists there too. Down point would be that there are buildings on top which let the view down..its hard to get even a clear 90 degree view without the buildings in it. However the views on the way down are incredible and I would still say it's definately worth it and very rewarding! JUST DONT DO IN HIGH SEASON OR HOLIDAYS!!!

Mid-september 2014. Weather was rainy some days before and it was really hard to decide do the climb or not reading all those whining off-season reviews. But in the end we decided to go (no, srsly, to be in sri lanka and not to climb Adam's peak is like to be and sri lanka and not to buy some fine tea). Looks like we got extremely lucky - sky was clear all night, bright stars, no rain, no fog, yes the wind is blowing - but it's a mountain, what do you expect, take some windproof jacket. You will be totally wet at the top too so take a spare dry t-shirt with you. There were like 10 more guys with us - all tourists - so no crowd like there is in season. Started at 2:20, finished at 5:10, sunrise was at 5:30 or something like that. Views are absolutely stunning and worth every step of that goddamn ladder (I hated all ladders for like 3 days after that climb). Sunrise is great but morning views when mist starts to go up are even better. Go for it, and you will be rewarded.

September, 2014. Out of season and we knew that the top would be closed, but decided to give the climb a try.....(the wife). We started out in a drizzle, then sunny, then foggy, then cold, then really ugly and windy. I dropped out at 7,000 feet and my wife went to the top and took some stunningly foggy photos that barely shows that she got there. Why on earth we attempted to climb this mountain is beyond me!!! We were the only ones on the hike but did encounter several groups of young men on their way up as we were limping down. If one is not a devotee, adherent or pilgrim climbing it is pretty pointless since not one person in one hundred thousand has ever heard of Sri Lanka much less Adam's Peak.

We went up in early September so off season. After reading in books and online that it would take 4hours and when fit 3 hours we started at 2:30 to be on the top before sunrise. A dark and unfortunately rainy walk took us only 2hours to reach the top, so we had to wait 1,5 hours being wet/cold. But it was worth it! Nice view, great sunrise, too bad the actual top gate was kept closed in this off season. So depending on the season you go up and how fit you are (we run 2x a week and go the the gym, pretty standard and not ironman fit or whatever) don't start too early ;)

1) We was climbed in augest, unseasson. No lighter, just 1 or 2 working caffe and rest point. 2) we start at 2'oclock am, but thats was our fault. In unseasson no reason to wake up so early. we was not ready with our equipments, so we was got all wet on the end of the way. During hole night was rain with the wind. On the top of the hill was not worked anything, but we must know that! thats why don't forget to take good rain protect close, good warm tee, some dry close. 3) soft of 2 hours we spend on the way. Yes our legs was ached terrible, and descent thought faster but more difficult. 4) if u will be lucky u will catch the sunrise. on the descent way u will see amazing waterfall.

It was tough but a good experience. Unfortunately weather wasn't great. If you decide to go there prepare for about 3 hours climbing up on stairs. going back there is a nice waterfall. I think it's a must do thing for those who like adventures.

We went off season, we went on our honeymoon, no we are not extreme hikers, but you only live once. It was cold, it was misty, it was middle of July. Just me, my newlywed wife and our guide provided by Slightly Chilled guesthouse in Nalatthaniya, and we went up the stairs like crazy people on a mission. The view up top can be good, but it was too misty to see anything. Also the guy who lives up at the top didn't let us use the restroom, not sure why. The way down sucks cause your thighs are trembling by now. Bring sweaters. We live in Washington DC, so we know cold weather, and this mountain is cold.

This is one of the best things one can do in Sri Lanka. As the common Sri Lankan saying says: "If you are in Sri Lanka and you don't climb Adam's Peak you are a fool, if you do it twice, you are a bigger fool" :)

We stayed in Hatton, roughly one hour fifteen from Dalhousie, the start of the climb. For the package, we used a local taxi driver called Saman. He can be contacted on +94 (0)771 978 992 or saman.hatton@gmail.com.  Extremely good value and always punctual, he also assisted in sourcing a guide. The climb is fairly long although takes less than the four hrs suggested. Even if the weather forecast isn't great, it is still worth the effort for the cloudforest you pass through on the descent. There are toilets along the way although bring your own loo roll!

Just came back from Adam's peak (July 22), ~6000 steps each way to reach the top and see nothing but clouds and mist. It did get us a good laugh at ourselves and all the other "crazy" tourists that went up :) My personal recommendation is to pass on it if it's not a high chance of sunshine at the top... your knees will thank you.
Exhausting, tiring, painful, but and absolute must do. You cannot go to Sri Lanka without hiking Adams Peak. Just make sure you don't go during pilmgramage season like we did!!

5200 stairs, if you are not used to walking you are definitely going to feel this one. Out of season did this in June, was raining most of the way. No other people on the route, just me and my friend. Got to the top, gate was locked, no foot print, rain so cloudy no view at all. We still enjoyed the walk, about three and a half hours up and down, we were told very slow with lot of rest should take about 6 hours.

Okay, so we were told that we should start walking at 2 am to get to the top in time for sunrise. So with no sleep, and no breakfast, we started this climb - and halfway up I told my boyfriend I had never been so exhausted in my life. And I actually think that was true. It is a really nice walk, and doing in at night is sort of an adventure (but bring a flaslight, or forget about it!), but if I were ever to do it again, I would not start at night. The sunrise people were talking so much about was nothing much. It gradually stopped being dark. That was it. But the view is great, and we looked down at the clouds, which was beautiful. So if you're in okay shape I would recommend the climb for sure.

We started at 9 in the moring and finished by 4 afternoon .it was extremely hard , for few days later we had dificulty in walking and sleeping . Will i go again? Surley yes its an adiction and the people around are cerry helpfull younwill be encourged by number of elderly people walking along the road .try it once in your life you will remember for years to come. Its adam peak!

Yes, it would be a nice trip, but the rain rains, the fog was everywhere, and I am not a nature love person, but wants to climb the peak, because of its importance for the Buddhists (and other religions) and after see Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, Sigiriya and Dambulla I think its a must. At 1st of July there was only 3 tourists before us at the bottom of the peak - theres a book of donations where you can write your name and donate the monk sitting by the book :) The actual fare is 1000 Rs. for person. But day before there was 16 tourists, than, when the weather is terrible, the tourists go to the peak also (but not the Sri Lankan people). I was only at half way (3 km), but my husband goes to the top (6 km and 6 km back). For him takes the on-and-back trip for 5 hours - also take pictures and has a dog-guard by his side. All the other tourists on the top has one dog :) For me at this weather the half-way was enough, at the top was also fog and rain, than I don't let nothing. It would be nicer at good weather, when is the season.

So, me being all so adventurous and ambitious travelled to Sri Lanka to climb this mountain.. I booked a near by hotel for overnight stay slept till 2 am and started off my journey towards the mountain alone but later I was joined by so many other climbers from all over the world . It was the sacred time of the month for Buddhist people but all I could see were foreign climbers including myself . It took me four hours to get to the top. Many women from Europe in better shape than me gave up before half way up. So it doesn't matter what shape you are .. You just have to keep going. Don't stop much just take 2/3 minutes breaks . Don't lug too much food like me or clothes . Just a stick to balance yourself. Trust me you gonna need it . A coat or sweater to wear when u reach the top because you will be sweating a lot and cold breeze at the top can make you sick I reached the top just at sunrise I couldn't see the mystical triangular mountain shadow. I couldn't see the Adams foot itself as you have to take special permissions to see it . So get your papers ready before you start the climb ..it was a huge disappointment for me as I wanted to see the foot print after such a long and tiresome hike . Don't start climbing any other time of the day or after the sun rises . You will get sun burnt . Best time is around 2 at night if you can climb in four hours and reach on the top at six.. I don't believe the reviews who say that they went up and came down in four hours total.. I was way ahead of the climbers who started out with me and still it took me almost four hours 3 hours and 50ish minutes ..Late November and December is the ideal time to climb . Don't spend much time on top as if your body starts to feel tired the hike down will kill you. It's even more challenging when u go down. I devised a hop hop technique lol. I held the hand of one of my fellow climber and hopped of the stairs . It helped a lot as I was hoping a couple of them at a time it saves time and it's easier on knees. But keep your age and weight in mind before doing this .. You might do more damage than good.. It took me three hours to get back to hotel from the top including the hike down. And full five days to recover. Sri Lankan people keep a balm handy you will see a lot of wrappers on the stairs as well it is a camphor smelling locally made balm for fifty cents .. Which will help you recover faster.. Old Sri Lankans when climbing apply it on the knees and joints I later discovered how all those grannies got to the top. There is a saying in Sri Lanka " you only climb Adams peak once" I say " marry the guy who will climb it for ya" lol . But to be honest if given a chance I will climb it again . And again and again. It gives you a sense of accomplishment that I was looking for .. For a long time. It's my most cherished memory. Happy climbing

We climbed Sri Pada in December 2013 on a poya day (religious festival) which means the experience was extra special as we climbed along with thousands of religious revellers singing and chanting religious songs which was such an inspiring experience. We were staying in Nuwara Eliya and a driver was organised for us by the guest house we were staying in which meant we had transport right to the bottom of the mountain and waiting for us at the end. There were 4 of us in the group, all in our 20s but of mixed ability - 2 very fit people, one smoker and one very unfit person (me). We started our climb at 2am at a nice, steady pace. The 2 fit people soon went ahead as they found the climb easier and the other two of us found it better to keep to our own steady pace without the pressure of keeping up with the others! We took plenty of water and energy bars with us but the monks serving free sweet tea and crackers along the climb were lovely and a welcome help in the chill of the evening. The steps to begin with are gentle but gradually become steeper and more frequent until the top where there's a railing to help pull yourself up. We were taking a breather every 20 steps by the end but were encouraged along by everyone around us and even the monks on their pilgrimmage were egging us on. Seeing the euphoric state people were in, singing and dancing as they got closer to the top, was truly amazing. Our friends made it to the top but felt uncomfortable squeezing for space amongst people praying so came down a few steps to a ledge where many tourists seemed to be settling. This is where we met them and watched the sun rise and it proved to be a beautiful spot. My partner proposed at this spot and it couldn't have been more perfect. After the sun rose, we could see the breathtaking views and appreciate the great climb we had managed. The climb down is very difficult, taking its toll on the knees and ankles but we came down a little faster than we climbed up. The festival vibe at the bottom of the mountain was brilliant and although going up stairs for the next three days was very painful, it was totally worth it. Take advantage of the toilets at the start of the climb as they aren't the best on the way up and there are none at the top and stick to your own pace. My legs were less painful the day after than my fit friend- she pushed her pace a bit too much and suffered for it the next day! I recommend this climb to everyone who's going to Sri Lanka. Magical.

We did it back in 2012 on Buddha's birthday and full moon night so it was a festival in itself, it took us almost 6 hours to reach at the top but worth the view, sunrise is amazing but do look for perfect triangle shadow on the other side which very few people know about , it is the view I can met forget while everyone was focused on sunrise I was looking for shadow and found it with Rainbow crown. You do get edible and cold rink stalls along the way and rest room facilities are available as well, might be difficult with kids , the higher it gets the steeper the stairs get so last leg is difficult  but once you are on top, you forget the pain. It took us 3 hours coming down but we enjoyed the experience and loved the fact we did it on full moon night which made it extra special. I would recommend doing it of you are a thrill seeker and try taking energy bars with you, you will need them.

We (my fiance and me) took a bus to Ratnapura and sleep their since we where too late to take the last bus to Siripagama. We were bagpacking so we wanted to take different way to go up and to go down. We had to carry all our stuff but it was alright (probably more pleasant without our bags). We begun our ascension around 3 pm in Siripagama, this is early but we wanted to see the jungle and landscapes before night. We saw many monks and monkeys on the way up. This hike has the particularity of being stairs all the way up. It does not mean it is easier, I found it quite tough and some parts are hard if you have vertigo (I have it, and I did it :)). I think it is better to have a good condition to do this trail. You can find snacks and water all the way up but not in the top. On the middle of the trek their is a cascade where you can take a shower (for men only and with your underwear). It is nice to change your clothe if you are sweating because when the night comes it is rapidly cold and you do not want to be wet. When you arrive at the top by this way, the first thing you see is the "police of Adam's peak". Some people had bad experience, in our case it was more like "do not leave your stuff without surveillance". We arrived in the top around 10 pm. We stayed and tried to sleep in the "cave", we were the only tourist and the locals were very friendly (sharing food and clothes). If you spend the night in the top, it is VERY COLD, even for a Swiss woman (bring a wind coat is a really good idea). It is true that you share the top with hundreds of other people, the toilets are smelling bad and you may not have the best view to see the sunset but it is an amazing experience and the landscape is great. The way down to Dalhousie was the most difficult thing in this trek: our legs were shaking and we felt like we were not going to make it. In Dalhousie we took a bus to Hatton and then to Kandy and went directly to bed. We had aches for 2-3 days after it, so do not plan to do the Knuckles directly after Adam's peak.

Adam's Peak (or Sri Pada) will always be one of Sri Lanka's top attractions no matter what I or anybody else says about it, but having walked to its summit, waited around a while, and walked back down, I left with a profound sense of jaded, bleary eyed ambivalence. On the one hand, the mountain - the highest climbable peak in Sri Lanka - is a striking geological phenomenon, a 2243m (7,369ft) conical spire rising vertically from the jungle, offering even a fit walker a considerable physical challenge rewarded with breathtaking and far reaching views. On the other hand, though, joining the procession of walkers trudging step by step up the mountainside through the dark feels a little like an overnight assembly line, an outdoor experience bereft of any sense of freedom, solitude or reflection. Ironically, by far the worst experience was topping out, where I and two Australians walking just behind me were stopped by official looking security guards wanting to know our names and nationalities, the purpose of which was never made entirely clear to us. Granted, they weren't exactly waving AK-47s in our faces, but there was still something slightly unsettling about the experience which left me feeling almost as if I shouldn't really be there. The protocol for climbing Adam's Peak is an early morning start with an extended break at the summit to watch the sunrise. Visitors should time their ascent well; arrive too early and you'll be shivering the hours away in desperation for sunrise, too late and there'll be limited space left for you to enjoy it. Although the summit area is relatively large, when there are literally hundreds of people there space is very much at a premium. Hanging off protective railings, as some folk try, is dangerous and likely to meet with official intervention. Although the ascent warms you up, you cool down quickly at the summit. Fleeces, hats, gloves (a lot of things you wouldn't normally wear in Sri Lanka) are recommended, if not downright essential. On a cold, clear night, however, the sky is a revelation, a canopy of constellations and planets with (in March 2014) Venus remarkably luminous, but Mars, Saturn and - just before dawn - even Mercury visible. Sunrise, when it eventually comes, is a welcome burst of light and warmth. There's something refreshingly primal about it. When you're done looking to the east though, it's worth taking in the view westwards to see the mountain cast a triangular shadow over the rolling jungle below. The rapid, bone jarring descent requires care and control. Knees and ankles are sorely tested. Heavily cushioned shoes are recommended. Trainers might actually be better than proper walking shoes. Whichever way you square it though you're going to feel it the next day, and probably for a few days after...

We took a bus to Dalhousie from Hatton which is only R75 but if you don't get a seat the very scenic hour long bus ride can be very uncomfortable. Taxi mini buses and Tuk Tuks are more than willing to take you but it costs around R1500. Accomodation in Delhousie is pretty average they tend to continuously turn the rooms over. We watched one couple check out and five minutes later another couple was checked into their room which wasn't even cleaned, same bed sheets etc Food situation isn't much better. I advise you get your snack food for the climb before you reach Delhouise as options are very limited. It's recommended you do the climb at night to witness the sunrise and the shadow of the mountain. It's a tough climb if your not in decent shape physically but if you pace yourself it's very achievable. It's not uncommon to witness three generations of Sri Lankans climbing together. The summit is a little disappointing as it resembles a run down toilet block with a small temple shrine on top. View once the  sun is up is pretty good. Worth the climb tho? That's really down to individual experience I guess. personally I enjoyed the view on the way down more. I recommend checking out  www.mountain-forecast.com you can check an accurate forecast for Adams Peak to find out if it's going to be raining, cloudy, windy etc Don't bother climbing in the rain at night if it's not going to be clear In the morning. Personally I'd stay in a larger town near by and climb as soon as I get to Delhousie bearing in mind it's a 5-6hr round trip (2-3hrs up) and (1.5-2.5hrs down). Bring a change of t-shirt or jumper as you get quiet sweaty on the climb and the wind chill on top can be severe if your soaked in sweat. Return buses can be busy but if you can afford it I recommend the Tuk Tuk option for speed and the ability to stop and photograph the amazing landscape.

Did the climb on Sunday 27th with a fit son, daughter and son's fiance.  Used the easiest path from Nallathanniya on both ways. Started at 11:15PM and reached the peak at 4:15AM with the whole party slowed down by myself.  This is the hardest I have done but the whole experience was awesome.  With good pacing, this is possible even for a moderately fit person.  There were lots of people climbing but not large enough to slow us. First 2-3km is a gentle walk uphill.  Then the hard part starts with a fairly steep climb of big steps.  This goes for a while and then reaches the steep climb to the peak.  Last part in fact is relatively easy since there are railings that you can hang onto and push yourself.   There are many rest areas along the way that you can buy food and drinks.  There are basic toilet facilities as well along the way where you pay Rs.20 to use. You can see the lit path to the top while climbing and this is a very pretty sight.  Views from the top are amazing.  There is a platform to view the sunrise outside of the temple area. We started the descent at 6AM and the views again were amazing.  Stopped along the way for a roti breakfast. Descent is in fact harder than the climb and by the end I could hardly feel my legs. Maintaining balance is another challenge.  Overall, this is an awesome experience and I am glad I did it before it is too late :-)

The climb is tough but for people in good shape it shouldn't be a problem. We were unlucky to have climbed Adam's Peak on a saturday: one of the last days in the season. It was very very very (!) busy. Buses full of pelgrims. At first we thought this was a nice thing but coming closer to the top it got very busy and dirty. People vomiting, really bad smells all around. The last 500 m standing in line with many people (Sri Lankans as well as tourists) brutally skipping the line! Very uncivilized behavior, didnt expected this to happen in Sri Lanka with it's friendly / polite people! We waited for an hour without moving and so we decided to go back as there was no movement in the line and we were not on time for the sunrise.

The walk up Adam's Peak is not easy, but it's so incredibly worth it. Stopping along the way for a cup of tea or a roti, and getting the top for sunrise was a great experience. I would recommend it to anybody. You don't have to be extremely for to climb either. We saw loads of old grannies (with pink handbags and sandals) climbing too. It was great to see. Amazing morning. Amazing experience.

It was one of the most challenging and exciting adventures I have ever had. My husband and I started the climb around 2.30 am. As the steps were getting steeper, we were falling into despair that we will never make it before sunrise, though we considered ourselves to be fit. It was really not easy! The sweat was soaking all our clothes. As it was a day after Sri Lankan new year, many local people at the same time were climbing down, clogging the way. Also a big stream climbing up. it got slow just before the peak where tge cold wind hit us. We cheated to take the line for climbing down, rather than waiting in the long line up, as it seemed we were never going to reach. It was 5 am when we finally got into a queue at the entrance of the temple, which was nothing impressive. One could definitely not see any 'foot'. But the view was just stunning... All shades orange, yellow, red and purple...amazing. Highly recommended for the breathtaking outlook and a personal physical challenge!

After joining the throng at 2am, I started on my journey to the peak. Coming to the end of the 6 month cycle, it was full of pilgrims who are no particular rush; some stopping for tea on the way; other frustratingly deciding to stop for a rest - or a sleep - in the middle of the path. Its hard work because of the number of steps and their gradient - and the multitude of old grannies and babies - who slow everyone down. There were a few times when i was sweating like a racehorse [and I'm relatively fit for 48] where I seriously battled with myself about turning back... When you get to the last 1000 or so steps the path divides into up on the right; down on the left, and the pace slows to crawling. A real moral test for westerners...do you respect the local Buddhists and Christians, or jump over into the other lane [often empty] and make it to the top in time for sunrise? Getting to the peak is worth it. I think.... Its an amazing perspective coz you're so high, and there's nothing like sunrise above the clouds. But its a shuffle to get a view, given the top isn't very well-organised, and everyone is squeezed into a small area. And by that stage I just wanted to have a cup of tea and some breakfast. Be aware there are 5,800+ steps to the peak, and after a while they get to you. But nothing like on the way down - which if you are 40+ can be agonising, due to the incessant pounding on your knees. Seasons April to December, path is NOT lit; December to April - pilgrim season. TBC

Incredible moment. Adam's peak is not only that climbing of 5200 stairs , it's much more than that.Iwas staying at the nice White house with 3 other guys ( swiss and estonian ). We began at 2.30. Funny at the beginning and become quiet. It really has somathing to see with the religious thing. At the top , waiting in a common room with families , pilgrims , tourists and out at the temple waiting for the su to rise and the peole singing. WOUAHHH !!! that's a moment and the way down , not the easiest but with the sun and smiling and a bit of time. One of my best moment for sure in the loving Sri Lanka.

We climbed Adams Peak in the early hours of Friday 25 April. We started the climb at 2:35am. It had been raining the night before so the path was wet and a bit slippery, but the weather was clear and not too cold until we got to the top. I thought I'd share some personal information to give others an idea regarding the difficulty level of the climb. I am a 33 year old female, average height and weight and my main exercise is running 5km about 3 times a week. I would say my fitness is average. The climb up took me about 2 hours 20 mins (including a few stops to catch my breath, especially towards the end) and at the top I felt roughly as tired as I do after a 15km run. The difficulty level was about what I expected from the information I had been given. The climb starts fairly easily and as it progresses the steps become steeper and more continuous. The locals (including lots of seniors) were climbing in bare feet, sandals and flimsy dresses. However, I recommend being a bit better prepared! I wore my usual running trainers which had grip and were good for the slippery parts, leggings and a gym vest. Although the path was mainly well lit, there were a few dark and uneven parts so it was well worth bringing a torch. When I got to the top I added a lightweight thermal top, a waterproof anorak and wrapped a sheet around my legs. I think I would have been too cold with anything less. The official sunrise time was 6am but we started seeing beautiful colours in the sky from about 5:30 onwards so it was worth getting to the top quite early, also to get a good spot to sit. We didn't encounter many people at the start of the walk and it only became busy in the last 50m or so from the top. We weren't worried about missing the sunrise at any stage of the climb. Coming back down was quite crowded at first but thinned out quickly. We left the top at about 6:15, and it took about 2 hours to get back down at a more leisurely pace and stopping to take photos in various places. I found my legs were a bit shaky on the way down but I did some stretches and drank plenty of water and they stopped shaking after a while. I also found zigzagging down the stairs helped a bit. Overall the climb was well worth it to see the beautiful sunrise and landscape below, but also to see the dedicated local pilgrims making their way to the top and engaging with them, they love saying hello or good morning... We saw many shoeless elderly ladies making the climb, a guy with only one leg on crutches, and families who were chanting and singing to keep up moral as they made their way up. I would definitely recommend this trek to those whose fitness levels are up to it.

So we started climbing at 11pm in Saturday 8th March on Sunday 9th and it was biggest mistake to do that at the weekend. Climbing was nice and easy until about 2:30am when we reach pilgrims be stack on one place.So we did one step per hour it was overcrowded craziness! ! So we want to give up with my girlfriend but there was no way to go back literally people everywhere. During that time when we're stuck we start to chat with one Sri Lankian guy and he suggested that we can climb with him so we did. Have to say we start to cheat bcs we went into the line for pilgrims who climb down from Adam's peak.Many time we're stop by security and that Sri Lankian guy told them that we are his friends etc...so we're allowed to do so. .. We reach a top of peak at 7.30am absolutely exhausted with his help! !! It was amazing experience we would love to do it again but during WEEKDAYS. Have to say it wasn't physically challenging but mentally!

Do not try and climb Adam's peak if it is around a holiday or weekend. The guide books mention that there is a que near the top, but they fail to explain that the que is hundreds of people crammed together on a staircase that does not move. After waking up at 2am to climb, there was no chance that we would even make it to the top due to the heavy crowds. Not worth the trip all the way out to Dalhoiuse...

We were planning to go to Adam's Peak and maybe it was bad planning but Adams Peak is nearly three and a half to four hours from Nuwara Eliya. We ended up not going as a result, that and the combination of locals saying that Sinhalese New Year means many more people trying to get to the top. We are glad we didn't go reading previous comments recommending not to go up on a public holiday. If you are intent on climbing plan to stay at Dalhousie night before or that day (so you can rest until 1 am) which is at the peak of the mountain so at least you only have the 7 hour climb !!

We have just returned from trying to do Adams peak. We left our hotel at 11pm as the owner said is would be busy due to the holiday/new year. It happened to be good Friday/Easter Saturday and new year was a few days before. We walked for an hour or two and then came the HUGE line! At 8am long after sunrise we still had not reached the top. Our friends who had walked some of the way 'off the track' had gotten further then us and we seen them on the way down. They told us that we would be waiting for at least another 2 hours to get to the top and it wasn't worth the wait. That was enough! The locals which we usually find extremely friendly, were pushy and at times a little aggressive towards us and our friends said the same when we got back to the hotel. We should have done a little more research about the different tracks because what we were hoping would be a great climb turned out to be one of the worst trips plan to date.

You can climb Adam's Peak/ Sri Pada also from the Ratnapura side. Its eleven km, Its heavy, but I did it and im not in such good shape, so anyone can do it. This route is less travelled than the Hatton route, so more quiet, I saw many animals just crossing or chilling on the steps before me. reptiles, monkeys, squirls, birds, butterflies. I went up in the afternoon, spend the night at the top and came down after sunrise. Take a thick blanket if you're going to sleep on top, its cold. Was the sunrise spectacular? No. But being at the temple on top after having worked so hard for it, in between the praying pilgrims and the sound of the temple bells, That makes it worth it. Ratnapura i found uninteresting and expensive to stay, so i stayed in Sri Palabaddala, the startingpoint village of the route. There are simple rooms for 800rs and you can eat amazing food and get all help you can imagine at Mallika's small restaurant. Ask for Mallika when entering the village or call 071-2009474/0773389394 and she'll make sure you are ready for the trip and get a good rest afterwards!

Climbed up the peak but as not in great shape as I thought I was took me 3.5 hours. Crowded as did it during pilgrimage but once on the top it was all worth it. The view, the spirituality and the history of the Buddha reportedly being there made everything worthwhile! Totally recommend it but be ready fir sore legs for a week after.

A general level of fitness is needed for this climb up steep and sometimes high steps. We left at 22.00 and the assent was relatively quiet as we passed Sri Lankan families pushing and pulling their elderly matriarchs up the mountainside. They would have spent all day for the climb up and another day for the climb down. The summit is somewhat haphazard, but what do you expect on top of a mountain in a limited space. We congregated in a room where you can lay down and sleep, so take a plastic sheet for the floor and a thin blanket or large towel. I helped the temple serve coffee and candy to the Sri Lankan pilgrims as a way of keeping warm. Sunrise was like watching a photographic print being developed in a bath of chemicals. Take a change of attire for the summit as you become sodden with perspiration and you need a jacket to keep warm. Wear good shoes and NOT flip flops. I saw one girl loose her control and she began involuntarily running down the uneven and steep steps only to end up in a heap concussed and a couple of teeth knocked out. I am happy to say her flip flops survived intact.

Decided to do adams peak as in the top 20 things to do in lonely planet whilst also sounding right up my street. However we all left unanimous in our disappointment. The walk itself is tough, certainly doable and not enough to deter me if the views at the top had been worth it, which they weren't. The authorities have built several ugly concrete buildings blocking the view from one of the main areas to wait for sunrise, around one of the other areas the trees have been allowed to grow to cover the view. The 'sunrise' was more a gradual change from night to day, we never actually saw the sun behind the clouds. I would not recommend this.

My first climb was on a Buddhist holiday in Feb 2014, and even though I left very early, by the time i got near the top there was a queue that was hardly moving. That's because there was several hundred people on the top waiting for sunrise and several hundred on the steps below trying to get up. Somehow I managed to get up just after sunrise and overall it was a great trek, amazing views and good experience. On the way down my legs were turning to jelly but I found a place that was giving free herbal tea and free calf muscle massages which was bliss. My leg muscles then ached for a week. I then returned to Maskeliya and decided I wanted to climb it again at a quieter time so I could get to the top with the hassle of so many people. (The problem is near the top the steep step path is divided into two by a handrail. Those going up must be on the right hand side and the path is narrow. Because people of all ages and physical states do this trek since many of them are pilgrims, there can be people holding up others at this part of the trek - The last few hundred metres to the top is slow going in pilgrim season.) So on my second time I thought I'd be sweet since I left an hour earlier and it was a normal weekday albeit Friday. However near the top I once again met traffic, which was nowhere near as bad as the previous time but still takes a bit of getting past without bumping people. I got to the top well before sunrise and take warm clothes because you stop trekking it quickly get's cold. Amazing views, and I think the trek is quite tough and a very long walk. Second time around my legs didn't ache in the days afterwards and coming down was easier but going up will always be tough. That's why climbing in the night is good because it's cool and you don't really know what you're in for. If you go in Buddhist pilgrim season do it on a normal weekday but not a Friday. Leave earlier than you'd think depending on your fitness it can take anywhere from 2 hours to 5 with an average of 3 to 4. One of the best things I've done in Sri Lanka in three trips covering several thousand K on a scooter. Must do! And it's free unlike some of the rip-off archeology sites further north.

as the path are all steps, you only require to have your legs and healthy lungs to climb it all. We started around 2am and arrived the top around 5.30am. took us around 3.5 hours to reach the temple at the top. We queued up and entered where it was believed to have the footstep of hanuman / adam whichever religion it relates to. it was cold up there at the temple when we had to sit and wait for the sun rise for about 30mins. we were freezing but thank god for the wind breaker and emergency blanket that we got. we managed to stay heated till sun rise. the morning prayer was a blessing while witnessing the sun rise from the temple. A pure and blessing morning to start the day. i have created a blog and spoken abit about adams peak for more personal experiences, you may browse it on : http://pinparadise.blogspot.com/2014/03/sri-lanka.html cheers Prana

The climb itself isn't as gruelling as I expected. Tough, but manageable if you are fit. However, we did the climb on a Sunday and I would advise against anyone doing the same unless well prepared. We left at 1:30am and reached the summit at around 5:30am. The crowds were in their thousands. The only reason we reached the top is because we followed some Sri Lankans down an unlit back pathway which then linked onto a quieter staircase. This happened around two-thirds of the way up. We saw other Westerners who had not taken this route when we were coming back down later on. They had around 4-6 hours of queuing ahead of them to reach the summit. We were very lucky and the top was full of people. The actual summit is small and so space to watch the sunrise is restricted too. Again, we were lucky to get a fairly decent spot. In hindsight, our experience was much more authentic and memorable to see the Sri Lankans on pilgrimage, but it was not an easy day. Coming down was ok, we arrived back by 8:30ish.

I climbed from Dalhouise/Nalathaniya side which is the shortest route. Its a painful and never ending climb. You should set 3-4 hours for climb, if you want to experience the sunrise. The views from dawn to sunrise and afterwards are awesome and should not be missed. It gets really cold in the night and after hot after sunrise, so pack accordingly but keep the weight light. 2 layers should be enough for the cold. Along the climb you'll find all services like food, water, bath, toilet and even place to sleep, but these might not be as per everyone's standards. Advice: Don't expect too much re these services and prices of all items increas as you climb up.

Its my Experience I wanna share with u all... Once in a lifetime u gotta go there and see the Sunrise. There is actually 3 main ways to reach the Top of SRIPADA(Adams Peak). 1.most famous,through Nallathanniya,from Hatton stn.(Always Crowded,but closest) 2.From Rathnapura Palabaddala (Moderate Distance about 12kms,but Continuous Steps) 3.From Kuruwita, Erathna where we chose to hike up the hill.(Longest Route around 20kms,but filled with nature,less tiring places to rest and to have a Bath)TIME: 08hrs if continous,14-20hrs if rested. **Take a Torch **some water bottles+light food **Wear Hiking shoes and preferably gears when u reach the Summit then u ll feel 'the great achievement' u made Watch this,I took it by myself the video of Sunrise(0630HRS) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WKHUPqLfMtc

Startet 01.00 am, was the almost the only one at the buttom, but Got the Wrong Way up, when my Gps Said 5 km, the Path suddenly ended. When i came down i talked to locals, they Said i was not the first to take the Wrong rute, the rute i took was for local The farmers... I was really really really mad, Can almost laugh of it today, almost! I even afsked the reception before going, if it was easy to find, "yes yes, go to start and up, can't go Wrong" CHECK IT IS THE RIGHT WAY UP, THERE ARE NO SIGNS!!!

We climbed at 1.15am and took just 2.40hrs to get up, with two short breaks, and then 2.10hrs down. I wouldn't consider myself fit although young and fairly active. It was tough in parts, with the steps very variable and sometimes broken. And the old and young being carried cause delays. We went on a Tuesday and made it up with no queues. DO NOT GO ON A WEEKEND. You cannot get to the top due to the queues as this is when most locals do the pilgrimage. Take a torch, and if you wana watch the sunset from the top be prepared for how busy it gets, the pick pockets and the 'sleeping rough'. We made it to the top around 4am, and went back down to watch the sunset from towards the bottom. We still got great views and missed all queues and crowds. There is food and drink at regular intervals so don't carry too much on you to slow you down. And be prepared for the days to come, the pain kicks in the following two days. But a feeling of great achievement.

We went to Adams peak Saturday 1st March and wanted to climb Sunday morning. We heard there would ve many locals so we desided to start early. 00.30 am we got a good start noted every 50 steps we took. There were many people but we had a nice pace. After 3000 steps still more than 2000 to the top or 500 meters height (1km  distance) we were not able to continue as the steps werw packed with people with NO movement. We were able to more one step every 10 min. Calculating we had to accept the hard truth, we were not able to make it to the top before sunrise. And we were pm thw west side. Not able to see anthing from where we were standing. So we gave up and started the hard climb down. It was a big Challenge to go there both up and down and we were sad not to get to the top. So we have to come back some other time. Bit next time on a week day. I used a wood stick as walking stick which I can recommend.

After much hype we decided to do the 2am hike up to Adams Peak. Rough guide tells you it's 5890 steps and tiring on your legs on the way down. This is a miss quote of the century. I'm 41 year old male avid gym goer and consider myself fit. The climb up with various size steps, broken boulders and dirt wore my legs and lungs out. The fact that it was dark you just carried on to the top. It was cramped, slow and the amount of locals taking their 97 year old grannies up the mountain was a joke. I've seen pigs being pulled to the slaughter house go quicker up steps. I couldn't believe the amount of locals trying to yank them up those god how many steps. So after 3 and a half hours you eventually make it to the top where it's now freezing cold you are warned that you will be robbed by pick pockets by the police. So instead of the police tackling this crime by actually having a presence up there they are half way down the peak taking foreigners details for their records!!? So at the top you and 1000 locals and another 400 foreigners trying to fight for space to see the sunrise you realise that it just isn't worth all the aggro. We decide to head down early knowing full well that with that amount if people trying to get down would take another 9 hours or so. After taking 40 or so steps down my right knee gave way and the agony was terrible. With no help, no way of getting down I had to tie my knee up with a scarf and fight through the pain. 4 hours later we made it to safety. I can not stress enough how tough and dangerous going up Adams Peak is. They say its a test of your faith I say it's a test of your sanity

My friend and I did the Adam's Peak with a guide starting at 2am on the Hatton route. At the start we were entertained by the sheer number of stalls selling badminton racquet sets! As we started to climb we could see that this was going to be tough, we climbed overnight on a Saturday so it was crowded and at two thirds of the way up we came to a complete stand still there were literally thousands of people and nobody was moving. At this stage both of us felt totally deflated, getting so far and facing the possibility of not making it to the top. However our guide was determined, he got us to scramble up a muddy bank through a forest (in the pitch black) and onto another route (sorry I can't think of the name of this one but it is the longer route approaching from the other side). As soon as we got onto the new route up, it was much better no crowds. We made it to the top for 5:30am and yes it was cold, I think it feels colder as you are very warm having climbed 5,500 steps to get to the top then you stop and wait for the sunrise. The queue for the temple was huge, but our guide got us int he back way for a quick peek. The sunrise is good, however the side from which you'd get the best view seems to be blocked with the water tanks which is a shame. We didn't loiter long after sunrise and headed down. It's not for the faint hearted, the steps are very steep with big drops off either side which of course you don't see on the way up in the dark. The views on the descent are fantastic and it was a clear day for us so we were lucky. Down hurts a lot, and the steps are very uneven and rocky, I did fall but fortunately not far - you need to watch your step closely. The toilet facilities get more grim as you go up, if you can wait I'd advise this. However if like us you need to visit the bathroom at the bottom it will be the most painful experience, girls to use a squat toilet after all those steps - OUCH! Like others who have reviewed the most inspiring part of this walk at the Sri Lankan people who walk barefoot or in flimsy flip flops, are carrying babies and children, helping old people - how they make it I'm not sure. Would we do it again? Probably not, but we are so glad we did it and have the jelly legs as a souvenir.

We arrived to Dalhousie on 14th February. There was full mion and long weekend, so everybody want go to summit. It was also very difficult to get to Dalhousie. We were driving about 6 hours from Kandy. We were allowed to go to Dalhousie only because we have reserved hotel with parking. Every where was lot of people. We still hear the pray. After short sleep, we start our descent at 11 p.m.. At the beginning it was easy. In 1 am we were in 2/3 of the descent and the way starts to be very crowded. After 1,5 hour, we have moved only about 500 metres. We were between hundred of local peoples. Some people were pushing up, some people were nice and help you if you are falling. At 3 we decided not to continue and return back to hotel. The way back was same as the way up. Very,very crowded. It took us 3 hours to get to the hotel. Interesting experience, but we do not see the sunrise.

The climb was tiring, long and the weather was super cold. Bring gloves cause the railing feel like ice when you touch it. I started climb around 0300 am and arrived after 2-1/2 hours just in time for sunrise. The sunrise was amazing but the crowds are too many (local & tourist). I would advice not to go to the temple right away but sir at the nearby stair and enjoy the sunrise. After that go behind the temple and see the infamous triangle shadow of sri pada. I spend a good 1-2 hours up there cause crowds start descending as soon as the sun rice ended. they distribute free ponggal rice for breakfast. Ring the bell near the stair to the temple (where the feet is located) and visit the temple & and so called feet (it is vertical and wrapped but huge). I took my time to descent so, it took me almost 2 hours.

What an experience , it was my first visit to this place and unfortunately we went on a weekend where the highest number of pilgrims turn out in the entire history ! , so i need not say anything further.. Luckily we were accompanied by two friends who had done this trail more than 3-6 times hence we had very little decision making to do as they knew exactly how to keep time during the entire walk. As a newbie to this here is a few tips to  all 1) Avoid any long weekend in sri lanka , It will be best if you could make it during a weekday 2) Always go with somebody who knows this trail , keep track of time is very important. 3) Remember it is not an easy climb up , take it slow and steady , you actually need you energy more towards the end of the trail , the beginning 3 hours is actually your approach to the main peak :) ( could be a spoiler )... 4) Your decent back, is more harder on your knees , so be care full ! 5) For those who cant stand the cold , take adequate clothing ! 6) There is enough and more places to buy snacks , but always check expiry dates , and remember all shops only serve vegetarian and the food let me say simply " be cautious what you eat " 7) Entire trek will take between 5-7 hours ( climb only ) . 8) last but not the least.. you need to have that "go" in you or else you could easily give up mid way . things to take with you , a torch in case you want to go to the public toilets( not really recommended ) . For your way back a dust mask , on your way back; you could encounter a lot of dust in case it is the dry season.

I like both the walk and the peak. The night walk meeting and talking to people on stands is a small magic. As it is night and all the people share the same goal these short talks have authentic atmosphere. You will meet a lot of people on the way up so there will be many opportunities to meet. And this becomes to be a bit of a problem once coming to the top. The peak was really full of people. This time we were lucky having an almost clear view. If comes to timing, we started at 2, having two longer tea breaks (not counting many short stops) just buying a time not to be on the top too early. Even though we were at the peak more then half an hour before sunrise waiting sweat in strong wind.

The average rating is about the experience of the walk rather than the peak, which being a natural site warrants a excellent rating. The walk is hard as it's mostly steps upwards, upwards, upwards! Mostly people start at about 2am to be up for sun rise. This is not for you if you don't like walking up steps or like sights of the beaten track. This sight is very busy! Made harder by those that suddenly decide to sit in the middle of the steps and rest, the sheer amount of people going up made it hard to move, but as I was adding to this number I probably shouldn't be cheeky enough to class that as an issue! What is inspirational is the families that bring the oldies out to climb, I saw at least three old people being carries up by younger members of their family. We were unlucky to not have a clear day and so saw no sun rise but there was a procession at the top which was interesting to see even if we didn't understand what was going on! It's one to tick off the 'must sees' for Sri Lanka but I don't feel as though you would miss out if you didn't give it a go!

We start our journey for Adam's Peak from White House approximately at 2:30am. Throughout our journey we passed by a large standing Buddha and tea estates until we reached the big arch that marks the beginning of the route to the sacred area. We bumped into many locals coming down from the peak; from as young as infants to elders about 70 years of age. Some routes are lighted while some, you might need help with a torchlight. Pathway is secure. Lots of tea stops in between too. Climbing up to the peak is extremely challenging for both physical and mental. Halfway, I personally feel about to give up as I can feel my legs are begging me to stop and my muscles are stretching to the max. But then I can't give up now since I am halfway closer to the peak! So we continue the journey and managed to catch the sunrise. The view from the top is awesomely superb, I totally forgot about the leg pain and all! When you're at the peak, look out for the mysterious shadow - a perfect triangle outline depicting the shape of the summit itself. It's amazing. Going down is quicker, but at this point of time, my legs feel like jelly already. Bring warm clothing along as it's cold at the summit. Some people is asking if there is a need to get a guide; I would say it's an option. You can still reach the peak without one. Best to climb out of pilgrimage season.

I am 57 about 8 kilos overweight and don't go to the gym or jog anywhere. But this climb is not so bad, and the sunrise is truly spectacular and worth the effort. What ads to the spectacle is the religious chanting that starts just as the sun comes up. Advise for the less fit, get a guide for Rp2000 this is a big help and if your lucky he might carry your camera bag. Take your time and have a an extended break at the last or second last tea house ( shack really ). And remember that as long as you are putting one foot in front of another you will make it. Going down can be a killer , your muscles are stressed until your get your lower foot placed so try to do that as quick as you can. Plan for a leisurely day on day 2 and 3 .

Stayed at the Greenhouse hostel - wasn't the nicest rooms, but the food was lovely and so close to the start of the walk is good. Started at 2:15am to see the sunrise. There are shops all the way up selling food, drinks so no need to carry much. The steps are tricky - a lot are uneven, stone, or large steps so take your time. Warm up and cool down afterwards, my leg muscles seized and couldn't walk for 2days! Wear warm clothes for the top to wait for the sunrise. Unfortunately cannot say this was an amazing experience, the pilgrims were heading down when we were heading up at 3am and the sunrise was 'ruined' by the haze. Toilets at the top are squat type. Big kudos to the army and workers climbing up the mountain with sacks of 15kg building materials for the temple.

We arrived mid afternoon at Slightly Chilled guesthouse at the foot of Adam’s peak. It was reasonably cheap and more of a backpacker type of place but we were only going to be there half the night anyhow and really just wanted a bead. There was a buffet dinner and lots of travellers making full use of the wifi. The steps to our room were steep, by mountain goats standards, but when we got to our modest room we were taken aback to see directly out of our window, from our bed, an uninterrupted view of the peak with the little lights, which would be our path to walk in the morning. It was quite humbling and slightly unnerving to witness the feat ahead. I can’t remember exact times now, but I had done all the reading and taken all the advice (I scour for every bit of info before travelling), and we set off half an hour before the recommended start time, I'm thinking we started at 1:30 am or 2am, but my memory may be failing me. We are both active types so had all the right gear on, quick dry layers, warm layers, the right lightweight backpacks etc. By about a quarter of the way up I was really wondering whether I had bitten off more than I could chew. To give some context, my partner is still playing club level football regularly and I sail competitively multiple times a week and do lots of yoga. I would say we are on the fitter end of average Australians. But this walk was tough. The incline was tough but one of the hardest bits was that in sections the majority of the steps were larger than one step, at least one that you can take in your stride. You really had to spring off your lower leg to leverage yourself onto the next step. In parts I was apologising to bf for stopping so often and slowing him up, sometimes we were stopping every 2-5 steps, just to get our breath. He was kind enough to say that he was very glad every time I stopped as he needed the stops also. We didn’t have too many breaks sitting down, maybe 1 or 2, and we got water along the way at the little shops, and some nuts and other things to supplement what we were carrying. We used a few of the bathrooms and were happy to have our own small packs of tissues and hand sanitisers. Every now and then we would be greeted by a 80+yo frail woman in no shoes making her way back down from the top … there’s no motivation quite like that :) Families of children, many of them very young, sometimes with their young mother piggybacking them. It was quite extraordinary. So we kept pushing on, keeping to the time schedule. We were well ahead of schedule, maybe 40 mins ahead and could see the top, less than 500m ahead, when the traffic started to slow down. At first we were quite happy for the reduced pace, but then we started to get colder from not keeping the pace and needed to put our fleece layers back on … as the sunrise drew nearer it became apparent to us this traffic jam would be our treks demise. Less than 200m from the top but with nowhere to go we stood there with the schoolgirl giggles while the sun rose and we stood on a thin cobbled path, 4 people deep in the crowd, our view fully obstructed by an overhanging tree and on the western side of the mountain. It was character building, but one of the moments of the trip I smile fondly when thinking back on. What else could you do hey? To get to the top took us about another hour or more. It was truly stunning up there and we were very glad we went. There seemed to be many elderly sick people up there and my mind boggles about how they made that journey. The walk down was long, using a different set of muscles and we were probably a little seized up by that point. We were glad to make tracks when we did because the heat of the day was setting in by the time we got back. We had a well-earned brekkie, a good shower and were on our way again.

Did the classic visit to the peak and started early, 1am from Hatton side. Saw the sunrise and then back down to the car at 9am. Can only say that this is the most spirituell experiance in Sri Lanka and do recommend that you do this.

This is a must in Sri Lanka. Locals do it at least couple times in their lifetime and we saw old people, barefoot folks got up and down with no problem. They take few hours more :) It's quite a hike, i read somwhere 5200 steps and there sure are lots of them. Just bring some snacks and water as the prices go higher the higher you get. You can stop for tea in the several stops. 2,5hours up the rop and less down should be enough. Watch the knees!

Trekking is always nice, Adam's speak trek is mostly human steps made in concrete (not a natural track). The view at the very top is nice but to be honest I had much more magnificent and scenic views elsewhere. The tourism crowd and pushy people willing to get the best photography is quite annoying and install a bad atmosphere. Be careful In Dalhousie, lot of guest houses to spend a night in is a total rip off, the price escalated from a 600-800LKR for the night to about 4000-7000LKR. Getting to Adam's speak a touristic season is quite easy, you can juggle between train/bus or tuk tuk

How to get there from Colombo? Start from Pettah Bus Station, Colombo, I took a kind of public minivan to Hatton. After 3 hours, I arrived in Hatton Bus Station. Then, a man from hostel picked me up to go to Dalhousie by private minivan. Travelers, who want to Adam’s Peak, usually stay in Dalhousie. There is hostel and guesthouse to stay before start to reach Adam’s Peak. From Hatton to Dalhousie, it took about an hour. I took a rest in Dalhousie. Then, I started my trip to reach Adam’s Peak at 2 a.m. by walk. Why I started so early? I want to see the sunrise from the top of the mountain. Local people said that it will take about 2 hours to reach the top. In fact, I did it more than 2 hours. *fiuuuuh* However, it was not end in smoke. The scenery was so amazing and the air was so fresh.

Climbing Adam's peak needs to be done between the full moons of December and May. As it is the season for the locals to climb and offer there tributes. However one could do the journey on whats being called "Off Season" from May to December of an year where the area gets a down pour thanks to the Monsoon rain. On season the roads are lit and there are three main ways to approach the Peak in which one road connects to the other two ( Rathnapura road connects to the paths that start from Kuruwitha and Hatton aka Nallathanniya.) One could use the Bus to get to all three starting points but i prefer to take the Train to Hatton which will take me max 5 hours and it is comfortable if I land my self on a 2nd class seat ( Rs. 290/- 17-01-2014) it leave the Fort Railway station. if you leave in the morning you ll reach Hatton by afternoon. From there you take the Bus that's parked outside to the foot of the hill. Have a bath from the stream next to the foot of the mountain as it is what becomes a one of the main four rivers of Sri Lanka. And if you have reached the hill too early in the day there are many lodgings that will charge around 4k for 4 people. Its easy to climb in the night under the shadow of darkness than walk in the scorching sun of the tropics. but expect company shops are either side to by stuff and liquids but be adviced the prices go up when the you get to the top. Spend the night in the Temple as the sunrise is just breath taking. You have the option of climbing down the same way or coming down from the other side which would more or less be a long walk than a decent. though it is scenic. and through villages and jungles and leads to a old village where you ll have to take a bus to Rathnapura town and could take a another bus to Colombo which will take 3 hours max to reach its destination...

Honestly, NOT WORTH IT.  your arrival is welcomed with the smell from the toilets and it doesn't improve from there. Views would indeed make a spiritual experience for sure but only without a huge pushy smelly crowd fighting for somewhere to stand/sit while police walk around yelling at the tourists to not stand on the back fence or stairs trying to get any type of view..  i think you would have to arrive by 4am if you wanted any type of unobstructed view, we had rows of people infront of us waving their iPads / tripods as high as they could above their heads trying to see something themselves, it was a sea of screens.  Then my buddy had his wallet stolen in the crowd and when we actually needed a cop, the guy was 100% useless and wouldn't even use his radio to verify no wallet had been found.   Followed by this disappointment, the walk down is painful and your legs will hurt for 3 days on average.

I was a bit apprehensive about this as I'm reasonably unfit. The first hour is alright but the second is torturous. Don't listen to people telling you how long there is to go, one man told me there was another hour and it really killed my spirits! I am so glad that I did it - such an incredible experience to be there for sunrise. I'd definitely do it again! Take small notes for the monks on the walk so you don't end up paying too much (it is a donation).

Worth the challenge. Its good to not think about the time or how long you have to go. taking each step as a glorious victory also helps. the descent is also easier if you do it quickly. Feels spiritual as you are with Sri Lankans and their pilgrimages in the climb; walk through clouds; and the footprint of Buddha. We had a quite a misty sunrise. but it was beautiful in its own way - the sun kept appearing and disappearing like a ship in the distance. People kept complaining. I guess you have to appreciate for what it is and can't expect to see the 'perfect' sunrise. if you're a sook, then investigate the weather beforehand and time your climb accordingly.

We really enjoyed our hike up to Adam's Peak--the view of sunrise from the top was amazing.  I had a hard time finding information on Ratnapura trail, so thought I would share our experience. Hatton trail is about 3 km while Ratnapura is about 8 km.  Both trails are well marked (no need for a guide), mostly have concrete stairs, have plenty of light during climbing season (no need to bring lamps), and have shops.  Hatton has a ton of shops almost to the top.  Ratnapura had some shops.  So no need to carry much water or food--you can buy along the way.  On the Ratnapura side we must have passed at least 8-10 stalls on our way down (many more on the very bottom). We started our trip to Sri Lanka in the north (Anuradhapura, Sigiriya, Polonnaruwa, Kandy) and then wanted to get to the southwest beaches without driving more than a couple of hours each day.  So hiking up Hatton side and coming down Ratnapura saved us lots of time.  We send our driver to pick us up on the other side.  I took him about 4-5 hours to drive around Adam's Peak.  We were able to get from Ratnapura trail head to Hikkaduwa in just over 3 hours. We hiked Jan 2nd.  We spent the night at Achinika holiday inn (ok for 1 night).  We woke up at 3 am and were at the trail head by 3:30.  It took us about 2 hours to get up--there were very few people on the trail, so no crowding.  We spent about an hour at the peak and then started walking down Ratnapora trail.  It's much prettier than Hatton trail and more natural.  The trail down is about 8 km of almost all stairs.  It took a bit over 4 hours and the last 2 km were really tough as one of my knees was in pain. It was dry season and we did not see any leaches.  it's also mostly concrete steps, so not sure where leaches would come from.

We stayed at white elephant hotel the night before (will review separately), left our hotel at 02:40AM and signed in with our donation at the bottom 02:55AM, passed through the large stone arch at 3:05AM and reached the top at 05:05AM with pretty much no rest stops - we were absolutely knackered. Being younger and healthy made it easier, but it was still very difficult and steep in parts. Would recommend scheduling in plenty of time of time for rest stops (plenty of little shops for food along the way). Wear good runners. Sunrise was just after 6, would recommend trying to save yourself a seat just down from the actual temple (facing east).

Set off at 4am and got to the top at just after 6 and I'm just averagely fit (and 50 years old) bought a load of peanut brittle and rotties for breakfast. You can buy in the two hundred odd stalls lined along the path.( this slightly detracts from the walk as they are somewhat tacky!),the walk is also lit by street lights so this spoils the view of the stars but means you do not need a torch ! It's tough as others have said but not too bad if you take it easy and also tip no 1 walk in zig zags . Tip no 2 is very important !! When you get to the final ascent and it's the steepest part where there is a sign saying stay to the right and railings to divide people coming up and down go to the left as there's no one using this as everyone's going up at this point ! The right queue as it will be by now and virtually stationary is for people going to see the foot! Also by going up this left line you can sneak round the back and queue jump everyone to go and see the fictitious foot print that you can't see anyway as it's covered up by the begging money so really don't waste your time, I was astounded how rubbish it was but amazed by how much money it was pulling in! But then I shouldn't be cynical as the walk was free , a first for me in Sri Lanka ! The views are amazing and I loved the walk. And would like to do it again at sunset which if it wasn't cloudy would be fantastic !

It's a 2 to 3 hour climb but steep and steps are uneven but well worth it.  Just make sure to get a spot  by the wall of the hat ton entrance or it will be difficult to see over the crowd which is packed at the top.

Left our hotel in Nuwera Elia at 9.00pm to reach the start by midnight.  Started walking at 1.00 am.  It was an amazing experience with only the 2 of us and our torch lights.  Managed to reach the top after 3.5 hrs and saw an amazing sun rise at 5.30ish. Going down only took 2.5hrs which for a couple in their 60's is not too bad.  Only about 30 people on the top because we did it 2 days before pilgrim season started but this made it all the more amazing due to lack of lights and the experience was fantastic, so many night noises and only the stars to look at. Not as tough as what we expected and certainly an experience not to be missed - agree with others the last hour is the worst going up, mainly because you do not know how much further you have to go and jelly legs coming down do not help.  Felt great the next day but calf muscles kicked in the day after despite a massage but nothing too bad.  It really is a must do experience.

Adam's Peak walk is a must do, walking alongside many Buddhist Sri Lankans. We stayed right at the bottom of the walk (at green house) and left at 3 am. We had one 15 minute break and a few 5 minute breaks, with a steady pace made it to the top at 6am. The last hour of walking was the hardest, up steep stone steps and a well used hand rail. It was cloudy and difficult to see the sunrise, and the peak was crammed full of people and a tangle of shoes. We moved lower down the mountain to see the sunrise then began the descent. Going down was also difficult as legs quickly turn to jelly and the uneven steps mean you can't rush down. Lazy girlfriend forgot to stretch afterwards and was complaining for days after the walk. Thoroughly recommend the trek, take some snacks and water although there is plenty of hot and cold food available to buy.

Climbing the highest peak of SriLanka is not for the light feet and the inexperienced. It's really high and tiring with never ending stairs till the top. Before we started off, mainly with the intention of watching an amazing view of sunrise, we heard that the ascend would take anywhere between 2 to 5 hours depending upon how fast one can climb the hill stairs. We started our ascend in the night 11PM, and were quite slow in the beginning, spending enough time clicking star trails and other night photography on the way. After around 1AM, we picked a little speed to climb the stairs and by 3AM, we already dead tired, but the stairs never seem to end. Although there're many small shacks on the way up, selling soft-drinks, snacks, tea and water, they're practically there to loot you with costs more than 2.5 times the normal cost of anything (which are anyway expensive in SL). So if you're on a tight budget like us, better to carry a couple of water bottles and some snacks (nice energetic sweets are available) from the bottom. Once we managed to reach the top by around 5AM, it's a small buddhist temple, flocking with a huge crowd already, most waiting for the sunrise. We barely managed to find a corner to sit and relax the aching feet, with the police making us get up from the stairs, and go elsewhere. Also being december night at such a height of 7,359 ft, it was quite chilling up there. But ultimately once the sun came out, all the pain just vanished looking at the beauty of the landscape and the sunrise through the scarce clouds at the horizon. Captured a lot of photos and then decided to start the painful descend at 6:30am. Took another 3 hours to reach down, and the feet were paining like hell.

Climbed 5km overnight (with lots of breaks) and it took nearly 7 hours. Totally worth it. Saw the breathtaking scenery of sun rise. Then the site of the sacred footprint. Rang the bell once as this is the first time I made the climb. Then Climbed down 8km  from Sri Pada to Pawanella (Ratnapura). Almost 9 hours. Saw lots of rare birds from Sri Pada to Pawanella road.

If you are in good shape Adam's Peak is probably one af the most rewarding experiences you can have visiting Sri Lanka. 2,5-3 hours of hard climbing over 5.200 stairs in the middel of the night together with hundreds of local pilgrims. Seeing the sunrise 6 o'clock in the morning while Buddhist monks play funny music is magic. Bring water, a little food and sweets, and warm clothes (it's could on the top). Ordinary trainers is sufficient, but be prepared that the 2 hours walk down all the stairs are much harder than going up.

This is not as difficult as many reviews suggest. It took us 2h40m bottom to top. We got up at 2am to see the sun rise from the top. My advice would be to go at about 5-6am. That way you still see the sunrise during the final part of your ascent, it won't be as cold at the top so you don't have to bring layers of clothing just in case and you miss the scrum at the top at sunrise. The main thing is the view from the top - which you get regardless of start time.

I love to climb hills and trek so this was a great walk. The added fun was that you have start at 2am to get to the top for the sunrise, so the walk is in darkness. As I was on holiday and not doing my regular level of exercise, I powered up to the top and got there a few minutes over two hours (I think that others do it around 3 hours). So I had a workout rolled into the journey too. It's steps all the way, at times quite steep, and not an easy walk at all, but people of all ages are making their way up, so it's possible to do even of you are the wrong side of young. The sunrise was pretty cool, with visible rays a la Caravaggio. Also, being so high and clouds so low, meant that the tops of the hills were poking out through the mist creating islands in the clouds (which actually I thought was more visually stunning that the sunrise). The only shame is that you have to share this Shangri La with many others at the top (cramped Into a small space). But I guess that they're thinking the same about me. Liked it and would do it again.

There are several routes to climb to the top. We took the hatton route. It is usually crowded during the season. We wanted to climb the stairs slowly so it took more than 4 hours. Start climbing at about midnight so that you can reach the top by sunrise to see the magnificent view. Take snaks and water. But there are shops on the way to the top, the prices increases as you go on to the top. TAKE A JACKET. Its really freezing. It will be a great workout for your legs.

may be it was the worst experience of my life. i came to see the adams foot print which is on top of adams peak. to get there during off peak times you must leave kandy at 6 am. by the time you will reach delhouse it will be 11 am. i took 3.5 hours to climb over 5000 stairs. it is very far way and very high. you will be testing your legs to the limit. most people take 4 hours to climb the stairs. when i reached there along with few other tourists the priest told us that it is closed. we cant see the foot print. it is only open during jan feb march and april. rest of all year it is closed. we requested the priest to open it for us but he flatly refused. everyone was so angry. he would not open it even for one minute. the room where the foot print is, is only open during the tourist season. BE WARNED. there is no point climbing all the way up just to see hills around you. THERE IS NO SIGN BOARD WITH OPENING OR CLOSING TIMES. It was sick joke for the us the tourists, as we all went up being told that it is open. the priest was just smiling at our plight. there are no toilets along the way. bring your won food and drinks as they are very expensive in the few stalls.  you will know why if you climb.

Out of the three main climbing routes to Sripada- Holy foot print of Lord BUDDHA most favourite and comfortable route among pilgrims is from Hatton, Nallathanni.I was managed to reached the summit in 03 hrs. and climb down in 02 hrs. after spending relaxing time of one hr. on the peak. Best season to climb I think month of November with very little traffic and good weather conditions just before the pilgrimage season starts from December to May. Although the altitude one has to negotiate is around 2300 meters you need to have strong legs specially during the climbing down due steepness of the mountain. Sripada is good to climb during day or night specially during the pilgrim season since the route is well lit.

By far the best experience I had in Sri Lanka. If you are able, start hiking between midnight and 2 AM to make the top by sunrise around 5 AMish. It is a spiritual, stunning moment to see the sun peak through and illuminate Sri Lanka's landscapes. Be sure to bring big bottles of water, sunblock, and some snacks on the way.
