Oh, and don't forget your flashlights. It was a difficult climb, esp in the end when you are faced with just stairs. And it gets chilly so make sure you are layering. Be sure to check the weather before you climb and hope for sunshine. Rain would probably sour the entire experience. Really, just do it. You won't regret it.

My wife and I climbed Adams Peak earlier this year and it was truly a life changing experience! We started the climb far too early at 10pm and reached the summit at 1am. Whilst we had packed jackets and some warm clothing, we weren't prepared for the 5hr wait sitting on cold concrete! Pack gloves, socks, beanies and something dry to change in to. It was all worth it though. The climb is exhausting but also meditative and spiritual, even though this wasn't something we were expecting! The locals are so friendly and have such a great spirit when climbing that it's infectious. At the top of the mountain, we met many other tourists and shared stories whilst waiting for the beautiful sunrise. This was one of the best travel experiences of our lives and a highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka.

One of the most mountain in Sri Lanka. It is sacred in relative to 4 religions due to the holy footprint on the summit. Buddhists believe it is of Lord Buddha's, Hindus deem it is the footprint of Lord Shiva, Muslims and most Christians consider it to be that of Adam,The holy mountain is shrouded in legend and history. .Although the journey was laid out with stairs all the way, the ascent was quite tiring and exhausting. Be sure to start the climb around 12 to 1 am, you will be able to reach the peak right on time for the stunning sunrise. But this depends heavily on the weather and visibility. But if all conditions favour you, your definitely going to have some of the most picturesque scenery while climbing . At the top of the peak, soon after dawn, the rising sun casts a perfect triangular shadow of the mountain on the surrounding landscape. Often the misty clouds make the shadow appear hovering over the sky upright and as the sun gradually rises the shadow disappears to the base of the mountain.  And in the surrounding dozens of mountain ridges will appear that poke through puffy clouds to sketch a mystical view. The surrounding is covered with dense forests that make up the Peak Sanctuary. Sri Pada is surrounded by a densely rainforest that makes up most of the Peak Wilderness Sanctuary. The cool misty forest resembles the forests found in the lower reaches of the Himalayas. Giant trees and thick moss rest everywhere and can also be seen along the routes. Rhododendrons bear large red blossoms and rare orchids like the Regal and the Chandraraja grow in the dark moist earth.Fresh water lavishly flows down from the Adam's Peak that feeds four large rivers at the lower slopes of the mountain. You will certainly feel a connection to nature and beyond when you crusade this place. NOTES: Avoid going on Full Moon; Poya days as there is more pigrims.

I climbed with four other people. We all agreed that it was one of the most amazing things we had ever done. Climbing through the night, the pain of the last few steps, meeting and chatting to new people, the atmosphere, the view from the top and also experiencing the Buddhist prayer ceremony just after sunrise all led to something none of us will forget. Our group had varied experience of Adam's Peak and I was one of two first timers, the majority of us were averagely fit and with plenty of breaks and support the climb is very manageable. I would happily recommend to anyone who likes the outdoors.

I climbed out of season so I knew I wouldn't get the best views from the top with the cloud. Left at 0230am and got to the submit at 0510 with heavy rain all the way. At the top is some big concrete buildings, one we waited in for sunrise and a small temple to see. All the way up is concrete steps and on the way down was some nice views of the waterfalls. I'm glad I did it but wouldn't do it again.

We climbed top of adam's peak at the beginning of september, the very low season. Only few people climbed (about 20 people). We began at 2.15 am, and took 2h40min to reach the top, with a lot of stops, but at a quite normal pace. Going down took 2hours or so. We met some people who did it in less than 2 hours, but it's quite useless, as everybody start at 2am, and that the sunrise in september is at 5.30 or so. The view was incredible, with clouds moving very fast, and it was totally cloudy 1h after. We met a lot of people who didn't even see the sun because of the thickness of the cloud. Climbing Adam's peak is nice to do (night hiking, more than 5000 stairs, that brings a lot of memories, and your legs won't forget easily), of course it is incredible with the view. But I think i'd do it even if the sky is not clear. No need of a guide, but better not go alone (walking in the night solo can be scary), and bring a good flashlight (can be find in any supermarket Kandy if you forgot it). A lot of people decide not to go because there is a risk of not having a view, and i think that is a shame if you have a not too bad stamina and if you like hiking.

Adam's Peak was amazing! I was surprised at how hard the climb was. I am quite fit (had completed a 1/2 marathon 4 months earlier) but I found this climb challenging.  We arrived in Dalhousie in the afternoon which was a real bonus. As it was February and during the pilgrimage period it was wonderful to wonder through the town before we started the climb. We watched bus load after bus load of locals arriving and departing. Everyone was happy and joyous and there was a 'party atmosphere'. We tried to get a few hours sleep before the ascent, but this was almost impossible due to the constant stream of buses and their musical horns rolling pass. We gave up and started the 'walk' at 1pm. Word of warning - try to avoid the weekends. We were their on a Friday night and the last 700 metres to the top was a nightmare due to the amount of people. However we arrived at the summit just before sunrise and it was worth every step/stair. Make sure you wear good joggers and take warm layers - it's really cold at the summit. If you get the chance this is a MUST to do in Sri Lanka. Absolutely loved it!

Out of the pilgrimage period, the 3-hour climb is usually done during the night, in order to reach the top at time for sunrise. However, that is only a good idea if the weather so permits. If not, a climb during the day is the best choice, in order to take a look at the beautiful forest surroundings.

We spend 3 hours walking from the bottom to the top. We started at 2.30 am, The walk has app. 5200 steps, so it is a hard walk for your knees ( and remember when you walk up, you also has to walk down - it takes 2-3 hours to get down) but if you are in this area, then Adam's Peak is a must. The view  is fantastic, we loved it, and when you walk you have the most fantastic view ever.

Climbing Sri Pada (or Adam's Peak) was great experience, although exhausting. We climbed from Dalhousie in mid February, and it was enjoyable, without too many people on the path.  We started 45 minutes before usual starting time and had a quiet climb. In the morning, when everybody started descending at the same moment, we were stuck several times on the first couple of flights of stairs, but after a while crowds spread. We missed the spectacular sunrise because of the clouds, but morning religious services on the top and pilgrims were also rewarding sight. Tea houses were opened all the way, and they have wide offering of food and drinks at reasonable prices (maybe they sounded reasonable to tired feet :) ) To fully enjoy the climb here are some tips: - It can get cold in the night. If you climb to catch the sunrise at the top, take some warm clothes in your pack, and something top protect you from the wind. - There is a temple at the top (building covers the whole top), and no-shoes rule is strongly enforced there. If you want to keep your feet warm, take extra socks for the occasion. - There is an area with stone benches (wide concrete steps) in front of the entrance that is protected form the wind. You can sit, or even lie down and still keep your shoes on while there.) - It takes a lot of steps to the top; many of them are steep and high. It is a hard climb and getting down is even harder. Do not go unless you are in a good shape. - Sri Pada is a place of pilgrimage. You can expect big crowds if you climb on the nights of the full moon or holidays. Check before you go.

Ok climb for beginners even though it rained throughout out whole 4 hours climb to the top! We even saw some guides and tourist wearing flip flops and shorts up! But personally, I would recommend against that and wear proper pants and shoes!
A great place for first time hiker....usually takes around 5 hours to reach the top..and the view is so awesome :)

Its Adam's Peak in English, Sri Pada(Holy Mountain) or Samanala Kanda (Butterfly Mountain) in Sinhalese. This is the only mountain where pilgrims and travelers alike from all faiths come to worship their Lord or Guru. How ever Its one of the holiest places for Sri Lankan Buddhists since they believe Lord Buddha in one of his visits to Sri Lanka visited Sri Pada on the invitation of God Saman and set his foot print on the mountain. The season to climb Sri Pada begins in December and end in May. It is very hard to climb the mountain in the other Months due to very bad weather. As you climb the summit you will see the breathtaking view of clouds beneath and other mountains and especially the sun rise which will be one of the rarest sites any visitor can see any where in the world. So if you are a adventurous tourist this is a must go site in Sri Lanka.

We started at 1:00 am. Walked slowly up through the night to end up on top in time for sunrise. It was a meditative walk in the night, and an awesome experience as the sun rose above the the surrounding mountain peaks. Absolutely surreal, it was because the mountain's shadow formed a pyraide figure in the mist on the shady side!

We also started the climb at 3 pm and it made for a great experience. There is still lots of large family groups doing the pilgramage and the majority of shops are closed so no one hassles you. It is gruling, harder then you would expect, but the people made it one of our best experiences in Sri Lanka. They offered us tea, biscuits, sugar packets, grapefruit, etc when they seen we were so tired. It touched us deeply because they were just as tired, some never had shoes, and some were 30 plus our senior! It took us 2 hrs up and 2 1/2 hrs down. We found coming down was harder then going up. Glad to do the majority of it in the light, the steps are kinda scary in some parts and the overhead light are burnt out in parts so it gets very dark. 3 police stations and maybe 4 bathrooms all spread out.

Went in low season. I believe it's 8km round trip, a lot of which is vertical :) Started off at about 2:30 from slightly chilled. You walk through the village, pretty obvious where to go. Lots of evidence of stalls along path which weren't open due to lack of tourists, so less hassle. 1st part of ascent is relatively gentle but not well lit, so you need a torch or smartphone or tag behind somebody who does. About 2/3 in to the climb, you get to steep steps, and they just get steeper. At this point, I was resting about every 100 yards. When you see the path lit up, you'll see an orange light at the top. Convinced that's not the top but a toilet block which is only about 75% of the way there. Started getting light around 5:10, so mild panic sets in at that point that you won't make it in time and you'll quicken the pace. You need to be close to above the timber line at that point. I got to the top at 5:45 just 5 mins before sunrise and was blessed as the cloud came in, 5 minutes after sunrise. As I wasn't at the top long, I remained in just a t-shirt and trousers and was perfectly warm. I'd started out with 3 tshirts, a jumper, under trousers and trousers, but that was way too hot to climb in and took them off about 1/4 of way in. Bring a backpack to store clothes if necessary plus water, you'll need lots, the climb is knackering. My legs still ache 3 days later. Not as scary as Sigiriya but 1 heck of a climb. Climb down is worse but there's lovely scenery including nice waterfalls. Made it back by 8.15.

My husband and I climbed Adams peak in the late arvo, starting around 3:30pm and reached the top by 5:30pm, hoping to see sunset but it was a white out. We enjoyed the climb, but it is difficult. It is true that you see local elderly and children doing the pilgrimage, so it is possible for the unfit, but I imagine very slow going and not very enjoyable! If you don't mind missing the sunrise, I would definitely recommend climbing in the arvo to avoid the crowds, cold and sleep disruption... Also recommend taking wet weather gear, the weather changed quickly on us and we got drenched on the way down.

We were not doing this for the pilgrimage but because we were told it was a great walk and like non other. It certainly provided the 'like non other'. It felt like we woke up early to trudge through 7km of the dodgy part of town in any foreign city. The walk is very well paved and lined with shops for at least the first 3km. At 2am, walking 5200 steps, the last thing you want is the constant hassling of shop owners trying to get you to buy things from them. This is how the walk felt to us. At the top it was overcrowded as the other reviews imply. There were spit and other coughed up substances lining the concrete available to you when huddling for warmth. The sunrise was spectacular (for three minutes) then began the pushing and shoving back down the 5200 stairs. Worthy to note... it was 40 degrees during the day but bitterly cold at the top at 5am. We had thermals, coats and a sleeping bag and were still cold. Bring something to line the concrete with, like a garbage bag, and thick socks as you have to remove your shoes at the top. Those that say it's a hard walk are pansy's. I had food poisoning, hadn't eaten in two days and made it easily. All I did was started earlier so I could take heaps of breaks. If you start at midnight you could do three mins of walking to one min break. We saw a pregnant women doing it, half a dozen senior citizens, and a lady carrying her son overtook us at one point. Oh yeah, half way down there was a one legged man on crutches asking for money. If he made it 2600 steps with only one leg... what's your excuse? All you need is 1L of water and a few small snacks and you'll be right. If you don't have these, you'll still be right as you can buy them at an inflated price all the way up.

Adam's Peak is a tough climb, me and my partner are 23 years old and we struggled the odd time. Not for children or the elderly! We started the climb around 2am in order to arrive at the peak for sunrise, which we did easily. It can be quite crowded, especially at the peak. Also it is very cold at the top, make sure you bring a jacket, although it was very hot on the climb down! The sunrise was beautiful and you feel a greaet sense of accomplishment after climbing this peak. I enjoy climbing so i had a nice time. If you dont like climbing you will probably not enjoy this very much! Expect your legs to be very painful the next couple of days!

This experience has the potential to be a monumental one. However, Pilgrim season means, yes, the stores are open and the path is lit up, but also means LOTS of people. Add to that I was there around Sinhalese New Year  - the busiest time of year. I started at 2am, and from 5am I was standing basically in the same spot, in a queue, on steps, after at least 4000 steps. Sunrise was still magnificent, the atmosphere with locals etc was wonderful, but it was frustrating to just give up on the peak due to the crowd.

Me and my wife climbed to adams peak in April 2013 (new year festival season) and by half way up we knew it was a bad decision. The climb is difficult to say the least and even being young 26 year old, didn't help a bit. We started at 1:30AM and managed to reach to the top by 9:00AM. Due to the new year season, it took us 2 hours to cover the last kilometer with queues as long as we could see ahead. What was worse was that the views were good but weren't worth the hardship and there wasn't any Adam's foot to be seen as it was coverved with a golden cloth. I would recommend that tourists should avoid this place and rather trek Horton's Plains. The return trip was even worse for the legs and the next two days of our tour we could only spend nursing them. I you are entirely bent upon going, avoid the festival season, and be prepared well in advance for climbing.

The climb is tough even in the cool of the morning. The recommendation to leave at 2.30 am (to be at the top at 5.30 am, ie: dawn) only applies to the fit as you need the entire 3 hours to make it. If you have less stamina start earlier and in any case as you reach the top it becomes a logjam up the single file stairs. This will slow you down regardless. At the top there is no room to move, get a viewing position and stick to it. We were on the steps next to what appeared to be the monk's admin office and chatted to the head monk. Thankfully the tourists are swamped by the hundreds of locals on the pilgrimage.

Omg, this was the most ridiculous thing I have ever done in my life! My friend and I began climbing Adams Peak at 3am and were nearly at the top by dawn (5:40) at which point we had had enough and were not going to climb another step. But if the climb was not challenging enough, the walk down was even harder. Our legs were like jelly all the way down and it took us about 2 1/2 hours to return. The climb is not for the faint hearted and you do have to be at least reasonably fit. Be warned, it can take you up to 4 days to recover. If you do intend to do this climb, get as much rest as possible beforehand (and not have a party the night before like we did) and allow yourself a beach day following the climb to allow yourself time to recover a little. Anyone considering this climb should think very carefully before doing it and follow the advice provided in other reviews! Good luck

Really hard climb. 5000 steps up and 5000 steps down. the way down was almost as hard as the 3hr climb up. Views at top are fab but personally I didn't feel it was worth the hell I endured for 6 hours starting at 2am!!

OK, let me start by saying that it wasn’t as hard as everyone’s making it sound.  It totally scared me hearing all these stories--I wondered if it wouldn't be too grueling.  Well, I’m here to tell you Don’t Worry. I’m someone who spent the last two years being seriously ill and largely bedridden.  I climbed up carrying everything I possessed (which was basically a backpack filled with extra clothes, a lonely planet guide, a camera, and a handbag).  And STILL I didn’t find this overwhelmingly challenging.  I started around 7 or 8 pm and took lots of breaks and drank lots of tea.  I could not have stretched the climb past midnight if I had wanted to. So, trust me, it’s really not that bad.  If I can do it, so can you.  You can stop anytime you need, even on the steps themselves.  Plus, the camaraderie of the local people climbing with you is something to behold.  It was a great climb! I have to give it 3 stars because it’s possible to be disappointed.  Like all “natural products”, variations can occur.  I went hoping to see the legendary sunrise…and it was cloudy, misty, and a giant loudspeaker directly obscured my vision.  I was kind of disappointed, because this was THE reason I wanted to visit Sri Lanka.  Just be open to the idea that it might not be the way it’s described in the guidebooks. Others have said going down is much harder, and that's true.  You just don't feel the exertion happening until it's WAY too late.  I read another review here that said the Ratnapura trail is less steep.  I followed that advice, and it’s not true…instead of going to the base of the mountain, it actually takes you out of the entire mountain RANGE.  It’s a much longer trail and goes much farther down.  The last 4 km in particular are mostly steep, rail-less steps.  I could hardly control my legs at that point--it really did leave my calves painfully stiff (as in, could hardly walk) for the next three days.  On the other hand, the trail did get me to the bus to Ratnapura.  Take a walking stick to lean on if you decide to go this route.

Our family of 4 climbed the peak in about 2.5 hours.  We left at 2 based on our guides recommendation and spent 2 hours waiting for the sunrise that unfortunately did not break through the high mountain clouds.  For anyone that does any exercise, 2.5-3 hours is enough to get up.  So with sunrise after 6, we left way too early and were very cold on top, even with extra clothes. We were just wet from the humidity sweat. The sutra chanting wnas interesting but definitely not the spiritual experience i was expecting.  Trip down was good in daylight to see what you missed on the way up in the dark.  What we found most annoying were the speakers playing commercials, constantly.  Not good!  Be aware that there are no first aid locations and crappy toilets and some stairs that are odd heights.  Easily doable for most people.

It was my second time to climb and I didi it at the end of the rainy season during daytime. Practically no people around which was enjoyable to watch the nature. The climb is strenuous under the heath, but with good training, excellent shoes and enough water  it is a rewarding experience.

Hope that none of you will need this information, but just in case... Note that there is no doctor or anything like first aid along the way nor in the whole Nallathanniya/Dalhousie. The closest hospital is in Maskeliya (14 km). I got quite seriously injured on Adam's Peak and had to see a doctor. Fortunatelly there is a private one by Laxapana Tea Factory - 10 minutes from Dalhousie by tuktuk (600 LKR return). It was like a way back in time... but the doctor was sane and well-educated. He did a good job. For few stitches and some pills he charged me 250 LKR. Laxapana is worth a trip anyway - easy, pleasant walk through tea plantages with nobody around except tea pickers and local kids... The tea factory is not usually open to public but if you ask to visit in the morning you can take an excursion later that day. If not interested in tea just keep walking, few minutes later you reach a small village. Regarding Adam's Peak the climb is indeed a good experience but a bit disappointing after all - crowds and teenagers with loud radios kill the atmosphere and the sunrise uncovers garbage all along the path. Not mystical at all. To be honest I enjoyed surroundings more than Adam's Peak itself.

I'll start by telling you what you're probably most curious about. I'm thirty three years old, I have a desk job, I don't go to the gym and I don't do any sports. We set out at 2 am and reached the top at 5 am. The worst part was actually reaching the top because we had an hour to wait for sunrise and were shivering like crazy. You don't feel the cold going up because the activity keeps your body burning, but once you reach high altitude and rest, it's more than a bit nippy. Considering me and my partner had built this up to be a really strenuous climb, we were surprised that it wasn't as bad as we expected. The best way to describe it is a tattoo. Some people tell you they're really painful, some people tell you they're not painful at all and then when you get one down it's about as painful as you expect it to be. Yes, it hurts, but its bearable. That's how we felt about Adam's Peak. Essentially, you're marching for three hours up a mountain, so yes it's hard, but its manageable. The trick is to get into a rhythm of slow pace rather than trying to belt your way up telling yourself that you can 'hack it'. Instead, take it slowly and your stamina will carry you through. The funny thing is that the first half is uphill and then halfway through it becomes constant steps and you think you're not going to achieve it. We saw a couple of girls from our guest house and when they stopped at one of the many places along the way, one of the girls said "am I stopping too often, it just feels like every time we start I'm tired again already". I know how she felt, but you reach a point where it doesn't bother you any more and you just plough through. The top largely depends on the weather, we had a cloudy day and therefore a very disappointing non-event for a sunrise. It doesn't feel like the top of a mountain either, there is a temple at the top and some houses so it just feels like being more at the top of a hill with a village. If you're expecting a spiritual experience, you may wind up being severely disappointed. I was surprised that on the way down, I didn't get the jelly knee syndrome I was expecting and again, it was hard but easier than I'd built it up to be. The fatigue only hit me, ironically, once we had got to the bottom. By that point, I couldn't be bothered with the twenty minute walk into town. I just wanted a shower and some food in my belly and that was the longest and hardest part for me. Overall, I'm glad I did it. The rewarding part was the sense of achievement at having done it rather than the experience once you're at the top of "beautiful views" or "spiritual experiences" of which I don't think Adam's Peak delivered either.

The journey to Adam's Peak was an experience in itself...the views of the mountains and tea plantations en route to Dalhouise were incredibly scenic. The climb is difficult but absolutely doable. We attempted the climb on our second night in Sri Lanka after having traveled for more than 30 hours to get to Sri Lanka and were successful.  We started the climb at 2:30 am and reached the top by 5:30 with two 10-15 minute breaks. The path is wide, clean, well paved and we went during season so it was for the most part well lit. The sunrise was nice, the shadow of the peak in the mountain mist is seen BEHIND the peak - on the opposite side of where the sun comes up. Some of the people seemed to be pointing to the sun and looking for the triangle there and were disappointed. But once the sun comes up walk around to the back of the temple and look out over the mountains and you may be able to see it, it last for about 30 mins or so. But even if you don't see it, the views from the top and of the mountains and valleys on the way down are worth it, the green rolling expanses of land covered in a light mist. And in the event you start losing stamina on the way up, take inspiration from the troops of petite elderly ladies dressed in white and barefoot slowly and steadily making the climb up!

we started at 1:30 am from our hotel, we reach the top at 4.00. It was a bit crowdy just before top on narrow stairs, so it is slowing down, take this into consideration when planning in season as there are a lot of local people who want to reach the top. I admired old people walking bare foot or in flip flops all the way up. It's a lot of stairs to go through but the view and sun rise from the top is totally worth it:-) hot when climbing and really cold on top in the night, so take extra clothes. We were waiting 1.5 h for sun rise wearing fleeces and jackets (probably only place in Lanka I put my jacket on..;-) Anyway I would recommend this to anyone who likes nice views from top of the mountain and anyone for whom Adam's peak is more than just another mountain. Great experience! :-)

I am in my mid 50's and knew I had not put in enough work prior to climbing Adams Peak - I found the last km or so extremely tough and had some doubts that we were going to make it to the top for sunrise. The encouragement from locals climbing not to mention the inspiration one gains watching elderly Sri Lankans being assisted to the top by family members was thankfully enough to help me keep going. The view of the sun rising over the mountains is amazing although I did find the crowd at the top a bit overwhelming. As others have said the climb down is also pretty tough. I was suprised that I was not particularly sore the next day - I used a walking pole and suspect that this may have taken some of the pressure off my knees. The other thing that came in really handy was a head torch for the toilets - they are quite dark. Although I found it difficult it was also one of the most rewarding experiences we had in Sri Lanka and I am really glad that we did it.

We climbed Adams Peak on NYE 2012 and climbed down on New Years Day 2013. Very romantic, but very busy. Dont let that put you off! It was the best thing we did during our holiday in Sri Lanka; a real experience. It's hard work though, so make sure you stretch, take decent trainers and dont try and run up! Take it easy and talk to people along the way; we met some interesting characters. Getting down is harder and we followed the locals by jumping/bouncing down the steps. It sounds bonkers, but it works; try it! Way easier on the knees than walking. Good luck with the climb- its very very worth it. Oh, and take a jumper and something wind proof as its cold at the top just before dawn...

ok, the best part is here - Adam's peak or sri pada. it 's not easy at all to reach Hatton, but during the road to the the place, it's amazing, and local shop owner could offer you the best honey, it is so rich and so natural, something that you would never imagine to find it at your country's high-end supermarket. We started the trip at 0215, and when i got back to the guest house, it is 11 o'clock in the morning, the stairs are scary, and your legs are killing you both during and after the climbing, but your heart will always encourage you to go, especially, so many local sri lanka people, both old and young, being so pious and patient, steadily going up together with you  ( which means a guide is unnecessary ). when the sun comes out, there are some many "OMG" scenes, but to me, i found most touching is when the local chanting sutra together with the buddhist master, of course i can't understand the language, whereas, the place, people and the time and the mood, would make you think, having the chance to witness such authentic pilgrimage is a kind of bliss and enlightenment. At last, if you think going down is a more easy job, then i have to say, sorry you 're wrong, at least not to the people who climbed sri pada.

It was a little daunting when I left at 2am to see the lights rising into the sky. I am 51 and reasonably fit. It was hard work. However inspiration is at hand especially when an 80 year old woman passes you! Just take it slow and have rest stops often.  it took me about 3.5 hours and was there in time for the sunrise. It does get chilly on top. I was a little disappointed as I expected it to be more spiritual. The views were fantastic. The litter was disgusting!!!. It's harder coming down and me knees took a pounding. All in all it is well worth and I had great sense of achievement after completing almost 5200 steps up and5200 down.

Truly unique experience. Reading all the trip advisor reviews convinced me to go, and I'm very happy I did. Started at 02.30, got to top at 05.30 (with several stops). Then took 2.5 hours to descend. It is the most beautiful setting for a temple I have seen in my life, and it is worth watching at least some prayer that lasts from 6am to 7am - the devotion amongst the local people is fascinating to witness.

Up at 2am in the morning and 3½ hours on the stairmaster - then you are there. Phew..! But the view is spectacular and a bit spiritiual eventhough I tend to be a practical person :-) Prepare for two days of sore legs...

First of all don't expect that this is a trek and you'll be alone on the top with full of flora and fauna around. You should understand that this is an importat piligrimme road and you will surrounded with a lot of locals and tourists. But this is an amazing experience to see old people climb on the mountain to visit the temple! And the views are very nice as well! Below — some useful tips that will make your climb easier: — Don't be afraid: the ascend isn't that difficult. The first part is easy, the second part will be harder. Leave more time for the rest-stops on the second part. Walk slowly and keep your breathing under control: one step — breath in, other step — breath out. — Don't be shy and stretch your muscles. Otherwise your whole body will hurt next days. — The ascend from the starting point will take you 2½-3 houes depending on how you're fit. You have to be on the top at 5.40-6 am. Don't come their earlier, there's nothing to do before sunrise. — Try to make your bags as light as possible. Take one extra t-shirt to change it on top (your first t-shirt will be wet), one bottle of water (you can buy water at any stall along the way), camera, bisquits (to have a snack on the top). — On the top there's a lot of people. The first building on the top on your right has kind of balconies (but without fence). Climb there. You'll have an unobscurred view from there.

I did this hike in August (well out of season). It is easy to catch a bus to nearby Hatton, from here there are some more irregular buses possible to change towards adams peak, or a rickshaw should be relatively cheap or perhaps covered by where you are staying. In August much of the area is closed and baron around adams peak. Though there remain a few lodges open and at good off-peak rates. If on a budget, bring a lunch-pack curry with you as there are no open cheap restaurants around at this time of year. After chatting to several people we thought to leave out at 2AM, in order to catch the sunrise. In hindsight this was definitely too early. Any old torch will suffice, and we walked much of the way without one. Also be aware that it is significantly colder here than the rest of the country. It was very nice and quiet for us, simply seeing a couple of others on the way. At the top we found a monk who led us to a waiting room out of the wind until the temple opened just before sunrise. All of the way up we were hoping for the weather to clear or to pop out of the top of the clouds.. but unfortunately not. The climb took around 2.5 hours, (21 year old couple) and was fairly strenuous with the steep ascent. I actually found it more difficult coming back down. Around 20 people made it to the top for sunrise but we barely noticed when the sun was actually up due to the clouds. The small temple grounds at the very top require bare-feet which was incredibly cold! The sense of achievement was great and it was an interesting experience. There are advantages of the peaceful time of year, but be aware of the weather, you may see nothing at all as we did.

Climbing Adam's peak was one of the most physically demanding things I have ever done, but it was well worth it! Your experience will be dependent on a number of factors: The weather, the condition of the trail (from garbage etc), and most importantly the people you are with. Luckily for myself the weather was mild, the grounds had just been cleaned, and I had the best company! We began climbing at 1am, and made it to the peak just after 3:30am. This gave us plenty of time to have a seat and observe the pilgrims around us. Do bring warm clothes (incl. touques, mittens, and scarves) as it gets quite cold while waiting for the sunrise. The image of the sun illuminating the misty mountains and valleys around us will be with me forever, it was so beautiful.

The best way to travel from Colombo-Fort  to Adam's Peak (Sri Pada) is by train which starts at 5.55 am or 8.10 am. It's better to buy/reserve 2nd class (Rs. 260) or 1st class (Rs. 750) train tickets to avoid large crowds which come to worship this Buddhist monument during its pilgrimage season which starts from December full moon to May full moon poya day. You should get down at Hatton station and take a bus to Delhousie (Nallathanniya). Usually there's a bus waiting outside the railway station during pilgrimage season or you may try a tuk-tuk. It would take about 1 1/2 Hrs to reach there. It's better if you can refresh yourself by getting a room in a B&B  at Delhousie and keep the luggage before climbing. The climb would take 5-6 Hrs and you may take rests along the way. There are small shops along the way; but prices would go up as you reach higher elevation. e.g. cup of tea - Rs. 30 at ground, Rs. 70 - near the top. Most of the travelers try to witness the sun-rise which occur after 5.30 am which is very breadth taking site. If you are planning to stay on top (in early morning); make sure you have adequate stuff to keep you warm. A good pair of socks, a jacket, pair of glows, hat may come handy since it might become very cold. Try to avoid week-ends or Holidays since large crowds tend to visit the place and you may have to wait along the way to reach the summit.

A good trip to tick off another attraction done box. Hard work getting to the top and an early night is definately needed before the 2am climb up the hill! Starts out ok, walking through the village and gradually gets steeper with the steps being constant at the peak. Would recommend starting early so as to get somewehere to sit at the top. A little dissapointed at the top, lots of maintenance repairs needed, very small area to view the sunrise. If you think it was hard going up its even harder coming down. I laughed when I saw a review someone had written about the steps shaking even the wobbliest of knees but it truely gets you! 3 days later and my calves are still stiff! Make sure you stretch after the walk to ease the muscular pain! Take something warm to wrap up in while you are waiting for the sun to rise at the top and some snacks/drinks would be ideal as its a long trek, took us about 5 hours in total and were keen fitness fanatics. Had to take off our shoes once we reached the peak, (it is a temple after all) so take some warm socks because the cold floor gets you pretty chilly! There are a number of stalls along the way selling random items of clothing, toys, flowers, snacks, drinks etc and a number of basic toilet facilties along the route.

I have been there 3 times, latest in last month and will go again. You can go there by bus from Colombo Central bus stand, but I suggest you go there by Cab. You can find a cab for less than 20,000 for both days. (It takes almost two days to go there and come back to Colombo)There are two inroads to the top of the hill. One through Hatton which is the famous rout and short, and the other one through Ratnapura, which is longer yet nicer and easy to climb. If you are to see the famous sun rise, start your journey around 2.30 from the bottom of the hill. If you want to take some time and are a stop-n-go person, start your journey around 12 am. If you go during the season, there will be small places selling tea n snacks and even meals. Season is from Dec to march. However it is so very crowded during the season. DO NOT go there on a long holiday (long weekends) as I have seen many tourists come down halfway from the hill due to the crowd rush. When you reach the summit, stay there until sunrise as that is the very reason many people reach the top other than the religious value.

This is one of the main reasons why I visit Sri Lanka! No, I did not do it for religious reasons. More so because as a tourist, as a curious fellow hiker, and of course to experience the breath-taking sunrise! Talking about sunrise, I started off with 2 fellow backpackers just before 3am from Delhousie (the Hatton side) to catch the sunrise. It was cold but the constant movement going up kept us warm. It was going to be really cold once we get there, so we'd brought warm clothes to wear once we'd reached the summit. It was tough going up, especially from mid-way onwards. The steps were steep and taller than usual. That didn't help giving the thighs cramp-like sensation. It's pretty easy to go up as there are steps almost all the way. If you like, you can actually spend the night in the few shelters along the way. Finally reaching the summit was a huge relief, to say the least. There were loads of people in the small surrounding compound waiting for sunrise. Following a friend's advice, I stayed just below the compound, near a small balcony. The climb and wait was worth it! When dawn began to break, we began to see the horizon creeping with an orange hue. It was not long before the sunny yolk began to peep behind the horizon. As the orange disc rose slowly, the horizon began to burn with an orange graduated to deep dark navy blue above. I'd seen many sunrises... this must be one of the most beautiful sunrise I'd seen ever. Of course, after the sun yolk has risen high, the rest rushed to the other side to see the famed triangle shadow. It was there for at least a good hour. Having read from a blog about the Ratnapura way, I'd decided before the climb to go down the other side. It was about 14 km and double the distance from Delhousie; however, the gradient was much more gradual and was probably much easier to get down. The forest trail to Ratnapura is UNESCO wilderness site and was a joy to walk down. The many trees' foliage was cooling and gives a pleasant feeling to pass thru. Reaching the foothill, there's an unmarked bus-stop where all the locals wait. The bus takes about an hour to snake thru the winding road before reaching Ratnapura. Absolutely must go!

We reached Dalhousie around 8pm because of a heavy rain. We had dinner in the accommodation that we rented for the night (White Elephant). We left almost 3am and good thing that there was no rain anymore when we started the journey up. There is no need for a guide and it helped that we had a small flashlight to help us in hopping around in some areas covered with water when then light from the path is not enough. The climbed was very tough for us but the rest stations and the encouragement of locals or people coming down, somehow helped us not to walk away from this idea. We were at the last 50m when the sunrise started coming up. Aaarrrgghh!!  Anyway, the beauty of the surrounding is still breathtaking and worth it. Now, the climb back down is just as difficult because our legs are really, really tired. We managed to reach the hostel after 3 hours. Too bad that there was no electricity in the area because of the rain from the previous night. So, the cold water from the tap brought more inconvenience to the tired muscles. =(

Despite waking up late (3am) and having to stomp up the steep steps through torrential rain the whole way up to get to the peak in time for sunrise, which didn't rise due to the clouds, climbing Adam's Peak has been the most enjoyable, inspiring and physically challenging experience I've had in Sri Lanka so far and I've been surfing up and down the coast since the start of January. I wouldn't advise doing it in flip flops and shorts like I did, as it is absolutely freezing at the top and pretty dodgy/ knackering walking down, so take some layers, give yourself 3.5 hours and enjoy some great local tea on the way up (30 rupees). Also take toilet roll and if you want to stay in the area look up The White House. The guys there sorted my girlfriend and I a really cute, clean shack, with our own bathroom, for 2500rupees a night including all meals. No haggling necessary at that price. Have fun.

Adam's Peak is a religious pilgrimage site for Buddhist, Hindi & Christian people and has many visitors each day. We went in February, which is at the height of the pilgrimage season. At first I thought this might be regrettable, as the path would be crowded. However, it was inspiring to see 70-year-old women hiking barefoot and fathers hiking while carrying infants/toddlers. Also, I was surprised to find the path to be paved steps the majority of the way and very well lit. It's a bit disappointing to nature lovers, but well-catered for the amount of visitors it receives each day.  I still recommend wearing athletic shoes and bringing a flashlight to be on the safe side. It is ideal to see the sunrise. To do so, I would recommend beginning the hike at 2 am. Wear light pants and a t-shirt to begin. Pack a hat, gloves and fleece as you will get cold near the top. Be prepared for some steep steps, but there are many places to purchase tea or food along the way. We did not stop until the "last hotel" before the peak which served great tea and Roti (bread). When you arrive at the temple, you will need to take off your shoes, so be sure to wear warm socks. I would also recommend bringing a blanket, as there is a lot of downtime at the top of the peak. At the top there were nearly a hundred people crowded together to stay warm, waiting for the sunrise. When the sun did rise, there was a religious ceremony, complete with drums banging and flutes playing. It was fascinating to witness. On the way down the views of the surrounding mountains, valleys, and lower temples are incredible. Be sure to take a camera. I hope you found this helpful and you enjoy your trip to Adam's Peak.

Extremely challenging to make it to the top, but as most of the reviews have testified, it is so worth it. Climbing with thousands of others to witness the beauty and magic of nature is something I will never forget. The climb itself though was nothing compared to the descent (for me at least) I figured I would have more difficulties coming down than going up, but when my knees started hurting half way down, I was secretly wishing that they would have built a cable car or at the very least cleared a path to the bottom where one might be able to slide down on a broken down piece of card board like I used to in the frigid cold of the mid-west winters...alas, no such thing. But, it is a couple days later and my calves still feel the soreness, but my aching knees are but a memory (thankfully). Do it! p.s. there is no actual fee per say, but the monks at the entrance to accept donations.

Though this is a Hiking Trip to the foreigners its pilgrimage for the locals (suppose to be - meaning not everyone thinks like so). This was my 2nd trip and 1st was when i was around 17, and details of which i do not recall very well. I do not recall great difficulties last time i climbed, this time i nearly gave up along the way but wanted to complete with the promise to myself that this would be the last... however was ashamed with all the old ladies in their 60s & 70s climbing down after making it up. Some looked fresh still and climbing down in style. There are a lot of Europeans who go and its apparent they are much tougher than us. However my wife and kid (8 years) made it up hours before me and my cousin did :S. By vehicle this is about 130KMs from colombo. From the Awissawella / Hatton (Nuwar Eliya) High way you need to go 37 Kms along a B grade road. Nearing Sri Pada there are quite a number of small guest houses. A lower end (but good) one we checked was around LKR 1700/+ full board. On our way back we had lunch at a small guest house called 'niwasa' and they charged us only about 150 rupees for a meal with 4 curries (tourists rates could be higher but dont complain as sri lanka is like 1/5th cheaper already than your country :D. I have seen eurpeans arguing or NOT buying stuff which we buy with no concern :D) The road is full of small shops from the start till a few kms up. This is proof of the amount of visitors this place has. There are people who carry stuff (such as gas cylinders) on their heads or backs and climb this 6+km route.. its incredible (and sad also). There are cadets who carry cement and sand as well (for building things ofcourse). Climbing in the night is recommended and the entire path is fully lit and in good condition. While you are getting near, you will see the entire route lit up and its a real far way up. There is a local warning that you should never say, 'how can i climb this' and if you do so you will never make it to the top. There will be a few times when you think you are there... BUT you are not there :D The sacred place is protected by God Saman. Its common for people to get blessing before starting. Musical instruments are not allowed to be taken. Been intoxicated is not adviced (you can fall to your own death ofcourse) and been dressed at least with a white top is best. Despite the cold you will have sweat. It is advised that you do not take this pilgrimage as a fun outing with shouting or any disrespect... it could anger God Saman which is not an advisable thing to do. Phone signals will work from time to time - both dialog and mobitel. Ofcourse try to travel light... there will be shops till the top to buy stuff but will be more expensive (which is very justifiable). There are toilets (but not many) and you have to pay either 10 or 20 ruppes for use. Litter bins are everywhere so no need to through anything anywhere else (unless its bio degradable). After about 1 km up, you come to the Siddhalepa Veda Piyasa. They have rooms there and a small restaurant. A good idea would be travel and come up to stay here in the morning - have your rest and start the climb in the night come back - rest and have a oil massage relax and go home. If you are weak or specially when you are climbing down and in bad condition... there are trishaws from the main entrance area to the car park which is about 1.5 km walk. Though it says its 5KM climb... IT IS MORE THAN THAT. 5 Km is calculated from the point which is designated as the sacred area... to get to this point i think there is about a 3km ascending walk. The view is good as its like you are looking from the highest point in Sri Lanka. However i felt i saw better while traveling in train in the hill country. If you are eating from the shops i would recommend NOT to eat 'filled short eats' - such as vegetable roti or rolls... last thing you need is a bad stomach. On my first trip one girl had such a problem and it was not fun for her. There are no Cool drinks but water or any bottled beverage is cool by default. Weekends will be very crowded and its better to go on a weekday during the season. Be careful cause if you injure yourself there are no helicopters to lift you back to safety. Nearly all who visited i noticed are from middle or lower class.. very very few higher class sri lankans were there. I suppose this not such a poch place for them to take a hike :D There is only one place for you to have a bath in the 'Seetha Gagula', not many do it and its very public. It is common for people to find a place to have a bath in Kithulgala.. However you may have to park and go in to find a place as we did not notice bathing places along the main road. My advice is to start early in the night (reviews i read from foreigners suggested to start around 2 - 3 am to reach the top at around 5-6 am) around midnight and climb with as less stress as possible. Going up is less stress on the legs but more tiring.. coming down more stress on the legs. A common tactic used is to climb cris cross - but it did not work for me. Allow about 2 days to recover after the climb. So if you are a foreigner and you have to fly the next day after Sri Pada visit...you may not enjoy going back home :D. A lady we met said she has climbed many times but will not come again along Hatton route as its too steep. Though rathnapura route is twice longer... its not strenuous and advice us to take that the next time. There is a local saying, a person who has never climbed siri pada is a fool and one who climbs more than once is also a fool :D This time i understood what it means.

I have visited Sri Lanka 3 times, in 1999, 2001 and latest 2005 (so it's been a while...but I plan to go back within a few years!). Each time, I climbed Adam's Peak and each time was a great experience I will never forget! For the first time and the second as well, I stayed at Green House Guesthouse, very close on the start of the climb. The guesthouse owners were super nice and on my 2nd trip, gave me a walking stick and their dog to accompany us. On my 3rd trip, we stayed in another guesthouse that wasn't as nice as Green House (can't remember the name) and we had a good guide with us. All of the climbs were in off-season. I was able to see the triangle on my 1999 trip--the weather was dry and perfect, despite it was in October (I think). Yes, it was cold over there, so warm clothes are a must! The second and third time it was rainy--very rainy--and it was really cloudy on the top. Still it was an amazing experience, despite of me having a stomach bug on my 3rd trip (talk about it being a pain in the butt...literally...being ill in the dark, wet mountain..ughhh! I don't know how I did it!). My legs were always super stiff and sore for days after each walk. Each time it took me about 3 hrs to 3,5 to get on top. I wanna go back someday, and want to go in off-season since the walk to me is more magical when it's dark and silent and there is no crowds, noise and lights around. If you go off-season, take some water, snacks and warm clothes!! A guide is a good idea for first-timers, but not necessary. Oh, and a good torch is a must as well! I will take rain gear too next time, and good hiking shoes. There are leeches, so I will definitely wear long pants and check for them frequently. Have fun if you go, it's unforgettable! PS: the review requires you to check the time when you visited...there were no options earlier than 2012 so I chose Dec 2012 but in reality I was there in 1999, 2001 and 2005 as I wrote:)

This was an incredibly experience and absolutely worth the hard walk! What an experience and what an incredible view up there!! We walked up Adam's Peak on the 30th of december 2012 and as this was close to new year and  not yet the high season there was not many people which was perfect. Our travel agent, Viraj at Sri Lankan Expeditions (excellent by the way!) booked a guide which we first thought was not necessary but it turned out being excellent having an experienced guide (12 years and probably thousands of walks there...). He was very nice, explained a lot during the walk, pointed out the best spot up there to wait for the sun rise and took us partly another way down which was a little bit easier for the knees and made us see a different view. We were lucky to have a superb sunrise and saw the famous triangle clearly, amazing! We started at 2am and got up at 5am and then waited on our privileged spot while eating the breakfast we brought. Do bring extra warm clothes as it's very cold once up there! You'll start and end in shorts&t-shirts but need trousers, warm sweater, windproof coat and hat&gloves on the top!  The walk up is quite hard but even harder down and tough for the knees... But it is so worth it! Yes, there are wild dogs that is irritating in the beginning but you soon forget about them. We had four that followed us all the way up&down! No problem with the smell people talked about in other reviews but that was maybe thanks to being there early in the season with less people on a not too hot day. I definitely recommend doing this, it's a once in a lifetime experience!

We did the climb during off-season (actually the day before the season started in December 2012). I have done this twice before during the season but this was by far the best experience.  We were told that you can't do it during off-season and were nervous until we went there. We were told they don't light the path before the season so we bought few flash lights. It was pitch dark most of the path but we had an amazing experience. There were lots of tourist who climbed with us at 2:30 am. It took us 3.5 hours to climb up and lot more time climbing down since we spent time specially taking pictures, talking to locals climbing and carrying heavy sacks for the temple and just people watching. Next night, we were able to experience the carnival like atmosphere in the town on the first day of the season and was able to worship the relic that was going to be carried up to the temple. It was a amazing.

If you've done this trek then you will know its worth every minute of the discomfort you will feel for 2 days afterwards. We took all our children - an experience they will never forget. Climbed twice now - just once more and I will be happy . If you visit Sri Lanka it's an absolute must x tough going but worth the magical experience - Sri Lankans run up and I huffed and puffed - but it's fantastic

We climbed Adam's peak just before the season so only a few tea houses were open and most of our climb was in the dark. That being said: we loved it! We suffered, but loved it :-) No crowds (apparently the 3h climb can take 10h in season because of the crowds) and a very special feeling to just rely on the beam of your torch. On the summit it is very very chilly because of an ice-cold wind. The owner of the White House guesthouse told us to bring a clean dry t-shirt to change and we are eternally grateful for this tip! We watched the sun rise and then saw the mysterious triangle appear in the sky. Being on a holy mountain watching this natural phenomenon is a truly spiritual experience. On the descent during daylight you see how beautiful the surrounding nature is and where the noises came from that you heard when you climbed up in the dark. We have some tips left: - as mentioned: take a clean dry shirt to change at the top - bring gloves - a guide is not needed, the trail is easy to find and there is only one way. Up the summit you have to make sure to take the same route down as you came up - take some cookies or snacks outside of the season - book an extra night after your climb to recover

Had a wonderful trip to Adam's Peak (Sri Pada). It is one of the best trips I ever had. This was my first time and look forward to try again. We started from Ratnapura and came down from Hatton. Started in the night to reach the peak in the morning to see the sun rise. It is so amazing and beautiful. On the top huge crowd (local and foreigners) to see the sun rise. It was so hard to reach the top tired and leg was so painful but really a worthy effort. Did not regret at all. Looking at the beauty of mother nature you forget the pain.

Here's a suggestion for you to consider. Get to Dalhousie during early afternoon. Commence climbing Adam's peak during daylight hours and take in the views as you climb, you'll have plenty opportunities for this as you're gasping for breath on a regular basis going up all the steps. Once you reach the top (you'll be nearly broken - unless you're an olympic athlete still in training!) there are two large concrete shelters where all the local (Sri lankans) are sleeping under blankets waiting for the sun to come up. Speak with the locals, they're delighted to chat, share a cup of tea (take your flask) and just chill (wrong word) cos it was freezing the night we were there. Unfortunately it hosed down with rain all the way to the top and down again, so we saw nothing at the top. Doing it this way will save you spending money for accomodation which you'll barely use and then once you come down jump intot the car / bus / whatever and sleep until your next destination.  PS. I doubt is a guide is required, just follow the steps like the 'yellow brick' road and keep heading up. As one guide said to us, once you reach the hand rails the going gets tougher, but you're nearly there... Beware, this is gruelling

Go during climbing season (January to May) when the crowds of pilgrims are there and tea shops and services open. Otherwise you'll be climbing a steep mountain, alone in the dark. Not much fun. The climb from Dalhousie is the easiest, but still strenuous. I was there on a long weekend so the trail and more so the summit were very crowded. Still, that added to the experience. Dalhousie has a carnival air to it as people are beginning the climb. It is inspiring to see so many elderly people climbing, or parents carrying their children. Most of the locals climb in flip-flops or even bare feet. Be sure to leave early enough to pause for tea enroute. You will want the rest anyway, but it adds to the experience. Take some time at the summit. Many people watched the sun rise, then headed straight down. I recommend staying to enjoy the atmosphere of the many worshippers, both Buddhist and Hindu. If you want to actually pass through the temple, allow half an hour to stand in line. It takes about 10 seconds to pass through it, and you won't see anything. The point is to enter an briefly worship and give an offering. I hiked out the Erathna route, about 14 kms down a rugged mountain trail. I do not recommend it unless you are adventurous and prepared. Having said that, I passed several older women climbing down in bare feet. If they can do it...

We started 2am and it took us a little less than 3 hours to reach the top, another 2 hours to get down. It is something special walking up the illuminated stairs in the middle of the night reaching the summit and observe a spectacular sunrise. We got caught in the middle of some local showers, but it felt rather refreshing during the climb. Some people, mostly locals as I understood decided to camp overnight at the temple, but I wouldn't recommend it. It's freezing cold and very cramped up. The local village does not really have much to offer besides Adam's Peak but I'm glad we decided to stay an extra night following the climb to rest out. We stayed at Hotel White Elephant, big, clean rooms, hot water, tasty dinner, wi fi and a very friendly manager. Hotel next door did seem like a better option but it was fully booked.

My boyfriend and I climbed Adam's Peak in November even though we were advised against it as it was not season. We ignored that and it was the best decision we took. =) We stayed at the Slightly Chilled guest house . They arranged a guide for us for LKR 2000. His name was Roshan. The climb started at around 2:15 in the night . Roshan met us at the guesthouse, armed with flashlights and was surprisingly clad in flipflops =). We were literally engulfed in the darkness , which is quite an experience if you have not climbed at night before. My torch failed , but luckily Roshan had a spare . The two and half odd kilmeters to the start of the actual climb went very fast , due to the adrenelin rush and the novelty of the night climb. The actual climb up was for sure not easy , however if you are reasonably fit it is do able and very rewarding . There are about 6000 steps , and the last section is a near vertical climb . Roshan helped us pace ourselves and encouraged us and kept up an easy banter , which really helped time pass and through the course of which we learnt he does the climb thrice to four times a week in his trusty flip flops. We met a few like minded climbers like our selves and swapped stories on the way up which was good fun, and helped time pass. As the first rays of light touch the valley , the climb gets slower , because it is steeper and you and cannot help but stop and gaze at the breathing view , which words and pictures do absolutely no justice to at all. As sunrise rose we reached the top(FINALLY) and just soaked in the view. We took some obligatory pictures and drank black sri lankan chai for LKR 70 a cup. We took a stroll around the temple at the top and would have loved to spend some more time there , but Roshan told us we needed to get going fast , as it would be really hot. The climb down took about three hours or so and was a lot slower , cause it got hotter and we did not have the promise of sunrise to spur us on . It was fun seeing all the scenery we had missed at night - vistas of waterfalls and, pine forests and tea gardens at the lower slopes- beautiful ! We had a quick stop and chat with a friendly buddhist monk at a small shrine a kilometer from the trail head, and finally stumbled back to the hotel, absolutely exhausted but oh so happy. We (especially me) could not walk much that day , but it was an amzing experience that we could not get enough of and has inspired us to do a trek in Nepal soon . =) My top tips would be - 1) GO OFF SEASON - I cannot stress on this enough , but the magic of Adams Peak is the serenity and the silence as you climb and take in the views 2) get a guide - this is a must if it is your first hike at night or to the area , we highly recommend Roshan - ask for him at Slightly Chilled Guesthouse 3) carry some light snacks and WATER BOTTLES to munch on  for energy as you climb and to avoid dehydration as the air is very dry 4) wear layered clothing as though it might be little chilly on the way up , it will be HOT on the way down 5) wear a good pair of shoes and socks , because if you dont climb regularly blisters are a certainity. 6) DO NOT underestimate this climb - it is 7 km each way - with a very steep ascent . Remember that it has stairs because of its steepness , so stairs do not make it easier, having said that , Adams Peak was probably our favorite part of Sri Lanka. An absolutely must do challenge. !

amazing experience, up at 12 midnight to get to the start of this amazing pilgrimage...it is not for the faint hearted...6,000 steps and 6 hours to reach the summit but the reward at the stop is amazing....stunning sunrises if you are lucky. We went out of season so it was pitch black on the way up but our amazing guide Neil (in his flip flops) was just fantastic...worth every step!!!

Left a bit early, if you're reasonable fit then it really doesn't take quite as long as everyone claims it will; as a result we spent a good hour in the heavy clouds and cold in the morning much to the concern of the resident monks. There's a little room on your right hand side just below the summit that you can wait in if you're early. Even thought he sun failed to rise, and cloud cover was so dense we could only see a few peaks poking through it was still worth the clamber up the 3800 or so steps, do it for dawn and then you can skip back down for breakfast and still have the whole day ahead of you. 4 out of 5, although 0 out of 5 for wheelchair access ;-)

This is very interesting hike. There is a season to climb this mountain (December to May) . Otherwise it's little bit hard to climb in off season because of weather. Also season time, there are much pilgrims and temporary shops available. I don't know about off season but during season time, there are public bus services available. Go to hatton town and wait for Dalhousie bus. Normally to climb, it takes 4-6 hours. (depend on you . ) Important Take only necessary things. Don't carry heavy things because it will slow you Take thick cloths. On the summit, it is cold in night time Take water, food with you. If you try to buy those on the way in temporary shops, it is double price. Careful with drinking water. keep remember there are only basic facilities Most important thing is this is a pilgrim place. Please behave yourself. I saw some foreign couples kiss each others on the way and on the summit. Please don't do that and think about sri lankan cultural and ethics. Sri lankan people climb this mountain to worship load Buddha’s footprint. Ware something nice and respect others also. Climbed and worship load buddha on 2012-12-31

Went out of season (14th-16th October 2012), which we were told wasn't possible, which just isn't true at all - it's perfectly possible.  In fact, I hear it can take up to 9 hours during pilgrim season due to the volume of people, and I suspect it would be very difficult if you wanted to stop and take rests (as we frequently did!). Climb took us 2 hours up and 3 down, left at 2:30am and reached in time for sunrise.... Weather was hit and miss, a couple went up the night before us and couldnt see anything at the top for thick cloud but our sunrise one day later was perfect. Advice - layers of clothes, to strip off one by one as you get hot climbing and to quickly put back on when you reach the freeeeeezing top. Wear covered ankles/legs, we heard of a couple of leach incidents.  Take a camera and plenty of water, You don't have to be super fit (as we managed and are probably "occasional exercisers") but there was some leg suffering for a couple of days after. Oh - take extra socks maybe? you have to take shoes off at the top and then if it's damp (which it is likely to be) you get wet socks... I hate wet socks.... MOST IMPORTANT ADVICE - there is a lovely lovely lovey family who own "Achinika's Holiday Inn" in Dalhousie.  We didn't get the chance to stay there as had pre-booked at. 'Slightly Chilled' but if we go back we will DEFINATELY be staying with Achinika and her family.  They had heard it was my birthday and invited me and my travelling companion over for dinner, bought me a birthday cake/present and spent time to try and find me a Sri Lankan Rupee made in the year of my birthday..... i've not known such genuine hospitality in all my travels.  Achinika's mum also offers traditional full body (you can't be modest) massage/body scrub which was a great experience :-) and much needed after climbing the peak! and her Dad has a taxi service with very reasonable prices for your on-going travels. Enjoy!

I made an 8-day-trip to Sri Lanka from 8/11/12 to 15/11/12.  On my fifth day of my visit there, I took a tuk tuk from Kandy at 2pm to Dalhousie, not far from Adam's Peak.  I could have taken a train to Hatton before going by tuk tuk to Dalhousie, but considering that the train would depart the Kandy Railway station at only 5pm and reach Hatton at 7pm, I decided to save time by going on a 2-hour-tuk-tuk-ride to Dalhousie from Kandy.  I reached Dalhousie at around 4pm, and checked into Slightly Chilled Guest House and Restaurant.  After 2 hours of rest, I put on my mountain-climbing-gear of a short-sleeved-collared-T-shirt, a pair of short pants and a pair of snickers before I left for the nearby Achinika Food Corner(0094-523530377) to have my dinner, get a packet of sandwich and torchlight. At about 7pm I walked towards the entrance to Adam's Peak.  I waited there for about an hour for other climbers to come by, but no one did.  So. I decided to start off on my own.  The torchlight came in pretty handy since it was pitch dark.  I could hardly see the trail without the torchlight.  Soon, after passing a couple of temples, I came across a fork of paths. One was a rocky path and the other was an-inviting-path to a flight of stone-steps leading to a brightly-lit-Buddhist-temple.  I took the road often taken, i.e. the stone-steps.  The steps led to an open-spaced-brightly-lit-temple, but no other paths were visible.  I was lost!  So, I decided to wait there for the other climbers to pass by.  More than an hour passed by.  Inquisitiveness got the better of me, so I walked back to the edge of the steps to  see if anyone was using tthe path that I had taken. After about 10 minutes I saw a few head-lights moving along the path I had taken.  I was overjoyed and looked on eagerly, but I was in for a surprise because upon reaching the fork of paths the head-lights moved along the other path, the road I had not taken.  I quickly switched-on my torchlight and dashed down the flight of steps towards the fork of paths to catch-up with them.  Soon, I managed to join them, a team of young Russian climbers.  I tried my level best to keep-up with their pace, but after climbing about 200 steps, I was panting heavily.  So, I had to stop to take a 5-minute-break.  I decided to change my tactics by climbing sets of 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 steps, and by increasing the number of steps in sequence.  I rested for about 5 minutes after each set.  I repeated the 500-steps-set for about 3 times before reaching the peak of the mountain, the end to the streak of 5200 stairs. Upon reaching the peak, all the climbers gathered in a cosy room there to keep warm, rest and rejoice.  After drinking a cup of hot plain tea, served there for about Rp100 each cup, all of us went to catch a view of the sunrise by sitting on the steps of the temple balcony facing east to await the sun.  The view was amazing!  From the peak, I could see blankets of clouds floating several hundreds of metres below.  Soon, it was bright and cold.  All of us gathered around a locked room at the peak, and were informed by the staff there that Adam's footprint is locked in the room, and that it will only be displayed to public during the festive season in December.  I was disappointed!  I'm sure the rest were as well.  After walking around the chilled peak for about 15 minutes I decided to leave the peak before I froze-up.  The morning breeze made it unbearable for me.  It was freezing cold. I tried rubbing my palms together to keep warm but it didn't stop me from shivering. I started decending using the steps slowly and carefully partly due to the unbearable cramp-pain on my legs.  Soon, I picked-up pace and was jiggling down the steps.  However, the cramps remained and as soon as I had reached a more leveled path I started staggering back to  the Slightly Chilled Guest House and Restaurant to take a bath and rest.  The leg-cramps made it difficult for me to walk.  I promptly remembered my father's advice, years ago, to take a hot-water-shower when faced with cramp problems.  Cold water will only worsen the pain!  So I took a hot-water-shower, and felt much better afterwards.  Then, after sleeping for about 2 hours, I packed-up my bags and checked-out from Slightly Chilled Guest House and Restaurant at 3pm.  Subsequently, I headed to the nearby Achinika Food Corner to catch the taxi service that they were providing to the Hatton Railway station.  Upon reaching Hatton, I took the 4.30pm train to Colombo.

We climbed Sri Pada in complete off-season (August, 4th) and yet enjoyed it a lot! Manager of White House in Dalhousie (where we stayed overnight) who had been on the peak more than 60 times (one can never know, but he seemed trustworthy) told us that in this period of the year there is no point to start the ascent around 3 a.m. (to watch the sunrise) because the sunrise will not be visible due to the clouds if we are not able to see the peak's top light at 1 a.m. (the peak is in clouds). On the contrary there might be short period of cleared up sky around 9 a.m. As we hadn't saw the light we decided to wait till 5.30 a.m. and than started the climbing with the day light. Tens of people we met on their way down near Dalhousie just confirm the prediction - they went for the sunrise and yet saw "just" gradually enlighten clouds and fog. We take an advantage of quite solo ascent - apart form several groups near Dalhousie we have met really few people on the way up and down as well. All the way up without seeing anybody was stunning experience - there weren't any shops, and the last part beneath the peak and the temple on the top itself was more like a ghost town. On the peak we got also very much cloudy view but the feeling was great anyway. On the descent the sky was quite clear so we can enjoy the beautiful view of the valley below us. Expect a Buddhist monk at the begging of the path who is expecting donation from the pilgrims. On the top of the mountain there is a group of men living there for the whole year and they are ready to offer you tea. Anyway - as there are no stalls during the off-season, be extra ready concerning the water and sweets or any other energy-suppliers! And if you are worry about the difficulty of the terrain - we made in even in trekking sandals :)

In reading the above reviews I didn't notice (or missed) anyone writing about coming down, which is considerably harder than going up. We were almost totally unable to walk the next day. I also did not notice anyone mention that the sunrise casts a shadow of the mountain that stretches all the way to Colombo. There is a bell one gets to ring at the top. Just one ding for every time you make the climb. When we made the climb in 1986 there was a coroner's shack at the bottom. There have been a climbers who did not survive.

If you start climbing at night, you pass by beautiful countryside, you do not realize, until you climb down. Water cascades, mountain view... 5200 stairs are tiring, but worth it:) Unfortunately the weather was not nice, and we saw sunrise behind the clouds. A man, who is living upstairs said that they show Buddha's/Adam's/Shiva's feet in December:)

Some people say there are 5200 steps to reach Adam's peak summit (2243m above MSL) from the little town of Dalhousie. I haven't personally counted  but what I can tell you is that climbing the peak is a rewarding experience. We started the climb at 3:10am in September. As we travelled in Off-Peak period, the path to the top was not lit and bringing few headlights  was helpful (bringing a raincoat is also a good idea). It took us 2h20min to reach the top and we had to wait until 6:00am that the warden opens the gates up there to get closer from the footprint. He offered us to have a warm cup of tea in his room in the meantime.After the sunrise on the way back to the village, we could see the tea estates and many little waterfalls, which gave a scenic taste to the stroll. PS: to reach Dalhousie from Hatton, you have to take a bus to Maskelia (1h) and then take another bus to Dalhousie (1 more hour). It's also possible to hire a tuktuk and if you haggle with the driver, you'll probably get a rate at around 1200Rs (LKR).

It was off the season and no shops along the way. We started at 3h in the morning and get in time at the top. Unfortunately, it was cloudy so nothing abut the special effect in the sky and the temple was closed as well... then we decided to get down by the other side..15.000 steps and 15km versus 5.000 and a few km for the other path. We arrived 6h later and exhausted. We took a 30 min. tuktuk to Ratnapura. The whole experience was spectacular. I'll do it again.

If you like working hard for a reward this is the attraction for you. The arduous climb is really hard work, around 5200 steps, so make sure you're fit or really determined, but the feeling of satisfaction you get when you reach the top is tremendous. And when the sun rises it lights up the beautiful and pristine landscape around. Make sure you catch the perfectly triangular shadow of the mountain at the back. If you like moths as well there are thousands of them right at the top. It may not be the most spiritual experience you have but it is definitely worth it for the view from the top. A really fun and worthwhile experience.

it's a wonderful sight when u r at the top .. but lots and lots of walk !!! u need to constantly climb for 3 or 3.5 hours .. but the temple at the top and the sunrise view can actually worth out your effort .. We found a nice place just near to the start of our climb named Punsisi Rest Inn with great service and wonderful view of Sri Prada !!!

I notice that a lot of the other reviewers complain about the 'stray dogs and the stench of urin'. I wasn't bothered by that or of the many shops along the way. Sri Lanka is one of the poorer countries in the world, and emerged from violent conflict not too long ago, so I can accept that everything is not tip-top. I think the walk was really nice, we started the climb at 2.30 and arrived at around 5.30 (we are a couple in our 30ies in normal good shape). Bring lots of warm clothes for the top, it's really cold! The sunset was ok, very crowded on the top. It's true that there are shops all the way along the trail, but we still enjoyed it a lot, the view to the lakes and forests around the mountain is very pretty, and it's a nice walk.
