The walk down is a lot harder on thighs/knees than the walk up, so you should be in ok shape to enjoy it. I can recommend an excellent driver if you need to go from Colombo to Adam's Peak. It's a 5 hours drive each way, he charged us 140USD return trip, and we got in a nice minivan for the two of us. Mohamed Razeek Tel: +94 777 770 876 apartment.tmt@gmail.com www.tmtbuyandsale.lk

My husband and I are both fit so we didn't find the walk that difficult. So we weren't overly disappointed when we got to the top and found a Buddha with flashing lights around it, lots of stray dogs, stinking urinals and obstructed views of the landscape. If you were unfit and not spiritual you could end up wondering why you bothered. Adam's peak is no mini inca trail - it is lined with shops and litter and features the occasional dog fight.

Very dificult road,many stairs that smells from urine. The sunrise is pretty but you can barely see it, since the roof of the building you standing  on it covers it. We are couple who likes hikes and wouldn't recomend this one.Long and no sights along the way.

Started walking at 1.30am and arrived at top at 4.30am. Sunrise began at 6.30am and was worth the wait. Freezing cold till the sun came up.Took 2 hours to descend. The whole walk is on steps so is very relentlessly steep. Very crowded at top while waiting for sunrise.

we climbed the peak with a guide (though you dont need one) as he was part of the package we paid for already. we were told that it was arduous and recommended different clothing. But i guess things have moved on. Now there is a tea shop with blaring music every 10 minutes - good distraction during the climb. the toilets were average (better than wat we expected from similar journeys). most of the way has railings to hold on to and you just climb stairs which were not steep. We did it at night, which i would recommend, so that you are there for the sunrise, we did it in May and it was still very cold at the top at 4 am. Please time it correctly, we did not adn ended up at 4 am with no place to stay, the 2 "rooms" were  full of people and we soon joined the masses. all the effort is worth with the sun rise, the sounds of the  early morning pooja preparations and you can see more things as you climb down. difficult to say whether we will do it again, but worth it for this time

We are not fit and still managed the climb. Yes it's arduous, but it is absolutely worth it to see the sunrise and the mysterious shadow. We started at 2.15 am (later than planned) and it took us three hours at a steady pace, arriving at 5.30 am. We had one stop for tea. It is imperitive if you are doing this in pilgirmage season to stay in Dalhousie and start early - you cannot over estimate the number of people. The last 45 minutes was basically a queue of locals - and therein lies another beauty of the climb,

heed the advice and start at 2am, it took me 2 3/4 hrs and i'm not the fittest, the town itself is littered with many stalls selling the same tatt but the walk itself has many stalls which are very welcoming at times. gentle start leading to punishing middle and easier top. it is very cold whilst waiting for sunrise. you're joined by many friendly locals making the pilgrammage, some singing, many hello's, at the top everyone mixes and bell ringing and worshipping. beautiful views, beautiful walk down although my legs were shaking a bit!

After reading so many positive reviews on the web and in guidebooks we were expecting something spectacular. What we found was a huge crowd of people walking up the stairs that look like a marketplace for the most part.  Maybe it just is not the kind of 'spiritual experience' we thought it would be. [I cannot imagine how the climb looks when it is full moon and gets really crowded]

We are two semi fit Kiwis and this climb is not to difficult, we took the dalihousie route and we got up at 2.30am and made ourway to the start of the climb we arrived at the gate (you will know this when you get there) at about 2.55am. We didnt really stop but we did go slow as we did not want to reach the top to early, we walked in light 3/4 pants and a tshirt but a light top is advisable for the walk at the start and near the top.  we arrived at the top at 5.10am sunrise started about 5.40am so we were quite cold luckly i had packed a completed change of clothes such as pants, gloves ( i have poor circulation), hat and hoodie which was an excellent idea as you do sweat going up. Not much at the top and disspointed, the structure is a shambles, there is no good look out just mostly into the other building or into walls, My suggestion is to take photos then head down below the top and situate yourself on the steps as the view is way better about 25m/ 50m from the top to see the sunrise. walking back down is the hardest bit, got the jelly leg syndrome about 1/2hour from bottom. we arrived at the bottom at 8.30am We enjoyed the experience and was inspiring to see the locals do the pilgrimage - I hear full moon time can be ridiculous. Good luck!

As a 41 year-old with average fitness and no training for this climb, I was very worried by some of the reviews below and I almost cancelled as I was concerned that the injuries would ruin the next week of my holidays if I couldn' t walk properly. I'm glad I went ahead! It's demanding, but it's not as gruelling as many suggest below. Yes, I was sore for a few days, but if I'd done any training at all, I'm sure I would have been fine, and it didn't stop me from doing anything in the following days. Yes, it's crowded and there are many shops, but understand, that this is a very important pilgrimage for many people, especially local Buddhists. The shops are there to provide them sustenance and mementos. Indeed, getting a sense of what this means to the pilgrims is a highlight of the trip - see them huddled at the top, or supporting each other, and see what this means to them. And coming down is an exhilarating feeling - I was on a high all day as a result. Some advice: while I didn't do any training, you probably should. Do plenty of hill and stairs in the week leading up. Don't carry anything (except your camera - some warmer clothing for the top, that you can wrap around your waist). Any food or drink can be bought on the way. Don't go too fast or too early - if you get there too much before sunrise, you start getting cold. Stretch! - take the time to stretch really well (quads and calves especially) at the start and after you finish and any time you might be stopping for a while. I'm sure this was a big reason I was okay. And by all means take breaks, but don't make them too long - that is no help. Do some carb-loading the day before, then eat things like bananas halfway into your ascent, and plenty of water throughout.

As recommended by everyone we started our climb at 2:30am. We were told by other travelers that it took them 2 hours so we were confident to reach at least in 2.5 hours. It took us 3 hours at the end to reach the summit and 2.5 hours again to come down as the steps do become irregular and steep. As tough as it is to go up, as tough it is to come down. But we did take our own sweet time and reached reasonably fit - but totally sweaty. Recommend to bring - apart from a camera of course - a new set of shirts, as it does get windy on top and a dry shirt feels like heaven. I agree with some other reviews that it is a tough climb, but definitely worth it. The view from the top was stunning, and the sunrise was amazing even so I have seen a number of sunrises before. We did not get annoyed by all the shops on the way as they did not try to sell anything to us.  As we have been warned by one of the guesthouses that we should not eat the roti that is sold due to old oil being used which might cause stomach pain, we did not try it. we also got warned of pick pockets once you are up and happily watch the sunrise. The warning was "There are 100 nice people, but 1 bad one, so be aware and take care of your valuables." We catched a spot at the staircase before the buildings start and had a lovely view. Would definitely recommend this to anyone travelling in Sri Lanka.

Most foreign tourists visiting Adams Peak start the climb at 2am whereas locals often climb up the evening before and spent the night at the summit. We decided to climb up just after dark. We left our bags with a guesthouse free of charge (we had dinner with them and tipped then for looking after our bags) and left at about 8pm. We reached the summit at 10:20pm - I think the hike up might have been quite a bit quicker for us because we left so early and so did not get caught behind anyone. I found that the climb (particulary the second half of the climb) was much harder than I expected and for the last 500m or so I had to stop frequently for short breaks. I have read the review below and note that I was also disappointed by how commercialised the route up is - many small stalls with flashy lights and loud music selling food and cheaps trinkets. At the summit there is a small temple and a hall like room where pilgrims sleep - which was full when we arrived at 10:20pm. There is also an open area with fires where pilgrims and other local people warm there hands and chant. We found a place overlooking this area and spent a couple of hours watching this and talking to local people before we tried to sleep. The walk up might have been very commercialised but this was anything but. It has quite an amazing feeling - very different from anything that I have ever experienced before. Trying to sleep was a challenge - I am aware of having spent the whole night shivering but don't think there was any point where I actually fell asleep. Despite being out of the ice cold wind where we were and despite having several layers of good qulaity thermals, jumpers and a jacket I was absolutely freezing to the point where some of my bones were aching (and I'm in my late 20s so this was not something that I expected). We were roused (from our shivering state) at dawn by some locals and moved across to the eastern side to see the sunrise. At first we were concerned that we would not be able to see anything as quite a crowd had formed and it was difficult to see over all the heads. We then climbed up onto the rock on which the little temple is built and had an amazing view from there. The sunrise was absolutely magnificent - gorgeous beyond belief. Everything (the sunrise, the awed crowd, the pilgrims making offerings) creating the most amazing atmosphere. Just after sunrise we moved around to the otherside of the temple where we were able to see the shadow of the peak on the clouds which was also amazing. Overall, despite how commercialised the walk up was, despite how tiring, despite my aching legs for days afterwards, despite the cold and the lack of sleep, this was one of the most amazing experiences that I have had and the absolute highlight of my trip to Sri Lanka.

We set off at 1.30am ready for an adventure and quickly realised it wasn't going to be one! There is a large path the whole way up and every 20m there's shops selling food and drink or if you prefer a cuddly toy or a Mickey Mouse figure! We made it to the top only to realise it is covered in buildings, no 360degree view! Sunset was nice but somewhat marred by looking over buildings.  The shadow was the only highlight. Coming down seemed to take forever and music blared out for most the way. I honestly wouldn't recommend this anyone.

Sri Pada (known as Adam's Peak in english) is THE holiest mountain in Sri Lanka. There are 4 routes to go up to the top, the most popular one being the Hatton - Dalhousie trail.  We took this trail to go up, as we sat in the bus from Hatton to Dalhousie, the bus conductor was kind enough to point out Sri Pada's peak, as the bus wade thorough the winding road. We took our own sweet time to climb up the mountain as we did not want to rush the climb and tire ourselves too early, as such we started the climb at 9 pm.  We knew we would take some breaks or short snooze along the way, hence the reason to start early. Along the way we met with other pilgrims, some young couples carrying babies, and some elderly individuals.  The zest and happiness on the face of the elders is infectious.  Not once did i heard any of them complain or saying they wanted to stop and go back down again.  It is as if they had set their minds on reaching to the top and nothing on this planet was going to stop them. At the top, it was a pity photography was not allowed on the place of worship, as i had wanted to take some snaps.  To reached the top with an hour to spare before sunrise was just amazing, pity sunrise was not as spectacular as what i had seen in some magazine photographs due to the weather this time of the year. I was humbled as i reached the top and thanked the devas for looking after us while we climbed up.  Would like to come up here again sometime, this time taking the Ratnapura trail instead.
Just back from Adams Peak and highly recommend the guide Anil Vithanage (adamspeak_dharma@yahoo.com) Good compnay, well informed and very personable Rise early and see the sunset

I climbed it with my 9 year old son in 3 and a half hours and it took us 3 hours to descend. It's very atmospheric on the way up with all the Buddhist shrines and the tea shops, even if you climb at night. At first my son outpaced me but as the steps got steeper he started to flag and I started to get worried. We decided to give ourselves small targets, like 300 steps before resting, and this is a good way of motivating yourself to continue. By the end of the climb the 300 steps became 50 steps! Also, thinking about all the obese or old people who make it up there is a good way of motivating yourself. Take warm clothing and good footwear and take it easy. Leave at least 4 hours to make it up. When we got to the top it was misty and we could hardly see anything. So this was a great disappointment after all that effort. But on the way down the views were amazing although it did rain constantly. When you descend the pressure on your knees and feet is incredible and I am still limping several days after the climb. In conclusion, I would say that you feel a great sense of achievement after having done the climb and it's a must-do experience in Sri Lanka. But it's damn hard.

We started our climb at 2:30am, and set off with a spring in our step.  Before long, we were slowing down and as the steps got more irregular and steeper we found ourselves having to stop more regularly to catch our breaths and relax our legs. We reached the summit around 5:30, and we're reasonably fit, so make sure you give yourself time, as it would be agony to put all that effort in and get there late. It's a tough climb, but definitely worth it.  The view from the top was stunning, and the sunrise and the shadow of the mountain were amazing and everyone you pass on the way up and down have only smiles to share. Sturdy shoes are probably advisable and definitely pack a camera.  As it is a tough climb you will sweat, and you might appreciate a change of t-shirt for the top.  Also it can get windy and chilly at the top so a warm top/coat/jumper is probably a good idea.  There are plenty of stalls selling food and drink on the way up/down at reasonable prices.  We had a tea and roti just before the top, both of which were very welcome and tasty. The climb down seems to take a long time and irregular large steps are tough on the way down as well as the way up.  Expect some wobbling legs by the time you get to the bottom - hopefully to a hearty breakfast to help you recover. Would definitely recommend this to anyone travelling in Sri Lanka.

I have previously climbed Adam's peak from the easier route which from Hatton and told myself that's it never again. However this year I had the opportunity to join a group of interns to climb it from Ratnapura side. Which is the longer and the harder route. In comparison with the Hatton route there are lesser number of shops and pit stops along the way, there were stretches of the pathway which had no lights. Unless you are a pro in climbing and you have a very very fit body my advice is DON'T do it. Especially if you have only 2 weeks to spend on holiday in Sri Lanka I'm sure you will not want to spend more than 5 days limping around!!

We began our climb from Hattonaround 1 in the morning. The staff at the little guest house gave us hot tea and a light breakfast. Fortunately a guide a with great dog found us, we accepted his offer thank goodness and set off. I had no idea what to expect., and I was well prepared with my fashionable Merril Shoes, no rain coat and minimum fitness. The 3 of us set off up mountain in pitch black.  We climbed up and down, and finally came to a spot with many people as well as a bit of lighting.. I thought well, I could not go much further, but at least I have managed. Alas, we were at the base of the climb! Bravely, I struggled on, the guide was amazing, he helped me, my friend was fitter than I so she powered on ahead. I lost the guide in the crowds, it was Good Friday as well as a full moon. I was so touched by the number of people who held my hand, encouraged me, telling me not far now... then in turn I had the audacity to help others. The sweet tea along the way no doubt saved me, something in the tea made me want to keep climbing. I also felt like such a whimp as old ladies passed me, people without shoes, (at least I had my very fashionable Merrils) people carrying children and others helping old people all struggled up the steep and very slippery steps. I crawled and heaved my way up, at last coming to a stop where more were descending that ascending. I thought not far surely... in reply to a desparate how far... a lovley man said about a kilometre. I looked up in the blackness and could see the thin trail dimly snaking its way up the side of a rock! I thought well I have got this far... so further up I stumbled and crawled, and at last the top. It was pouring with rain and I could not see a thing.... fortunately theguides pooch found me, wandering aimlessly around the top, and managed to take me to my friend and his master. I did wonder why on earth I had not stayed in my bed.. exhausted we started the trek down. The brake muscles on the way down were well and truly tested, and the proof of the climb lived on for many days as getting out of bed became a painful experience, as did walking down stairs, however, the overall experience was one I will never forget. It was a truly remarkable, and I will never forget the friendship shown  me by everyone on the way up those huge steps. Willing hands helped, big smiles encouraged, and sympathetic tea servers handed me sweet tea, not even bothering to ask for the  small fee for the tea. There is something in that tea.... it kept me going, and I would not have missed that experience of Adams Peak for all the tea in Sri Lanka.

Our itinery was turned upside down because of accomodation issues due to the ongoing cricket world cup being held in Sri Lanka. Due to this, we had to do Adam's Peak right at the very end of our 8 day trip, without the initially intended R&R at the beach after the climb. Anyhow, we were not about to miss out on going up Adam's Peak, even though it meant having to get back to Colombo the same day after coming down from the mountain and then flying home very early morning the next day. We made our way to Dalhousie (the staging point) by van from Kandy where we had spent the previous day. The last part of this road journey took us through tea plantations, as far as the eye can see. The roads then began to be bumpier. Most of the second half of our journey to Dalhousie were through tea plantations. We got to our inn, the Watshala by 3pm and it was raining. The hotel arranged for someone to accompany us up Adam's Peak the next morning and it was a 1.30am start as the wife thought that she would be mega slow and we were told that it could get quite busy later on. From our Inn, we could see the lighted path up to the summit in the distance and it seemed miles away - actually 7km we were told. We had to walk about 15 minutes from the Watshala Inn to the start point of the trek up but it took much longer as we encountered a wild boar on the road which refused to budge, and in fact threatened to charge at us! I must say that the walk up was not as difficult and it took us about 2 hours and 40 minutes. The wife took 3 hours. When we reached up the summit, we found that many were already up at the summit, mostly pilgrims, all huddled up in blankets and the like - taking up almost every available space in and around the temple. One has to take off his/her shoes before going up a final flight of steps into the temple proper but it is ok to walk around (at the lower level) with shoes on. Photography is also prohibited  in the temple at the upper level. To be honest, it was not as cold as anticipated and a two pieces of clothing should be sufficient - I had a wind proof jacket and a quasi-thermal shirt. A Russian gentleman we came to be acquainted with wore shorts! (although admittedly, he regretted it). We went up to the temple proper and queued to go up to where the statue was placed. There was a continuing stream of pilgrims in the queue. A fantastic atmosphere. And of course, each would ring one of two bells after they have offered their prayers. Thereafter, most tourists would go back down to a slightly lower level (although some hung around in the temple grounds itself), out of the temple and hang around for sunrise. Sunrise was of course beautiful and music/chants from the temple signals sunrise. Then immediately after sunrise, our guide then ushered through the crowd to the other side of the complex to view the shadow. We did see it but because it wasn't a very clear day, the shadow of Adam's Peak only lasted for a very short while. The walk down was also very interesting and there was a bottleneck at the beginning of the steps down from the complex at the summit. We were chatting with monks and other pilgrims and travelers all the way down. This helped but did not entirely take away the feeling of shaky and achy knees! Coming down seemed somewhat longer. All in all, a fantastic trek up. A different sort of trek I must say - atmospheric and uplifting. We all felt so 'part of it' if you know what I mean. If you have the strength and don't mind the journey, it is a must do when in Sri Lanka during the January-May pilgrimage season- especially if you want to experience the sights, sound and the people..and of course, the scenery from the top. We had shower and a late breakfast back at our Inn and then it was off to Colombo - an almost 5 hour drive. On the way down in the tea plantations however, we chanced upon a Hindu celebration of sorts which had 'khavadis' and a few men being dangled on a bamboo pole - on hooks to their skin - Oouch! Tips/Observations: 5,400 steps (because there are new ones - so the old signs and info that there are 4,800 steps or so may not be entirely correct anymore - so we were told by our guide); Mineral water is sold at shops that line the entire walk up, so there is no need to carry too much with you - There was even a "Panadol' tent which we were told was a courtesy tent for those needing light medical treatment; Bring some small change for toilet stops; Bring a change of clothes in your daypack so that you can get off that sweaty one when you reach the top - less cold this way; sunglasses for the trip down; good sturdy shoes/ mid cuts but there is no need for heavy rigid trekking boots which actually impede movement when doing steps all the way up; sticks are useful if you have weak knees; headlamps are not needed during the pilgrimage season as it is lighted all the way up but having a torch is useful as for the dark 'patches' so that you can see the steps clearly - in our case, it came in handy to help 'scare' the wild boar away; The toilets are not in the best of conditions but they try. You will see rubbish all over but I suppose when you get about 1,500 people every night, with shops and eateries all the way up, it is quite difficult to control. However, don't let these little things bother you. Happy walking.

I almost gave up climbing Sri Pada as I woke up with an upset stomach (it has nothing to do with the food at Slightly Chilled). Took some medication and decided to go for it. I left my hotel "Slightly Chilled" at 1.30am. Hotel staff said "You should start at 2am. Freezing  up there". Don't listen to them. I would rather start earlier and stop more frequently during the climb to catch my breath and rest my legs. Frankly speaking, as I am writing this review now, I can't really recall how I got up there. All I can say is, it really helps a lot by climbing in the dark. The route up is lighted but I try not to stare and focus on the steep staircases for too long. Just tackle each flight of stairs as it comes. I rested at almost every drink stall and even sat on the steps (halfway up the flight of stairs) when my legs could not take it. There are toilets along the way so please drink plenty of water as you will perspire a lot. The trekking pole certainly helped me a lot especially when there are no hand rails to depend on. I must also thank the locals who climbed with flip flops. They gave me the determination to continue. One local saw me drifting to sleep (felt drowsy due to the medication) and offered me some food.  One stall owner said "You are almost there. 20 more minutes". Really??? I think I took another 45 minutes. I reached the top at 5.30am. Initially, I did not feel cold but while waiting for sunrise at 6.15am, it starts to get colder but not freezing. Anyway, no sunrise as it was foggy. Slightly disappointed, I made my way down at about 6.45am. I thought the way down would be much easier but I was wrong. Very wrong!!! My left leg started to ache badly with every step I took. It started to rain and we could not rest outside the drink stalls as the benches are wet. When we stop to rest, we could feel our legs wobbling by themselves. Fortunately I had my friend's shoulder and trekking pole to depend on. The route back to the hotel seemed forever. I kept asking my friend "Are you sure we took this route just now?" My friend said we should stop and have some breakfast at one of the drink stall to replenish my energy but I refused. I kept mumbling that I am not hungry but thirsty and I want to get back to the hotel as fast as I can and lie down on the bed. To make things worst, my shoulders and neck starting aching as well. I lost all interest in enjoying the scenery and began to feel frustrated. I felt like I am going "insane". Finally, we reached the hotel at about 10.45am. My friend insisted that I should take my breakfast. Glad I heeded his advice. I felt so much better after that. Breakfast  tasted awesome (A BIG THANK YOU to Slightly Chilled)!!! My leg muscles ached for 3 days. I thought the recovery was quite fast after the 9 hours climb. Must be the Ayurvedic Balm recommended by my driver, Hamar (YOU ARE THE BEST) plus stretching. Despite the aches, we could still climb stairs and slopes but going down, ouch! ouch! ouch! I recovered in time for Mihintale (1840 steps) and Sigiriya (1200 steps). After Sri Pada, all the other staircases appeared to be "easy". Well, if you can, do train for the climb to prevent muscle aches. I wanted to but did not due to a busy work schedule. Fortunately I have been doing stretching frequently so it  helps. Staying positive and be mentally prepared is very important but I guess for me, all crumbled while on the way down. Guess I was really exhausted and dehydrated. I told my friend I would like to do it again because we did not see the sunrise but is there an easier way down??? My friend said he will wait at Slightly Chilled............

We walked the Adam’s Peak in January. It was a great experience but really wet and really cold. If you want to do that trek make sure you have proper clothes and prober shoes. We had good rain jackets, proper shoes and even an umbrella, but still we were soaked wet because it was raining the whole night. We started around 2.00am and finished around 7.00 am. In the travel guide is written that you have to walk up four hours and down 3 hours. For sure it depends how fast you walk, but if there are a lot of people who are walking up or down, then it can take you even longer because mostly you can’t pass them. It was a really good experience, but on the other hand if it’s already raining when you want to start, then I probably would think about if you really want to do it or not. We have been to the very top and if it’s bad weather you can see nothing at all. There is no view and no sunrise, you are probably better off if you go on daytime.

WOW - what can I say..... I had planned this to be a romantic ramble up a mountain on Valentines Day. Not so. Firstly, the journey from Tissa to Dal Housie took closer to 7hrs than the 3 to 4 that I had estimated. The roads are not great, steep and winding. The actual climb was really really tough. I am a young 32yr old female - I go to the gym 3/4 times a week, participate in 5/10k runs, am the ideal weight for my height and think of myself as lets say, 7/10 on fitness. I struggled. I never thought it would be easy, but equally, did not think it would be so hard. We had to stop and rest at least 10 times on the way up - even thought we started out at 2.30am I was stilled soaked with sweat after the 1st 30mins. It took us around 3.5hrs and it is pretty much constant steps from about 2hrs in. The last 30mins are a constant steep flight of steps that you have to hold onto the hand rail for. It was nice at the top, but it was cloudy, really busy and to be honest, was not the spiritual magical place I had hoped it to be. The trek down was almost as bad. My legs were shaking and again we had to rest quite a few times. There were lots of elderly people, families, and we even saw a pregnant woman doing the climb, but we have no idea how half of these people made it to the top. But I suppose , it is a pilgrimage and not meant to be easy. I am pleased that I did it, but the fact that it took 7hrs to get to, then another 3hrs to get away from with 8hrs of back breaking effort in the middle, as a holiday maker who only had 2 weeks in Sri Lanka and not a pilgrim, I would probably say give it a miss.

On out 12day trip around the island we tried to hike a bit. Adam's Peak was the top location on our list. We stayed at Upper Glen Bungalows and at on Feb 18 1am we started our drive to Dalhousie. Dalhousie was almost empty when we arrived. Our driver stayed at the car (and had a good sleep) but our guide also wanted to climb Sri Pada. Termperature was OK and up we went. Somewhere on the way we lost our guide. His endurance was not as good as ours but we met him again at the top. Up there a very cold and strong wind was blowing and everyone was trying to hide and get a bit of sleep while waiting for the sunrise. And then the light came. It was a wonderful experience seeing the sunrise with all the pilgrims giving their prayers. Looking to the other side of the mountain we also could see the shadow of the peak of Sri Pada on the clouds. A truly unique experience

My wife asked me to take her to Adam's Peak after seeing a picture of sunrise over the peak in the Srilankan Airline magazine. Though we were scheduled to stay in Bentota area for a week and decided before our arrival in Srilanka to avoid any long journeys within the country as they could be quite tiring, but I am glad that I listened to her. We took a five hours drive up in the hill country side through some head-spinning winding roads to reach the Slightly Chilled hotel (not bad for a night or two) at the base of Adam's peak. We were told that the ascent starts at 2-2.30 AM in the morning to view the sunrise on the peak as the climb takes at least 3 hours for first timers. A guide is also highly recommended as passing through the forest in the night can be quite adventurous on your own. Also, the guide brought a torch for us, which is absolutely necessary for the climb during the night. We started the climb at 2.30 AM and it was quite an experience. Around 5,200 steps in 3 hours through the sounds of water falls, wind blowing through the forests, the flowing rivers...simply amazing!. We could only imagine what's around us as it was pitch dark. However, one thing we could see clearly after turning our torches off during the water breaks were the bright stars in the clear sky. Absolutely gorgeous! We reached the peak at around 5.30 AM where we were greeted by couple of residents of the peak. The peak and the route was empty due to off season, beside 3 more tourist who took the climb that night. We were told that it could take 8-9 hours to reach the peak in the pilgrimage season weekends. It was freezing cold up there and we used the hot tea cups that the peak residents gave us to warm our hands while we waited for the famous Adam's peak bell to open. The sunrise scene was gorgeous though it was a bit cloudy that morning and it is said be better on clear days. Around 6, we were allowed in the bell and famous Adam's step mark area of the peak. It was a great sense of achievement to ring the bell for the first time but we couldn't see the step mark in the stone as it opens only in the pilgrimage season  for public viewing. Shoes were not allowed in this area and with freezing cold, we couldn't stay for more than 5 minutes in that area of the peak. The descent is better than the ascent in the sense that you can now view the beautiful fauna around you in the morning light. The highlight of the trip came at around 50% descent mark. The waterfalls, lush green mountains, the clouds flowing over the mountains, the sunrise, the lake in the distance...STUNNING!! The last 25% of the descent was a bit difficult for us as we could feel it in our legs now...five hours of constant ascend and descend...the fact that we were not wearing any climbing shoes or joggers was adding to the pain...but remember, we were originally on a beach vacation, so wouldn't make sense to bring soft sole toe covered shoes with us you know! ;) Anyway, it was worth every step and we hope to do it again some day!
